FastAPI — Complete Reference

Scope: App creation & routing, path/query/body parameters, request bodies with Pydantic, response models & status codes, dependency injection, async endpoints, middleware & CORS, authentication (OAuth2/JWT, API keys, RBAC), error handling, background tasks, task queues (Celery/RQ), WebSockets & streaming (SSE), file uploads, database integration (SQLAlchemy sync/async), rate limiting & pagination, caching (Redis), lifespan events, configuration, observability (structured logging), testing, deployment (Uvicorn/Gunicorn/Docker), API versioning, throttling, resilience patterns (retry/backoff, circuit breaker), REST semantics (PUT vs PATCH, URL vs URI, status codes), gRPC with FastAPI, and a complete mini-project. FastAPI 0.100+ with Pydantic v2.

1. Fundamentals & App Creation

FastAPI is a modern, high-performance Python web framework built on Starlette (ASGI) and Pydantic. It derives request validation, serialization, and interactive OpenAPI docs directly from standard Python type hints.

from fastapi import FastAPI

app = FastAPI(
    title="My API",
    description="Production-grade API",
    version="1.0.0",
)

@app.get("/")
async def root():
    return {"message": "Hello, World!"}

# Run:      uvicorn main:app --reload
# Swagger:  http://localhost:8000/docs
# ReDoc:    http://localhost:8000/redoc
# Schema:   http://localhost:8000/openapi.json
•

Why FastAPI?

Built onPerformanceAuto docsType hintsAsync-nativeDI built-in
FeatureDetail
Built onStarlette (ASGI) + Pydantic (validation)
PerformanceOn par with Node.js / Go (async + Uvicorn)
Auto docsSwagger UI (/docs) & ReDoc (/redoc) generated automatically
Type hintsDrive validation, serialization, and documentation
Async-nativeFirst-class async/await support
DI built-inDepends() for clean, testable composition
•

ASGI vs WSGI

WSGI (Flask / Django)         ASGI (FastAPI)
─────────────────────         ──────────────
Synchronous only              Sync + Async
One request at a time         Concurrent requests
Served by Gunicorn            Served by Uvicorn / Hypercorn
No native WebSockets          WebSockets, HTTP/2, long-lived connections
•

Install

pip install "fastapi[standard]"      # includes uvicorn, etc.
# or minimal:
pip install fastapi "uvicorn[standard]"
2. Routing & HTTP Methods

Each path operation maps an HTTP method + path to a handler ("path operation function").

@app.get("/items")          # Read (list)
@app.post("/items")         # Create
@app.put("/items/{id}")     # Full update
@app.patch("/items/{id}")   # Partial update
@app.delete("/items/{id}")  # Delete
•

Path Parameter with Enum

Enums constrain a path parameter to a fixed set of values and document them in Swagger.

from enum import Enum

class ModelName(str, Enum):
    alexnet = "alexnet"
    resnet = "resnet"
    lenet = "lenet"

@app.get("/models/{model_name}")
async def get_model(model_name: ModelName):
    return {"model": model_name.value}

# GET /models/resnet   -> {"model": "resnet"}
# GET /models/foo      -> 422 Unprocessable Entity

Order matters: declare fixed routes (/users/me) before parametric ones (/users/{id}), otherwise me is captured as an id.

3. Path, Query & Body Parameters

FastAPI infers parameter source from the function signature: - declared in the path string (/items/{id}) → path parameter - a simple type (int, str, float, bool) not in the path → query parameter - a Pydantic model → request body

from fastapi import FastAPI, Query, Path, Body
from typing import Optional

# ── Path parameters ──────────────────────────────────────
@app.get("/items/{item_id}")
async def get_item(item_id: int = Path(..., title="Item ID", ge=1)):
    return {"item_id": item_id}

# ── Query parameters with validation ────────────────────
@app.get("/items/")
async def list_items(
    skip: int = Query(0, ge=0),
    limit: int = Query(10, ge=1, le=100),
    q: Optional[str] = Query(None, min_length=1, max_length=50),
):
    return {"skip": skip, "limit": limit, "q": q}
•

Auto-validation in action

@app.get("/users/{user_id}")
async def get_user(user_id: int):
    return {"user_id": user_id}

# GET /users/42    -> {"user_id": 42}
# GET /users/abc   -> 422  (int coercion fails)
•

Query Parameter Constraints

Query() accepts min_length, max_length, pattern (regex), ge/le/gt/lt, title, description, deprecated.

@app.get("/search")
async def search(
    q: str = Query(..., min_length=3, max_length=50, pattern=r"^[a-zA-Z]+$"),
):
    return {"q": q}
•

Body + Path + Query Together

class Item(BaseModel):
    name: str
    price: float

@app.put("/items/{item_id}")
async def update_item(
    item_id: int,                       # path param
    item: Item,                         # request body
    q: Optional[str] = None,            # query param
    importance: int = Body(default=1),  # extra singular body field
):
    return {"item_id": item_id, "item": item, "q": q, "importance": importance}
4. Request Bodies with Pydantic

Pydantic models define the shape, types, and validation rules for the request body. Invalid data is rejected with a 422 before reaching your code.

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from typing import Optional

class Item(BaseModel):
    name: str
    description: Optional[str] = None
    price: float = Field(..., gt=0, description="Price must be greater than 0")
    tax: Optional[float] = None

@app.post("/items")
async def create_item(item: Item):
    total = item.price + (item.tax or 0)
    return {"name": item.name, "total_price": total}
•

Nested Models

class Address(BaseModel):
    street: str
    city: str
    zip_code: str

class User(BaseModel):
    name: str
    age: int
    addresses: list[Address]

@app.post("/users")
async def create_user(user: User):
    return user

# Body: {"name": "Ada", "age": 36, "addresses": [{"street": "1 Rd", "city": "London", "zip_code": "EC1"}]}
•

Field Validators in Request Models

from pydantic import BaseModel, field_validator, model_validator, EmailStr

class UserCreate(BaseModel):
    username: str
    email: EmailStr
    password: str
    confirm_password: str

    @field_validator("username")
    @classmethod
    def username_alphanumeric(cls, v: str) -> str:
        if not v.isalnum():
            raise ValueError("Username must be alphanumeric")
        return v

    @model_validator(mode="after")
    def passwords_match(self):
        if self.password != self.confirm_password:
            raise ValueError("Passwords do not match")
        return self

Validation errors raised inside validators are returned as a structured 422 response listing each failing field.

5. Response Models & Status Codes

response_model controls exactly which fields are returned and how they are serialized — preventing accidental leakage of internal fields (e.g., hashed passwords) and producing accurate OpenAPI docs.

from fastapi import status
from datetime import datetime

class TaskResponse(BaseModel):
    id: int
    title: str
    created_at: datetime
    model_config = {"from_attributes": True}  # read ORM attributes (was orm_mode)

@app.post(
    "/tasks/",
    response_model=TaskResponse,
    status_code=status.HTTP_201_CREATED,
    summary="Create a new task",
    response_description="The created task",
)
async def create_task(task: TaskCreate):
    task_db = save(task)   # returns an ORM object
    return task_db         # filtered to TaskResponse fields
•

Field Filtering Options

@app.get(
    "/items/{item_id}",
    response_model=Item,
    response_model_exclude_unset=True,         # omit fields left at default
    response_model_exclude={"tax"},            # drop these fields
    response_model_include={"name", "price"},  # keep only these
)
async def read_item(item_id: int):
    ...
•

Union Response Model (Polymorphic Output)

A response_model may be a Union of models when an endpoint can return one of several shapes.

from typing import Union

class Cat(BaseModel):
    name: str
    meows: int

class Dog(BaseModel):
    name: str
    barks: float

@app.get("/animals/{animal_id}", response_model=Union[Cat, Dog])
def get_animal(animal_id: int):
    ...   # return a Cat or a Dog; OpenAPI documents both via anyOf

For input bodies, prefer a discriminated union (a Literal tag + Field(discriminator=...)) so Pydantic dispatches in O(1) and produces a clean oneOf schema — see the Pydantic reference.

•

Documenting Multiple Responses

from fastapi import HTTPException

@app.get("/tasks/{task_id}", responses={
    200: {"model": TaskResponse},
    404: {"description": "Task not found"},
})
async def get_task(task_id: int):
    task = db.get(task_id)
    if not task:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="Task not found")
    return task
•

Common Status Code Mappings

OperationCodeConstant
GET success200status.HTTP_200_OK
POST created201status.HTTP_201_CREATED
DELETE no content204status.HTTP_204_NO_CONTENT
Bad request400status.HTTP_400_BAD_REQUEST
Unauthorized (not logged in)401status.HTTP_401_UNAUTHORIZED
Forbidden (no permission)403status.HTTP_403_FORBIDDEN
Not found404status.HTTP_404_NOT_FOUND
Validation error422status.HTTP_422_UNPROCESSABLE_ENTITY
Rate limited429status.HTTP_429_TOO_MANY_REQUESTS
Server bug500status.HTTP_500_INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR

401 vs 403: 401 = "who are you? authenticate first" (missing/expired token). 403 = "I know who you are, but you are not allowed".

6. Dependency Injection

Depends() declares reusable, composable functions or classes that FastAPI resolves and injects automatically. It cleanly separates cross-cutting concerns (DB sessions, auth, pagination) and makes them trivially overridable in tests.

•

Function Dependency

from fastapi import Depends

def common_parameters(skip: int = 0, limit: int = 100):
    return {"skip": skip, "limit": limit}

@app.get("/items")
async def read_items(commons: dict = Depends(common_parameters)):
    return commons
•

Generator Dependency (Setup / Teardown)

A yield dependency runs setup before the yield and teardown after the response — ideal for DB sessions, file handles, and locks.

def get_db():
    db = SessionLocal()
    try:
        yield db          # provided to the endpoint
    finally:
        db.close()        # always runs after the response

@app.get("/items/")
async def list_items(db: Session = Depends(get_db)):
    return db.query(Item).all()
•

Class-Based Dependency

class Pagination:
    def __init__(self, skip: int = 0, limit: int = 10):
        self.skip = skip
        self.limit = limit

@app.get("/items")
async def list_items(pagination: Pagination = Depends()):
    return {"skip": pagination.skip, "limit": pagination.limit}
•

Sub-Dependencies (Chained)

Dependencies can depend on other dependencies. FastAPI resolves the whole tree and caches each dependency per request.

def get_current_user(db=Depends(get_db), token: str = Depends(oauth2_scheme)):
    user = db.query(User).filter(User.token == token).first()
    if not user:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=401)
    return user

@app.get("/me")
async def read_me(user=Depends(get_current_user)):
    return user
•

Global Dependencies

Run a dependency for every route (e.g., an API-key check):

app = FastAPI(dependencies=[Depends(verify_api_key)])
# or per-router: APIRouter(dependencies=[Depends(verify_api_key)])
7. Routers & Project Structure

APIRouter splits an app into modular, independently testable files (like Flask Blueprints).

# app/routers/tasks.py
from fastapi import APIRouter, Depends
from app.dependencies import get_db

router = APIRouter(prefix="/tasks", tags=["tasks"])

@router.get("/")
async def list_tasks(db=Depends(get_db)): ...

@router.post("/")
async def create_task(db=Depends(get_db)): ...
# app/main.py
from fastapi import FastAPI
from app.routers import tasks, users, auth

app = FastAPI(title="My API", version="1.0.0")
app.include_router(tasks.router)
app.include_router(users.router)
app.include_router(auth.router)
•

Recommended Project Layout

my_project/
├── app/
│   ├── main.py            # FastAPI app instance, lifespan, router includes
│   ├── config.py          # Settings (pydantic-settings)
│   ├── database.py        # DB engine, session, get_db dependency
│   ├── dependencies.py    # Shared dependencies (auth, pagination)
│   ├── routers/           # APIRouter modules (items.py, users.py, auth.py)
│   ├── models/            # SQLAlchemy models (table mappings)
│   ├── schemas/           # Pydantic schemas (API contracts)
│   ├── crud/              # Data-access functions
│   └── utils/             # security.py, helpers
├── alembic/               # DB migrations
├── tests/                 # conftest.py, test_items.py, ...
├── requirements.txt
├── Dockerfile
└── docker-compose.yml

Separation of concerns: SQLAlchemy models describe tables; Pydantic schemas describe API request/response shapes. Keep them distinct so the DB layer and API contract can evolve independently.

8. Middleware & CORS

Middleware wraps every request/response — used for logging, timing, headers, compression, and (browser) CORS.

•

Custom Middleware (Timing)

import time
from fastapi import Request

@app.middleware("http")
async def add_process_time_header(request: Request, call_next):
    start = time.perf_counter()
    response = await call_next(request)
    duration = time.perf_counter() - start
    response.headers["X-Process-Time"] = f"{duration:.4f}"
    return response
•

Class-Based Middleware

from starlette.middleware.base import BaseHTTPMiddleware
import logging

class RequestLoggingMiddleware(BaseHTTPMiddleware):
    async def dispatch(self, request, call_next):
        response = await call_next(request)
        logging.info(f"{request.method} {request.url.path} -> {response.status_code}")
        return response

app.add_middleware(RequestLoggingMiddleware)
•

CORS

from fastapi.middleware.cors import CORSMiddleware

app.add_middleware(
    CORSMiddleware,
    allow_origins=["https://mysite.com"],  # avoid ["*"] in production with credentials
    allow_credentials=True,
    allow_methods=["*"],
    allow_headers=["*"],
)
•

Other Built-in Middleware

from starlette.middleware.gzip import GZipMiddleware
from starlette.middleware.trustedhost import TrustedHostMiddleware

app.add_middleware(GZipMiddleware, minimum_size=1000)
app.add_middleware(TrustedHostMiddleware, allowed_hosts=["example.com", "*.example.com"])

Middleware executes in registration order on the way in and reverse order on the way out.

9. Authentication (OAuth2, JWT, API Keys, RBAC)
•

JWT — How It Works

A JWT is a compact, URL-safe, SIGNED (not encrypted) token: HEADER.PAYLOAD.SIGNATURE

  HEADER     {"alg": "HS256", "typ": "JWT"}
  PAYLOAD    {"sub": "user123", "exp": 1717000000, "role": "admin"}   <- readable!
  SIGNATURE  HMAC-SHA256(base64(header)+"."+base64(payload), SECRET_KEY)

FLOW:
  1. Client POSTs credentials to /token
  2. Server validates, signs a JWT with SECRET_KEY, returns it
  3. Client sends "Authorization: Bearer <token>" on each request
  4. Server verifies signature + expiry on every request

KEY POINTS:
  - Never put secrets in the payload (it is only base64, not encrypted)
  - Always use HTTPS; set short expiry (15-60 min) + refresh tokens
  - HS256 (symmetric) for single service; RS256 (asymmetric) for microservices
•

OAuth2 Password Flow with JWT

from datetime import datetime, timedelta
from fastapi import Depends, HTTPException, status
from fastapi.security import OAuth2PasswordBearer, OAuth2PasswordRequestForm
from jose import JWTError, jwt
from passlib.context import CryptContext

SECRET_KEY = "your-secret-key"
ALGORITHM = "HS256"
ACCESS_TOKEN_EXPIRE_MINUTES = 30

pwd_context = CryptContext(schemes=["bcrypt"], deprecated="auto")
oauth2_scheme = OAuth2PasswordBearer(tokenUrl="token")

def verify_password(plain, hashed): return pwd_context.verify(plain, hashed)
def get_password_hash(password):    return pwd_context.hash(password)

def create_access_token(data: dict, expires_delta: timedelta | None = None):
    to_encode = data.copy()
    to_encode["exp"] = datetime.utcnow() + (expires_delta or timedelta(minutes=15))
    return jwt.encode(to_encode, SECRET_KEY, algorithm=ALGORITHM)

async def get_current_user(token: str = Depends(oauth2_scheme)):
    credentials_exception = HTTPException(
        status_code=status.HTTP_401_UNAUTHORIZED,
        detail="Could not validate credentials",
        headers={"WWW-Authenticate": "Bearer"},
    )
    try:
        payload = jwt.decode(token, SECRET_KEY, algorithms=[ALGORITHM])
        username = payload.get("sub")
        if username is None:
            raise credentials_exception
    except JWTError:
        raise credentials_exception
    return get_user(username)   # fetch from DB in a real app

@app.post("/token")
async def login(form_data: OAuth2PasswordRequestForm = Depends()):
    user = authenticate_user(form_data.username, form_data.password)
    if not user:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=400, detail="Incorrect credentials")
    token = create_access_token(
        {"sub": user.username},
        timedelta(minutes=ACCESS_TOKEN_EXPIRE_MINUTES),
    )
    return {"access_token": token, "token_type": "bearer"}

@app.get("/users/me")
async def read_users_me(current_user=Depends(get_current_user)):
    return current_user
•

Bearer API Token (Simple)

from fastapi.security import HTTPBearer, HTTPAuthorizationCredentials
import secrets

security = HTTPBearer()
API_TOKENS: dict[str, str] = {}

def verify_token(creds: HTTPAuthorizationCredentials = Depends(security)):
    if creds.credentials not in API_TOKENS:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=401, detail="Invalid token")
    return API_TOKENS[creds.credentials]

@app.get("/protected")
async def protected(user: str = Depends(verify_token)):
    return {"message": f"Hello {user}!"}
•

Bearer API Token — Full Issue + Verify Flow

A self-contained opaque-token scheme: a login endpoint mints a random token (secrets.token_hex) and maps it to a user; protected routes validate the bearer token via a dependency. (Opaque tokens are stateful — they require server-side lookup, unlike self-contained JWTs.)

from fastapi import FastAPI, Depends, HTTPException
from fastapi.security import HTTPBearer, HTTPAuthorizationCredentials
import secrets

app = FastAPI()
security = HTTPBearer()
API_TOKENS: dict[str, str] = {}          # token -> username

def generate_token(username: str) -> str:
    token = secrets.token_hex(32)
    API_TOKENS[token] = username
    return token

def verify_token(creds: HTTPAuthorizationCredentials = Depends(security)) -> str:
    if creds.credentials not in API_TOKENS:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=401, detail="Invalid token")
    return API_TOKENS[creds.credentials]

@app.post("/auth/login")
def login(username: str, password: str):
    # verify credentials against a DB in a real app
    return {"token": generate_token(username)}

@app.get("/protected")
def protected_route(user: str = Depends(verify_token)):
    return {"message": f"Hello {user}!"}

API key header is an alternative for service-to-service auth: APIKeyHeader(name="X-API-Key") as a dependency. Use Security() with SecurityScopes for OAuth2 scope-based authorization.

•

Role-Based Access Control (Dependency Factory)

from enum import Enum

class Role(str, Enum):
    admin = "admin"
    user = "user"

def require_role(required: Role):
    def checker(current_user=Depends(get_current_user)):
        if current_user.get("role") != required:
            raise HTTPException(status_code=403, detail="Insufficient permissions")
        return current_user
    return checker

@app.get("/admin-dashboard")
async def admin_dashboard(user=Depends(require_role(Role.admin))):
    return {"msg": "Welcome, admin!"}
10. Error Handling
•

HTTPException

from fastapi import HTTPException

@app.get("/items/{item_id}")
async def read_item(item_id: int):
    if item_id not in items_db:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="Item not found")
    return items_db[item_id]
•

Custom Exception + Handler

from fastapi import Request
from fastapi.responses import JSONResponse

class ItemNotFoundException(Exception):
    def __init__(self, item_id: int):
        self.item_id = item_id

@app.exception_handler(ItemNotFoundException)
async def item_not_found_handler(request: Request, exc: ItemNotFoundException):
    return JSONResponse(status_code=404, content={"detail": f"Item {exc.item_id} not found"})

@app.get("/items/{item_id}")
async def read_item(item_id: int):
    if item_id not in items_db:
        raise ItemNotFoundException(item_id)
    return items_db[item_id]
•

Overriding the Validation (422) Handler

from fastapi.exceptions import RequestValidationError

@app.exception_handler(RequestValidationError)
async def validation_exception_handler(request: Request, exc: RequestValidationError):
    return JSONResponse(
        status_code=422,
        content={"detail": exc.errors(), "body": exc.body},
    )
11. Async, Background Tasks, Task Queues & WebSockets
•

async def vs def

import httpx

@app.get("/sync")
def sync_endpoint():
    return {"msg": "runs in a thread pool"}     # def -> threadpool, won't block the loop

@app.get("/async")
async def async_endpoint():
    async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:    # async def -> runs on the event loop
        resp = await client.get("https://api.example.com/data")
    return resp.json()

Rule of thumb: use async def for I/O-bound work with awaitable libraries (async DB/HTTP). Use plain def for CPU-bound or blocking sync libraries — FastAPI offloads it to a thread pool so the event loop stays responsive.

•

Background Tasks

BackgroundTasks runs a function after the response is sent — in the same process. Good for quick side effects (emails, logging). For heavy/long jobs or retries, use Celery/ARQ.

from fastapi import BackgroundTasks

def write_log(message: str):
    with open("log.txt", "a") as f:
        f.write(message + "\n")

@app.post("/send-notification")
async def send_notification(email: str, background_tasks: BackgroundTasks):
    background_tasks.add_task(write_log, f"Notification sent to {email}")
    return {"message": "Notification queued"}

A dependency can also accept BackgroundTasks and schedule work — handy for cross-cutting side effects (audit logs) without touching every endpoint:

def log_dependency(background_tasks: BackgroundTasks, q: str | None = None):
    if q:
        background_tasks.add_task(write_log, f"Query: {q}")
    return q

@app.get("/items")
def read_items(query=Depends(log_dependency)):
    return {"query": query}
•

Task Queues (Celery / RQ) — durable background jobs

in the same processtask queueworkersOffload work that isStay in-processProducer

BackgroundTasks runs in the same process, so it is not durable — a restart, crash, or scale-down kills pending work, there are no retries, and CPU-heavy jobs still hog the worker. For anything that must survive a restart, be retried, scheduled, or run off the request path, offload it to a real task queue: the API enqueues a job and returns immediately, while a separate pool of workers does the heavy lifting.

Client → API (enqueue job, return 202) → [Broker/Queue] → Worker pool (does the heavy work)
                                                    │
                                          (optional) Result backend ← worker stores result/status

When to reach for a queue

Offload work that is: - Slow (video/image processing, PDF/report generation, ML inference). - I/O-heavy or flaky (third-party API calls, sending email/SMS). - Schedulable (nightly reports, cleanup, reminders). - Burst-prone (smooth spikes by buffering work).

Stay in-process (BackgroundTasks) when the work is cheap, loss-tolerant, and "after this response, same process" is good enough (a log line, one email).

Architecture: producer, broker, worker, result backend

ComponentRole
ProducerYour FastAPI app; serializes a job and pushes it to the broker (.delay() / .enqueue()).
BrokerThe queue that holds jobs until a worker is free (Redis, RabbitMQ, SQS).
WorkerA separate process that pulls jobs and executes the task function.
Result backendOptional store for a task's return value/state so you can query task.status / task.get().

Broker vs result backend (a classic interview question): the broker delivers tasks to workers; the result backend stores their outcomes. You always need a broker; you only need a result backend if you care about results/status. Storing every result bloats the backend — disable it (ignore_result=True) when you don't need outcomes.

Message brokers compared

BrokerNatureStrengthsWatch out for
RedisIn-memory storeExtremely fast, simple, ubiquitousCan lose data on crash unless persistence (RDB/AOF) is on
RabbitMQFull AMQP brokerDurable, rich routing, acks, DLQsMore moving parts to operate
Amazon SQS / GCP Pub/SubManaged cloud queueAuto-scaling, no ops, durableVendor lock-in, at-least-once semantics, latency

The broker is the buffer that lets producers and workers run independently and at different speeds. Choose Redis for speed/simplicity, RabbitMQ/SQS when you need durability and routing.

Celery — the industry standard

# tasks.py
from celery import Celery

celery_app = Celery(
    "my_app",
    broker="redis://localhost:6379/0",       # where tasks are delivered
    backend="redis://localhost:6379/1",      # where results are stored (optional)
)

celery_app.conf.update(
    task_serializer="json",                  # JSON, not pickle (security)
    accept_content=["json"],
    task_acks_late=True,                     # ack AFTER success (at-least-once)
    worker_prefetch_multiplier=1,            # don't hoard messages on one worker
    task_track_started=True,
)

@celery_app.task(bind=True, max_retries=3, default_retry_delay=60)
def process_video(self, video_id: int):      # pass an ID, not the whole object
    try:
        video = db.get(Video, video_id)       # fetch fresh state inside the task
        transcode(video)
    except TransientError as exc:
        # exponential backoff: 1s, 2s, 4s ...
        raise self.retry(exc=exc, countdown=2 ** self.request.retries)

Enqueue from a FastAPI endpoint — .delay() is the convenient default; .apply_async() exposes scheduling (countdown/eta), routing (queue), priority, and expiry:

@app.post("/videos/{video_id}/transcode", status_code=202)
def transcode_video(video_id: int):
    process_video.delay(video_id)                          # returns immediately
    # process_video.apply_async(args=[video_id], countdown=30, queue="video", priority=5)
    return {"status": "queued"}

Run the worker as a separate process (it survives web restarts and scales horizontally), and query results when you have a result backend:

celery -A tasks worker --loglevel=INFO --concurrency=4 -Q video,default
res = process_video.delay(123)
res.id            # task id
res.status        # PENDING / STARTED / SUCCESS / FAILURE / RETRY
res.ready()       # True when finished
res.get(timeout=10)   # block for the return value (needs a result backend)

Compose tasks into pipelines with Canvas — chain (sequential, pass each result on), group (parallel), chord (a group then a callback with all results):

from celery import chain, group, chord
chain(fetch.s(url), parse.s(), store.s())()
group(resize.s(img) for img in images)()
chord((crunch.s(x) for x in chunks), summarize.s())()

Acknowledgement & acks_late: a worker acks a message to tell the broker "done — delete it." By default it acks when it picks up the task (crash mid-task ⇒ message lost). With acks_late=True it acks only after success, so a crash redelivers and the task runs again — safer, but the task must be idempotent.

RQ — the simpler alternative

RQ (Redis Queue) is a lighter, Redis-only alternative — easy to read and debug, fewer features.

from redis import Redis
from rq import Queue
from jobs import heavy_task

q = Queue(connection=Redis())
job = q.enqueue(heavy_task, "arg1")     # returns immediately
print(job.id, job.get_status())          # queued / started / finished / failed
# run the worker:  rq worker

RQ supports scheduling (rq-scheduler), retries, and a dashboard (rq-dashboard), but for multi-queue routing, complex workflows, and big scale, Celery is the more complete tool.

Choosing: BackgroundTasks vs RQ vs Celery

ToolBrokerStrengthsUse when
FastAPI BackgroundTasksNone (same process)Zero infra, trivialLight I/O after a response, loss-tolerant
RQRedis onlySimple, easy to debugStraightforward durable jobs, small/medium scale
CeleryRedis/RabbitMQ/SQSRetries, scheduling, routing, Canvas workflowsComplex/large-scale, scheduling, multiple queues

BackgroundTasks dies with the process; RQ/Celery run separate worker processes that survive restarts and scale out. (ARQ is a popular async-native alternative when you want asyncio workers.)

Reliability patterns

  • Idempotency (the cardinal rule). Queues are at-least-once: a crash after the work but before the ack redelivers the job, so it runs again. Make running N times == running once — use DB UPSERTs, dedupe on a unique job/event key, and pass an idempotency key to external APIs.
@celery_app.task(acks_late=True)
def send_invoice(order_id: int):
    if InvoiceLog.exists(order_id):       # dedupe guard
        return
    send(order_id)
    InvoiceLog.mark(order_id)
  • Retries — backoff + a cap. Combine exponential backoff (don't hammer a struggling dependency), a max-attempts cap (avoid retrying a "poison" task forever), and idempotency.
  • Dead-letter queue (DLQ). Where messages go after exhausting retries; isolates poison messages so one bad job doesn't clog the main queue, and gives you a place to inspect, alert, and replay.
  • Pass IDs, not objects. Send the primary key and re-fetch inside the task — smaller messages, no staleness, faster serialization.
  • JSON, not pickle. pickle executes arbitrary code on deserialization (a spoofed broker message ⇒ RCE). JSON is safe and language-agnostic — another reason to pass simple IDs/dicts.

Scheduling periodic tasks

ToolScope
Celery BeatCompanion scheduler that enqueues tasks on intervals/crontab schedules
APSchedulerIn-process scheduling for simpler apps
System cronLowest-tech: cron calls a management command
from celery.schedules import crontab

celery_app.conf.beat_schedule = {
    "nightly-report": {"task": "tasks.generate_report", "schedule": crontab(hour=2, minute=0)},
    "every-5-min-healthcheck": {"task": "tasks.healthcheck", "schedule": 300.0},  # seconds
}

Run exactly one Beat process — multiple schedulers double-fire every schedule.

Scaling & concurrency models

Scale by running more workers (and more processes/threads each); the broker distributes jobs. Match the worker pool to the workload:

Celery poolMechanismBest for
prefork (default)OS processesCPU-bound work (sidesteps the GIL)
gevent / eventletGreen threadsI/O-bound work (many concurrent network calls)
soloSingle processDebugging only
celery -A tasks worker --pool=prefork  --concurrency=8    # CPU-bound
celery -A tasks worker --pool=gevent   --concurrency=200  # I/O-bound

Monitoring & observability

  • Flowerweb dashboard for Celery (tasks, workers, rates, failures).
  • Queue deptha growing backlog means workers can't keep up → scale out (the classic early warning of an overloaded system).
  • Task latency & failure/retry rateexport to Prometheus/Grafana.
  • Structured logging keyed by task id; alerts on DLQ size, retry spikes, worker liveness.

Broker failure & high availability

The broker is a single point of failure: producers can't enqueue (.delay() fails — degrade gracefully), workers sit idle, and unprocessed jobs can be lost if Redis has no persistence (RDB/AOF). Mitigate with broker HA (Redis Sentinel/Cluster, RabbitMQ mirrored queues), persistence, and producer-side error handling.

Best-practice checklist

  • ✅ Offload anything slow/flaky/scheduled; keep request handlers fast.
  • ✅ Make every task idempotent (at-least-once delivery will re-run jobs).
  • ✅ Retries: exponential backoff + max attempts + DLQ for poison messages.
  • ✅ Pass IDs, re-fetch inside the task; keep messages small.
  • ✅ JSON serialization, never pickle from an untrusted broker.
  • ✅ acks_late=True + idempotency for crash safety.
  • ✅ One Beat scheduler; prefork for CPU, gevent/eventlet for I/O.
  • ✅ Monitor queue depth, failure rate, worker health; alert on backlog/DLQ.
  • ✅ Make the broker durable + HA; handle enqueue failures in the producer.

Cross-links: the at-least-once + idempotency model mirrors webhooks in 34_API_Consumption; concurrency-model trade-offs (prefork vs gevent) are detailed in 17_Concurrency.

•

WebSockets

from fastapi import WebSocket, WebSocketDisconnect

class ConnectionManager:
    def __init__(self):
        self.active: list[WebSocket] = []

    async def connect(self, ws: WebSocket):
        await ws.accept()
        self.active.append(ws)

    def disconnect(self, ws: WebSocket):
        self.active.remove(ws)

    async def broadcast(self, message: str):
        for conn in self.active:
            await conn.send_text(message)

manager = ConnectionManager()

@app.websocket("/ws/{client_id}")
async def websocket_endpoint(ws: WebSocket, client_id: int):
    await manager.connect(ws)
    try:
        while True:
            data = await ws.receive_text()
            await manager.broadcast(f"Client #{client_id}: {data}")
    except WebSocketDisconnect:
        manager.disconnect(ws)
        await manager.broadcast(f"Client #{client_id} left")
12. File Uploads & Streaming (SSE)
•

Single & Multiple File Uploads

UploadFile uses a SpooledTemporaryFile (small files in memory, large files spilled to disk) and exposes .filename, .content_type, async .read(), .write(), .seek(), .close().

from fastapi import UploadFile, File
import shutil, os

@app.post("/upload")
async def upload_file(file: UploadFile = File(...)):
    os.makedirs("uploads", exist_ok=True)
    path = os.path.join("uploads", file.filename)
    with open(path, "wb") as out:
        shutil.copyfileobj(file.file, out)
    return {"filename": file.filename, "size": os.path.getsize(path)}

@app.post("/upload-multiple")
async def upload_multiple(files: list[UploadFile] = File(...)):
    return [{"filename": f.filename} for f in files]
•

Large File — Stream to Disk in Chunks

@app.post("/upload-large")
async def upload_large(file: UploadFile = File(...)):
    with open(f"uploads/{file.filename}", "wb") as f:
        while chunk := await file.read(1024 * 1024):   # 1 MB chunks
            f.write(chunk)
    return {"filename": file.filename}
•

Server-Sent Events (SSE) — LLM-style Streaming

StreamingResponse with text/event-stream streams server-to-client output token-by-token over plain HTTP.

from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse

async def generate_stream(prompt: str):
    async for chunk in llm.astream(prompt):
        yield f"data: {chunk.content}\n\n"
    yield "data: [DONE]\n\n"

@app.post("/chat/stream")
async def chat_stream(prompt: str):
    return StreamingResponse(generate_stream(prompt), media_type="text/event-stream")

13. Database Integration (SQLAlchemy)
•

Sync Setup

# database.py
from sqlalchemy import create_engine
from sqlalchemy.orm import declarative_base, sessionmaker

SQLALCHEMY_DATABASE_URL = "sqlite:///./app.db"
engine = create_engine(SQLALCHEMY_DATABASE_URL, connect_args={"check_same_thread": False})
SessionLocal = sessionmaker(autocommit=False, autoflush=False, bind=engine)
Base = declarative_base()
# models.py — SQLAlchemy table mapping
from sqlalchemy import Column, Integer, String, Float
from database import Base

class ItemDB(Base):
    __tablename__ = "items"
    id = Column(Integer, primary_key=True, index=True)
    name = Column(String, index=True)
    price = Column(Float)
# schemas.py — Pydantic contracts
from pydantic import BaseModel

class ItemCreate(BaseModel):
    name: str
    price: float

class ItemResponse(ItemCreate):
    id: int
    model_config = {"from_attributes": True}   # read ORM attributes
# main.py
from fastapi import FastAPI, Depends, HTTPException
from sqlalchemy.orm import Session
from database import SessionLocal, engine, Base
import schemas, models

Base.metadata.create_all(bind=engine)
app = FastAPI()

def get_db():
    db = SessionLocal()
    try:
        yield db
    finally:
        db.close()

@app.post("/items", response_model=schemas.ItemResponse, status_code=201)
def create_item(item: schemas.ItemCreate, db: Session = Depends(get_db)):
    db_item = models.ItemDB(**item.model_dump())
    db.add(db_item); db.commit(); db.refresh(db_item)
    return db_item

@app.get("/items/{item_id}", response_model=schemas.ItemResponse)
def read_item(item_id: int, db: Session = Depends(get_db)):
    item = db.query(models.ItemDB).filter(models.ItemDB.id == item_id).first()
    if not item:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="Item not found")
    return item

Async SQLAlchemy (asyncpg)

from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import create_async_engine, AsyncSession
from sqlalchemy.orm import sessionmaker
from sqlalchemy import select

engine = create_async_engine("postgresql+asyncpg://user:pass@localhost/db", echo=True)
async_session = sessionmaker(engine, class_=AsyncSession, expire_on_commit=False)

async def get_db():
    async with async_session() as session:
        yield session

@app.get("/items")
async def list_items(db: AsyncSession = Depends(get_db)):

14. Rate Limiting

Rate limiting caps requests per client per window, protecting against abuse, brute-force, resource exhaustion, and runaway third-party cost. Exceeding the limit returns 429 Too Many Requests.

AlgorithmHow it worksTrade-off
Fixed WindowCount per fixed slot (per minute)Simple; bursts at window edges
Sliding WindowRolling windowSmooth; slightly more state
Token BucketTokens refill at a steady rate; each request spends oneAllows controlled bursts (AWS, Stripe)
Leaky BucketRequests drain at a fixed rateSmooths spikes (Nginx)
•

With slowapi

# pip install slowapi
from fastapi import FastAPI, Request
from slowapi import Limiter, _rate_limit_exceeded_handler
from slowapi.util import get_remote_address
from slowapi.errors import RateLimitExceeded

limiter = Limiter(key_func=get_remote_address)
app = FastAPI()
app.state.limiter = limiter
app.add_exception_handler(RateLimitExceeded, _rate_limit_exceeded_handler)

@app.get("/")
@limiter.limit("5/minute")
async def homepage(request: Request):     # `request` param is required by slowapi
    return {"message": "Welcome!"}

@app.post("/login")
@limiter.limit("3/minute")                # stricter limit for auth
async def login(request: Request):
    return {"token": "abc123"}
•

Distributed Rate Limiter with Redis

A shared Redis counter (atomic INCR + EXPIRE) enforces a consistent limit across many app instances.

import redis.asyncio as redis
from fastapi import Request, HTTPException

redis_client = redis.from_url("redis://localhost:6379")

async def check_rate_limit(client_id: str, max_requests=100, window=60) -> bool:
    key = f"rate_limit:{client_id}"
    current = await redis_client.get(key)
    if current and int(current) >= max_requests:
        return False
    pipe = redis_client.pipeline()
    pipe.incr(key)
    pipe.expire(key, window)
    await pipe.execute()
    return True

@app.middleware("http")
async def rate_limit_middleware(request: Request, call_next):
    if not await check_rate_limit(request.client.host):
        raise HTTPException(status_code=429, detail="Rate limit exceeded")
    return await call_next(request)

Useful headers: X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, X-RateLimit-Reset, and Retry-After (on a 429).

15. Pagination

Pagination returns large result sets in manageable pages, keeping responses fast and memory low.

StrategyURL exampleProsCons
Offset?page=3&size=20Jump to any pageSlow at large offsets; shifts on insert
Cursor?cursor=abc&size=20Consistent, fast for all pagesCan't jump to arbitrary page
Keyset?after_id=100&size=20Very fast (indexed)Needs sortable unique key
•

Offset-Based (with Metadata)

import math
from fastapi import Query, Depends

class PaginationParams:
    def __init__(self, page: int = Query(1, ge=1), size: int = Query(20, ge=1, le=100)):
        self.page = page
        self.size = size
        self.offset = (page - 1) * size

@app.get("/users")
def list_users(p: PaginationParams = Depends(), db: Session = Depends(get_db)):
    total = db.query(UserDB).count()
    rows = db.query(UserDB).order_by(UserDB.id).offset(p.offset).limit(p.size).all()
    return {
        "data": rows,
        "meta": {
            "page": p.page,
            "size": p.size,
            "total_items": total,
            "total_pages": math.ceil(total / p.size),
            "has_next": p.page < math.ceil(total / p.size),
            "has_prev": p.page > 1,
        },
    }
•

Cursor-Based (for Large Datasets)

import base64, json
from typing import Optional

def encode_cursor(uid: int) -> str:
    return base64.b64encode(json.dumps({"id": uid}).encode()).decode()

def decode_cursor(cursor: str) -> int:
    return json.loads(base64.b64decode(cursor))["id"]

@app.get("/users/cursor")
def list_users_cursor(cursor: Optional[str] = None, size: int = Query(20, ge=1, le=100),
                      db: Session = Depends(get_db)):
    start_id = decode_cursor(cursor) if cursor else 0
    rows = (db.query(UserDB).filter(UserDB.id > start_id)
              .order_by(UserDB.id).limit(size + 1).all())
    has_more = len(rows) > size
    rows = rows[:size]
    next_cursor = encode_cursor(rows[-1].id) if has_more and rows else None
    return {"data": rows, "next_cursor": next_cursor, "has_more": has_more}
16. Lifespan Events & Configuration
•

Lifespan (Startup / Shutdown)

The modern replacement for the deprecated on_event("startup")/on_event("shutdown"). Load models / connect to resources before serving, and clean up on shutdown.

from contextlib import asynccontextmanager
from fastapi import FastAPI

@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app: FastAPI):
    # Startup: load ML model, connect DB
    app.state.model = load_model()
    await database.connect()
    yield
    # Shutdown: clean up
    await database.disconnect()
    app.state.model = None

app = FastAPI(lifespan=lifespan)

For ML serving, load the model once at startup, not per request.

19. Caching (Redis)

Caching stores the result of expensive work (a DB aggregation, a model inference, a third-party call) so repeated requests are served from memory. Redis is the standard shared cache — it survives across workers/instances and supports TTL expiry.

import redis.asyncio as redis
import json

redis_client = redis.from_url("redis://localhost:6379")

@app.get("/expensive/{item_id}")
async def get_expensive(item_id: int):
    cache_key = f"item:{item_id}"
    cached = await redis_client.get(cache_key)
    if cached:
        return json.loads(cached)                 # cache HIT

    result = expensive_computation(item_id)       # cache MISS
    await redis_client.set(cache_key, json.dumps(result), ex=3600)  # TTL 1 hour
    return result
•

Response Cache with ETag

An ETag (hash of the body) lets clients/proxies revalidate with If-None-Match and get a 304 Not Modified instead of re-downloading.

import hashlib, json

def etag_cache(data: dict) -> dict:
    content = json.dumps(data, sort_keys=True)
    etag = hashlib.md5(content.encode()).hexdigest()
    return {"data": data, "ETag": etag, "Cache-Control": "max-age=3600"}
•

In-Process TTL Cache (Single Worker)

For per-process memoization without Redis, a simple TTL decorator works (lost across workers/restarts):

import time
from functools import wraps

def cache_with_ttl(ttl_seconds=60):
    def decorator(func):
        cache = {}
        @wraps(func)
        def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
            key = (args, tuple(sorted(kwargs.items())))
            if key in cache:
                result, ts = cache[key]
                if time.time() - ts < ttl_seconds:
                    return result          # HIT
            result = func(*args, **kwargs)
            cache[key] = (result, time.time())
            return result                  # MISS
        wrapper.cache_clear = cache.clear
        return wrapper
    return decorator

Cache invalidation is the hard part: prefer short TTLs, or delete/overwrite the key on writes. Never cache user-specific data under a shared key.

20. Observability & Structured Logging

Structured (JSON) logs are machine-parseable, so log aggregators (ELK, Loki, Datadog) can index every request by method, path, status, and duration. structlog is the common choice.

import structlog
from fastapi import Request

logger = structlog.get_logger()

@app.middleware("http")
async def log_requests(request: Request, call_next):
    logger.info("request_start", method=request.method, url=str(request.url))
    response = await call_next(request)
    logger.info("request_end", status=response.status_code)
    return response
•

Correlation IDs

Tag every request with a unique ID so logs across services can be stitched into one trace. Read an inbound X-Request-ID or generate one:

import uuid

@app.middleware("http")
async def correlation_id(request: Request, call_next):
    cid = request.headers.get("X-Request-ID") or str(uuid.uuid4())
    structlog.contextvars.bind_contextvars(correlation_id=cid)
    response = await call_next(request)
    response.headers["X-Request-ID"] = cid
    return response
•

Prometheus-Style Metrics

logsmetricstraces

Export counters and gauges for scraping (use prometheus-fastapi-instrumentator in production):

class MetricsExporter:
    def __init__(self):
        self.counters: dict[str, int] = {}
        self.gauges: dict[str, float] = {}
    def inc_counter(self, name, value=1):
        self.counters[name] = self.counters.get(name, 0) + value
    def set_gauge(self, name, value):
        self.gauges[name] = value
    def export(self) -> str:
        lines = [f"{n} {v}" for n, v in self.counters.items()]
        lines += [f"{n} {v}" for n, v in self.gauges.items()]
        return "\n".join(lines)

Observability rests on three pillars: logs (what happened), metrics (how much/how fast), and traces (the path of one request). FastAPI integrates with OpenTelemetry for distributed tracing.

21. API Versioning & Throttling
•

API Versioning

Evolve your API without breaking existing clients. Three common strategies:

# 1) URL prefix (most common, discoverable)
v1_router = APIRouter(prefix="/v1")
v2_router = APIRouter(prefix="/v2")

@v1_router.get("/items/")
async def list_items_v1(): ...   # old format

@v2_router.get("/items/")
async def list_items_v2(): ...   # new format

app.include_router(v1_router)
app.include_router(v2_router)

# 2) Sub-apps (when versions diverge heavily)
# app.mount("/v2", v2_app)

# 3) Header-based: inspect an `Accept-Version` header in middleware
•

Throttling vs Rate Limiting

rejectsdelays

Both manage excess traffic but differ in mechanism:

FeatureRate LimitingThrottling
PurposeEnforce a request quotaControl traffic speed
ActionReject excess requestsSlow / queue requests
Response429 Too Many RequestsDelayed processing
GoalAbuse preventionTraffic smoothing

Rate limiting rejects requests over the quota (see §14). Throttling delays them so processing stays under a target rate:

import time

class Throttler:
    """Enforce a minimum interval between processed requests."""
    def __init__(self, min_interval: float = 1.0):
        self.min_interval = min_interval
        self.last_time = 0.0
    def wait(self):
        elapsed = time.time() - self.last_time
        if elapsed < self.min_interval:
            time.sleep(self.min_interval - elapsed)
        self.last_time = time.time()

API gateways (AWS API Gateway, Kong, NGINX, Apigee) implement rate limiting, throttling, and per-key quotas at the edge — often the best place to enforce them.

22. REST Semantics (PUT vs PATCH, URL vs URI, Status Codes)
•

PUT vs PATCH

PUTentirePATCHpartial
  • PUT replaces the entire resource. Fields omitted from the body may be removed/reset. Idempotent.
  • PATCH applies a partial update — only the provided fields change. Usually idempotent.
# PATCH implemented correctly with exclude_unset:
@app.patch("/items/{item_id}", response_model=Item)
def patch_item(item_id: int, payload: ItemUpdate):
    stored = get_item(item_id)
    update_data = payload.model_dump(exclude_unset=True)  # only what the client sent
    for key, value in update_data.items():
        setattr(stored, key, value)
    return stored

Given a stored {"name": "John", "age": 25, "city": "Delhi"} and a body {"age": 30}: - PUT → resource becomes {"name": "John", "age": 30} (city dropped). - PATCH → resource becomes {"name": "John", "age": 30, "city": "Delhi"}.

•

URL vs URI

URIURL

A URI identifies a resource (/user/123, urn:isbn:123456789). A URL is a URI that also says where and how to access it (https://api.company.com/users/123 — protocol + domain + path). Every URL is a URI; not every URI is a URL.

https://api.company.com/users/123
│       │               │
│       │               └─ Path
│       └─ Domain
└─ Protocol
•

Full HTTP Status Code Reference

307 vs 302409 Conflict
1xx INFORMATIONAL
  100 Continue            101 Switching Protocols (WebSocket upgrade)

2xx SUCCESS
  200 OK                  201 Created            202 Accepted (async)
  204 No Content (DELETE)

3xx REDIRECTION
  301 Moved Permanently   302 Found              304 Not Modified
  307 Temporary Redirect  308 Permanent Redirect (preserves method)

4xx CLIENT ERROR
  400 Bad Request         401 Unauthorized       403 Forbidden
  404 Not Found           405 Method Not Allowed 408 Request Timeout
  409 Conflict            410 Gone               413 Payload Too Large
  415 Unsupported Media   422 Unprocessable (FastAPI validation default)
  429 Too Many Requests

5xx SERVER ERROR
  500 Internal Server Error  502 Bad Gateway
  503 Service Unavailable    504 Gateway Timeout

307 vs 302: 307 guarantees the method is preserved (a redirected POST stays a POST); 302 historically let clients switch to GET. 409 Conflict fits optimistic-locking / duplicate-create cases.

23. Resilience Patterns (Retry, Circuit Breaker)

When your API calls flaky downstreams (third-party APIs, other microservices), wrap those calls in resilience patterns so transient failures don't cascade.

•

Retry with Exponential Backoff + Jitter

Retry a failing call with exponentially increasing delays, adding random jitter to avoid thundering-herd retries:

import time, random

def retry_with_backoff(func, max_retries=5, base_delay=1, max_delay=60):
    for attempt in range(max_retries):
        try:
            return func()
        except Exception as e:
            if attempt == max_retries - 1:
                raise
            delay = min(base_delay * (2 ** attempt) + random.uniform(0, 1), max_delay)
            time.sleep(delay)
•

Circuit Breaker

openshalf-openclosesgraceful degradationtimeoutsbulkheads

After N consecutive failures the breaker opens and fails fast (no calls reach the dead downstream); after a recovery timeout it goes half-open to test one call, then closes on success.

import time

class CircuitBreaker:
    CLOSED, OPEN, HALF_OPEN = "closed", "open", "half_open"

    def __init__(self, failure_threshold=3, recovery_timeout=5):
        self.failure_threshold = failure_threshold
        self.recovery_timeout = recovery_timeout
        self.failures = 0
        self.state = self.CLOSED
        self.last_failure_time = None

    def call(self, func, *args):
        if self.state == self.OPEN:
            if time.time() - self.last_failure_time > self.recovery_timeout:
                self.state = self.HALF_OPEN
            else:
                raise RuntimeError("Circuit is OPEN")
        try:
            result = func(*args)
            if self.state == self.HALF_OPEN:    # recovered
                self.state = self.CLOSED
                self.failures = 0
            return result
        except Exception:
            self.failures += 1
            self.last_failure_time = time.time()
            if self.failures >= self.failure_threshold:
                self.state = self.OPEN
            raise

Related patterns: graceful degradation (return a cached/default response when the primary fails), timeouts (never wait forever on a downstream), and bulkheads (isolate resource pools so one failing dependency can't exhaust all workers). Libraries: tenacity (retries), pybreaker (circuit breaker).

24. gRPC with FastAPI

gRPC (Google Remote Procedure Call) is a high-performance RPC framework using Protocol Buffers (compact binary) over HTTP/2. A common architecture uses FastAPI as the external REST gateway and gRPC for fast internal service-to-service traffic.

•

REST vs gRPC

FeatureRESTgRPC
ProtocolHTTP/1.1HTTP/2 (multiplexing)
Data formatJSON (text)Protobuf (binary)
ContractOpenAPI / loose.proto file / strict
StreamingNot nativeBidirectional streaming
PerformanceGood~7-10x faster
Browser supportFullLimited (needs grpc-web)
Code generationOptionalBuilt-in (multi-language)
Best forPublic APIs, webMicroservices, internal APIs
•

Four Communication Patterns

  1. Unary Client --request--> Server, Client <--response-- Server (like REST)
  2. Server Stream Client --request--> Server, Client <--stream---- Server
  3. Client Stream Client --stream---> Server, Client <--response-- Server
  4. Bidirectional Client <--stream--> Server (both directions at once)
•

Protobuf Definition (.proto)

syntax = "proto3";
package user;

service UserService {
    rpc GetUser (GetUserRequest) returns (UserResponse);
    rpc ListUsers (ListUsersRequest) returns (stream UserResponse);  // server streaming
    rpc CreateUser (CreateUserRequest) returns (UserResponse);
}

message GetUserRequest { int32 user_id = 1; }
message CreateUserRequest { string name = 1; string email = 2; int32 age = 3; }
message UserResponse { int32 id = 1; string name = 2; string email = 3; int32 age = 4; }
message ListUsersRequest { int32 page = 1; int32 size = 2; }
•

gRPC Server

pip install grpcio grpcio-tools
python -m grpc_tools.protoc -I. --python_out=. --grpc_python_out=. user.proto
# generates user_pb2.py and user_pb2_grpc.py
import grpc
from concurrent import futures
import user_pb2, user_pb2_grpc

class UserServicer(user_pb2_grpc.UserServiceServicer):
    def __init__(self):
        self.users = {1: {"id": 1, "name": "Alice", "email": "alice@example.com", "age": 30}}

    def GetUser(self, request, context):
        user = self.users.get(request.user_id)
        if not user:
            context.set_code(grpc.StatusCode.NOT_FOUND)
            context.set_details("User not found")
            return user_pb2.UserResponse()
        return user_pb2.UserResponse(**user)

    def ListUsers(self, request, context):     # server streaming
        for user in self.users.values():
            yield user_pb2.UserResponse(**user)

def serve():
    server = grpc.server(futures.ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=10))
    user_pb2_grpc.add_UserServiceServicer_to_server(UserServicer(), server)
    server.add_insecure_port("[::]:50051")
    server.start()
    server.wait_for_termination()
•

FastAPI Gateway Calling gRPC

RESTgRPC
from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException
import grpc, user_pb2, user_pb2_grpc

app = FastAPI()
channel = grpc.insecure_channel("user-service:50051")
user_stub = user_pb2_grpc.UserServiceStub(channel)

@app.get("/api/users/{user_id}")
def get_user(user_id: int):
    try:
        resp = user_stub.GetUser(user_pb2.GetUserRequest(user_id=user_id))
        return {"id": resp.id, "name": resp.name, "email": resp.email}
    except grpc.RpcError as e:
        if e.code() == grpc.StatusCode.NOT_FOUND:
            raise HTTPException(404, "User not found")
        raise HTTPException(500, "Internal error")
┌──────────┐  REST/JSON   ┌──────────┐  gRPC/Protobuf   ┌──────────┐
│ Frontend │ ───────────► │ FastAPI  │ ───────────────► │  User /  │
│ (Browser)│ ◄─────────── │ Gateway  │ ◄─────────────── │ Order /  │
└──────────┘              └──────────┘                  │ Payment  │
                                                        └──────────┘

Choose REST for public/browser-facing APIs and quick prototyping; gRPC for low-latency internal microservice calls and streaming. They coexist well behind a FastAPI gateway.

25. Complete Mini-Project: Notes API

A full CRUD service tying together Pydantic schemas, path/query params, response_model, status codes, error handling, partial updates (PATCH with exclude_unset), and background tasks.

from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException, Query, BackgroundTasks
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from typing import Optional
from datetime import datetime
from uuid import uuid4

app = FastAPI(title="Notes API", version="1.0.0")

notes_db: dict[str, dict] = {}   # in-memory store

# --- Schemas ---
class NoteCreate(BaseModel):
    title: str = Field(..., min_length=1, max_length=100)
    content: str = Field(..., min_length=1)
    tags: list[str] = Field(default_factory=list)

class NoteUpdate(BaseModel):
    title: Optional[str] = Field(None, min_length=1, max_length=100)
    content: Optional[str] = None
    tags: Optional[list[str]] = None

class NoteResponse(BaseModel):
    id: str
    title: str
    content: str
    tags: list[str]
    created_at: str
    updated_at: str

# --- Background audit log ---
def log_action(action: str, note_id: str):
    with open("notes_audit.log", "a") as f:
        f.write(f"[{datetime.utcnow().isoformat()}] {action}: {note_id}\n")

# --- CRUD ---
@app.post("/notes", response_model=NoteResponse, status_code=201)
def create_note(note: NoteCreate, bg: BackgroundTasks):
    note_id = str(uuid4())
    now = datetime.utcnow().isoformat()
    notes_db[note_id] = {"id": note_id, **note.model_dump(),
                         "created_at": now, "updated_at": now}
    bg.add_task(log_action, "CREATE", note_id)
    return notes_db[note_id]

@app.get("/notes", response_model=list[NoteResponse])
def list_notes(skip: int = Query(0, ge=0), limit: int = Query(10, ge=1, le=100),
               tag: Optional[str] = None):
    notes = list(notes_db.values())
    if tag:
        notes = [n for n in notes if tag in n["tags"]]
    return notes[skip: skip + limit]

@app.get("/notes/{note_id}", response_model=NoteResponse)
def get_note(note_id: str):
    if note_id not in notes_db:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="Note not found")
    return notes_db[note_id]

@app.patch("/notes/{note_id}", response_model=NoteResponse)
def update_note(note_id: str, update: NoteUpdate, bg: BackgroundTasks):
    if note_id not in notes_db:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="Note not found")
    stored = notes_db[note_id]
    for key, value in update.model_dump(exclude_unset=True).items():   # partial update
        stored[key] = value
    stored["updated_at"] = datetime.utcnow().isoformat()
    bg.add_task(log_action, "UPDATE", note_id)
    return stored

@app.delete("/notes/{note_id}", status_code=204)
def delete_note(note_id: str, bg: BackgroundTasks):
    if note_id not in notes_db:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="Note not found")
    del notes_db[note_id]
    bg.add_task(log_action, "DELETE", note_id)
26. Quick Reference Cheat Sheet
APP                                  PARAMETERS
app = FastAPI(title=..., version=)   Path("...", ge=1)      path param + constraint

@app.post / put / patch / delete     Body(default=1)         singular body field
                                     Pydantic model arg      request body

RESPONSE                             DEPENDENCIES

SECURITY                             ASYNC / TASKS

Depends(get_current_user)            def endpoint             runs in thread pool
