20.4 Cursor-Based Pagination (For Large Datasets)

from datetime import datetime
from typing import Optional
import base64
import json

class CursorPaginatedResponse(BaseModel):
    data: list[UserOut]
    next_cursor: Optional[str] = None
    has_more: bool

def encode_cursor(user_id: int) -> str:
    return base64.b64encode(json.dumps({"id": user_id}).encode()).decode()

def decode_cursor(cursor: str) -> int:
    data = json.loads(base64.b64decode(cursor))
    return data["id"]

@app.get("/users/cursor", response_model=CursorPaginatedResponse)
def list_users_cursor(
    cursor: Optional[str] = Query(None, description="Pagination cursor"),
    size: int = Query(20, ge=1, le=100),
):
    # Determine starting point
    start_id = 0
    if cursor:
        start_id = decode_cursor(cursor)
    
    # Filter items after cursor
    filtered = [u for u in fake_users_db if u["id"] > start_id]
    items = filtered[:size]
    has_more = len(filtered) > size
    
    next_cursor = None
    if has_more and items:
        next_cursor = encode_cursor(items[-1]["id"])
    
    return CursorPaginatedResponse(
        data=items,
        next_cursor=next_cursor,
        has_more=has_more,
    )

Request: GET /users/cursor?size=3

{
  "data": [{"id": 1}, {"id": 2}, {"id": 3}],
  "next_cursor": "eyJpZCI6IDN9",
  "has_more": true
}

Next page: GET /users/cursor?cursor=eyJpZCI6IDN9&size=3

{
  "data": [{"id": 4}, {"id": 5}, {"id": 6}],
  "next_cursor": "eyJpZCI6IDZ9",
  "has_more": true
}

20.5 Pagination with SQLAlchemy

from sqlalchemy.orm import Session

def get_users_paginated(db: Session, page: int, size: int):
    total = db.query(UserDB).count()
    users = (
        db.query(UserDB)
        .order_by(UserDB.id)
        .offset((page - 1) * size)
        .limit(size)
        .all()
    )
    return users, total

@app.get("/users")
def list_users(pagination: PaginationParams = Depends(), db: Session = Depends(get_db)):
    users, total = get_users_paginated(db, pagination.page, pagination.size)
    return {
        "data": users,
        "total": total,
        "page": pagination.page,
        "pages": math.ceil(total / pagination.size),
    }
21. gRPC — What, Why & How with FastAPI

21.1 What is gRPC?

gRPC (Google Remote Procedure Call) is a high-performance, open-source RPC framework.

REST API:                          gRPC:
──────────                         ──────
JSON (text-based)                  Protobuf (binary, compact)
HTTP/1.1                           HTTP/2 (multiplexing)
Request-Response only              4 patterns (unary, streaming)
Language-agnostic (loosely)        Strongly typed contracts (.proto)
Human-readable                     Not human-readable
~100ms for typical call            ~10ms for typical call

21.2 REST vs gRPC Comparison

FeatureRESTgRPC
ProtocolHTTP/1.1HTTP/2
Data formatJSON (text)Protobuf (binary)
ContractOpenAPI / loose.proto file / strict
StreamingNot nativeBidirectional streaming
PerformanceGood7-10x faster
Browser supportFullLimited (needs grpc-web)
Code generationOptionalBuilt-in (multi-language)
Best forPublic APIs, webMicroservices, internal APIs

21.3 gRPC Communication Patterns

1. Unary RPC (like REST):
   Client ──request──→ Server
   Client ←─response── Server

2. Server Streaming:
   Client ──request──→ Server
   Client ←─stream──── Server  (multiple responses)

3. Client Streaming:
   Client ──stream───→ Server  (multiple requests)
   Client ←─response── Server

4. Bidirectional Streaming:
   Client ←──stream──→ Server  (both directions simultaneously)

21.4 Protobuf Definition (.proto)

// user.proto
syntax = "proto3";

package user;

// Define the service
service UserService {
    rpc GetUser (GetUserRequest) returns (UserResponse);
    rpc ListUsers (ListUsersRequest) returns (stream UserResponse);  // server streaming
    rpc CreateUser (CreateUserRequest) returns (UserResponse);
}

// Define messages
message GetUserRequest {
    int32 user_id = 1;
}

message CreateUserRequest {
    string name = 1;
    string email = 2;
    int32 age = 3;
}

message UserResponse {
    int32 id = 1;
    string name = 2;
    string email = 3;
    int32 age = 4;
}

message ListUsersRequest {
    int32 page = 1;
    int32 size = 2;
}

21.5 gRPC Server in Python

pip install grpcio grpcio-tools

# Generate Python code from .proto
python -m grpc_tools.protoc -I. --python_out=. --grpc_python_out=. user.proto
# Generates: user_pb2.py, user_pb2_grpc.py
# grpc_server.py
import grpc
from concurrent import futures
import user_pb2
import user_pb2_grpc

class UserServicer(user_pb2_grpc.UserServiceServicer):
    def __init__(self):
        self.users = {
            1: {"id": 1, "name": "Alice", "email": "alice@example.com", "age": 30},
            2: {"id": 2, "name": "Bob", "email": "bob@example.com", "age": 25},
        }
    
    def GetUser(self, request, context):
        user = self.users.get(request.user_id)
        if not user:
            context.set_code(grpc.StatusCode.NOT_FOUND)
            context.set_details("User not found")
            return user_pb2.UserResponse()
        return user_pb2.UserResponse(**user)
    
    def CreateUser(self, request, context):
        new_id = max(self.users.keys()) + 1
        user = {
            "id": new_id,
            "name": request.name,
            "email": request.email,
            "age": request.age,
        }
        self.users[new_id] = user
        return user_pb2.UserResponse(**user)
    
    def ListUsers(self, request, context):
        """Server streaming — yields users one by one"""
        for user in self.users.values():
            yield user_pb2.UserResponse(**user)

def serve():
    server = grpc.server(futures.ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=10))
    user_pb2_grpc.add_UserServiceServicer_to_server(UserServicer(), server)
    server.add_insecure_port("[::]:50051")
    server.start()
    print("gRPC server running on port 50051")
    server.wait_for_termination()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    serve()

21.6 gRPC Client

# grpc_client.py
import grpc
import user_pb2
import user_pb2_grpc

def run():
    channel = grpc.insecure_channel("localhost:50051")
    stub = user_pb2_grpc.UserServiceStub(channel)
    
    # Unary call
    response = stub.GetUser(user_pb2.GetUserRequest(user_id=1))
    print(f"Got user: {response.name}, {response.email}")
    
    # Create user
    new_user = stub.CreateUser(
        user_pb2.CreateUserRequest(name="Charlie", email="charlie@ex.com", age=28)
    )
    print(f"Created: {new_user.name} (ID: {new_user.id})")
    
    # Server streaming
    print("\nAll users:")
    for user in stub.ListUsers(user_pb2.ListUsersRequest(page=1, size=10)):
        print(f"  - {user.name} ({user.email})")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    run()

21.7 FastAPI + gRPC (Hybrid Architecture)

A common pattern: FastAPI serves external REST clients, gRPC handles internal microservice communication.

# main.py — FastAPI gateway that calls gRPC services
from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException
from pydantic import BaseModel
import grpc
import user_pb2
import user_pb2_grpc

app = FastAPI()

# gRPC channel to user microservice
channel = grpc.insecure_channel("user-service:50051")
user_stub = user_pb2_grpc.UserServiceStub(channel)

class UserCreate(BaseModel):
    name: str
    email: str
    age: int

@app.get("/api/users/{user_id}")
def get_user(user_id: int):
    try:
        response = user_stub.GetUser(
            user_pb2.GetUserRequest(user_id=user_id)
        )
        return {"id": response.id, "name": response.name, "email": response.email}
    except grpc.RpcError as e:
        if e.code() == grpc.StatusCode.NOT_FOUND:
            raise HTTPException(404, "User not found")
        raise HTTPException(500, "Internal error")

@app.post("/api/users")
def create_user(user: UserCreate):
    response = user_stub.CreateUser(
        user_pb2.CreateUserRequest(
            name=user.name, email=user.email, age=user.age
        )
    )
    return {"id": response.id, "name": response.name}
┌──────────────┐      REST/JSON      ┌─────────────────────────┐
│   Frontend   │ ──────────────────→ │   FastAPI               │
│  (Browser)   │ ←────────────────── │   Gateway               │
└──────────────┘                     └──────┬──────────────────┘
                                            │ gRPC/Protobuf
                              ┌─────────────┼──────────────────┐
                              ↓             ↓             ↓
                       ┌───────────┐ ┌───────────┐ ┌───────────┐
                       │   User    │ │   Order   │ │  Payment  │
                       │  Service  │ │  Service  │ │  Service  │
                       └───────────┘ └───────────┘ └───────────┘

21.8 When to Use gRPC vs REST

ScenarioUse RESTUse gRPC
Public API✅❌
Browser clients✅⚠️ (needs grpc-web)
Microservice-to-microservice⚠️✅
Real-time streaming⚠️ (WebSocket)✅
Mobile apps✅✅
Low latency required⚠️✅
Polyglot services✅✅
Quick prototyping✅❌
22. Complete Mini-Project: Notes API

A complete CRUD API for notes demonstrating all major concepts together.

# notes_app.py
from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException, Depends, Query, BackgroundTasks
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from typing import Optional
from datetime import datetime
from uuid import uuid4

app = FastAPI(title="Notes API", version="1.0.0")

# --- In-memory Database ---
notes_db: dict[str, dict] = {}

# --- Schemas ---
class NoteCreate(BaseModel):
    title: str = Field(..., min_length=1, max_length=100)
    content: str = Field(..., min_length=1)
    tags: list[str] = []

class NoteUpdate(BaseModel):
    title: Optional[str] = Field(None, min_length=1, max_length=100)
    content: Optional[str] = None
    tags: Optional[list[str]] = None

class NoteResponse(BaseModel):
    id: str
    title: str
    content: str
    tags: list[str]
    created_at: str
    updated_at: str

# --- Background Task ---
def log_action(action: str, note_id: str):
    with open("notes_audit.log", "a") as f:
        f.write(f"[{datetime.utcnow().isoformat()}] {action}: {note_id}\n")

# --- CRUD Endpoints ---
@app.post("/notes", response_model=NoteResponse, status_code=201)
def create_note(note: NoteCreate, bg: BackgroundTasks):
    note_id = str(uuid4())
    now = datetime.utcnow().isoformat()
    notes_db[note_id] = {
        "id": note_id,
        **note.model_dump(),
        "created_at": now,
        "updated_at": now,
    }
    bg.add_task(log_action, "CREATE", note_id)
    return notes_db[note_id]

@app.get("/notes", response_model=list[NoteResponse])
def list_notes(
    skip: int = Query(0, ge=0),
    limit: int = Query(10, ge=1, le=100),
    tag: Optional[str] = None,
):
    notes = list(notes_db.values())
    if tag:
        notes = [n for n in notes if tag in n["tags"]]
    return notes[skip : skip + limit]

@app.get("/notes/{note_id}", response_model=NoteResponse)
def get_note(note_id: str):
    if note_id not in notes_db:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="Note not found")
    return notes_db[note_id]

@app.patch("/notes/{note_id}", response_model=NoteResponse)
def update_note(note_id: str, update: NoteUpdate, bg: BackgroundTasks):
    if note_id not in notes_db:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="Note not found")
    stored = notes_db[note_id]
    update_data = update.model_dump(exclude_unset=True)
    for key, value in update_data.items():
        stored[key] = value
    stored["updated_at"] = datetime.utcnow().isoformat()
    bg.add_task(log_action, "UPDATE", note_id)
    return stored

@app.delete("/notes/{note_id}", status_code=204)
def delete_note(note_id: str, bg: BackgroundTasks):
    if note_id not in notes_db:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="Note not found")
    del notes_db[note_id]
    bg.add_task(log_action, "DELETE", note_id)
23. Interview Questions & Answers

Fundamentals

•

Q1: What is FastAPI and why is it called "Fast"?

Runtime performanceDeveloper speed

FastAPI is a modern Python web framework for building APIs. It is "fast" in two ways: 1. Runtime performance — built on Starlette (ASGI) with async support, it achieves performance comparable to Node.js and Go. 2. Developer speed — type hints + Pydantic auto-generate validation, serialization, and documentation, reducing boilerplate code by ~40%.

•

Q2: How does FastAPI differ from Flask?

FeatureFlaskFastAPI
Type systemNo built-in validationPydantic + type hints
AsyncRequires extensionsNative async/await
DocsManual (Swagger via flask-restx)Automatic OpenAPI
PerformanceWSGI (slower)ASGI (faster)
DINo built-inBuilt-in Depends()
•

Q3: What is ASGI? How is it different from WSGI?

WSGIASGIUvicornHypercorn
  • WSGI (Web Server Gateway Interface) handles one request at a time synchronously.
  • ASGI (Asynchronous Server Gateway Interface) supports async, WebSockets, HTTP/2, and long-lived connections.
  • FastAPI runs on ASGI servers like Uvicorn or Hypercorn.
•

Q4: What is the role of Pydantic in FastAPI?

Data validationData serializationData parsingSchema generation

Pydantic handles: - Data validation — incoming request data is auto-validated against model schemas - Data serialization — Python objects → JSON (response models) - Data parsing — JSON → Python objects
- Schema generation — generates OpenAPI/JSON Schema for docs

•

Q5: What happens when you use def vs async def for an endpoint?

  • async def → runs directly on the async event loop. Use for I/O-bound operations.
  • def → FastAPI runs it in an external thread pool to avoid blocking the event loop. Use for CPU-bound or sync library calls.

Path / Query / Body

•

Q6: How does FastAPI determine if a parameter is a path param, query param, or body?

path stringsimple typePydantic model
  • If declared in the path string (/items/{id}) → path parameter
  • If it's a simple type (int, str, float) and NOT in the path → query parameter
  • If it's a Pydantic model → request body
  • Use Body(), Query(), Path() to override defaults
•

Q7: How do you add validation to query parameters?

from fastapi import Query

@app.get("/search")
def search(q: str = Query(..., min_length=3, max_length=50, regex="^[a-zA-Z]+$")):
    return {"q": q}

Dependency Injection

•

Q8: Explain Dependency Injection in FastAPI.

FunctionsGenerator functionsClasses

FastAPI's DI system uses Depends(). Dependencies can be: - Functions that return values - Generator functions (with yield) for setup/teardown (e.g., DB sessions) - Classes (callable objects)

Dependencies can depend on other dependencies (sub-dependencies). FastAPI resolves the full dependency tree, caches results per-request, and handles cleanup.

•

Q9: What is yield in a FastAPI dependency and when is it useful?

beforeafter

A dependency with yield runs code before the yield (setup) and after (teardown):

def get_db():
    db = SessionLocal()
    try:
        yield db        # provide the DB session
    finally:
        db.close()      # cleanup after response

This is perfect for resource management (DB connections, file handles, locks).

Security

•

Q10: How do you implement JWT authentication in FastAPI?

  1. Create a /token endpoint that accepts username/password and returns a JWT.
  2. Use OAuth2PasswordBearer(tokenUrl="token") to define the token scheme.
  3. Create a get_current_user dependency that decodes and validates the JWT.
  4. Add Depends(get_current_user) to protected endpoints.

Libraries: python-jose (JWT), passlib (password hashing).

•

Q11: How do you handle role-based authorization?

Create a dependency factory that checks the user's role:

def require_role(role: str):
    def checker(user=Depends(get_current_user)):
        if user.role != role:
            raise HTTPException(403, "Forbidden")
        return user
    return checker

@app.get("/admin", dependencies=[Depends(require_role("admin"))])
def admin_panel(): ...

Middleware & CORS

•

Q12: What is middleware in FastAPI?

every requestevery response

Middleware is a function that processes every request before it reaches the endpoint and every response before it's sent back. Common uses: logging, CORS, authentication, timing, rate limiting.

•

Q13: How do you enable CORS in FastAPI?

from fastapi.middleware.cors import CORSMiddleware
app.add_middleware(
    CORSMiddleware,
    allow_origins=["http://localhost:3000"],
    allow_methods=["*"],
    allow_headers=["*"],
)

Database

•

Q14: How do you integrate SQLAlchemy with FastAPI?

  1. Create engine + SessionLocal in database.py
  2. Define SQLAlchemy models (table mappings)
  3. Define Pydantic schemas (API contracts)
  4. Create a get_db() dependency with yield
  5. Use Depends(get_db) in endpoints
•

Q15: What is from_attributes = True (formerly orm_mode) in Pydantic?

It tells Pydantic to read data from ORM model attributes (e.g., item.name) instead of expecting a dict (item["name"]). This is required when returning SQLAlchemy model instances as Pydantic response models.

Background Tasks & WebSockets

•

Q16: When should you use BackgroundTasks vs Celery?

BackgroundTasksCelery
Use caseLightweight (email, logging)Heavy (ML, video processing)
BrokerNone (in-process)Redis / RabbitMQ
Retry logicNoneBuilt-in
MonitoringNoneFlower dashboard
ScalingSame processSeparate workers
•

Q17: How do you handle WebSockets in FastAPI?

Use @app.websocket("/ws") and accept the connection. Maintain a list of active connections. Use receive_text() / send_text() for communication. Handle WebSocketDisconnect for cleanup.

Testing

•

Q18: How do you test a FastAPI application?

Use TestClient from fastapi.testclient (built on httpx):

from fastapi.testclient import TestClient
client = TestClient(app)
response = client.get("/items")
assert response.status_code == 200

For async tests, use httpx.AsyncClient with ASGITransport.

•

Q19: How do you override dependencies in tests?

app.dependency_overrides[get_db] = lambda: test_db_session

This replaces the real dependency with a test version. Reset after tests with app.dependency_overrides.clear().

Advanced

•

Q20: What are Lifespan Events in FastAPI?

Lifespan events replace on_startup / on_shutdown (deprecated). Use an async context manager:

from contextlib import asynccontextmanager

@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app: FastAPI):
    # Startup: load ML model, connect to DB
    ml_model = load_model()
    yield {"ml_model": ml_model}
    # Shutdown: cleanup
    ml_model.close()

app = FastAPI(lifespan=lifespan)
•

Q21: What is response_model_exclude_unset?

When set to True, the response only includes fields that were explicitly set by the user. Fields with default values that were not changed are excluded. Useful for PATCH operations.

•

Q22: How do you handle file uploads in FastAPI?

Use UploadFile which provides: .filename, .content_type, .read(), .write(), .seek(), .close(). It uses SpooledTemporaryFile (stores small files in memory, large files on disk).

•

Q23: How do you version your API in FastAPI?

URL prefixSeparate appsHeader-based

Common approaches: 1. URL prefix: APIRouter(prefix="/v1/items") 2. Separate apps: Mount sub-apps with app.mount("/v2", v2_app) 3. Header-based: Custom middleware to check Accept-Version header

•

Q24: What is APIRouter and why use it?

APIRouter is used to organize endpoints into modular groups (like Flask Blueprints). Each module defines its own router with a prefix and tags, then the main app includes them via app.include_router().

•

Q25: Explain the request lifecycle in FastAPI.

Client Request
    ↓
ASGI Server (Uvicorn)
    ↓
Middleware Stack (in order)
    ↓
Route Matching
    ↓
Dependency Resolution (+ sub-dependencies)
    ↓
Request Validation (Pydantic)
    ↓
Endpoint Function Execution
    ↓
Response Serialization (response_model)
    ↓
Middleware Stack (reverse order)
    ↓
Client Response
•

Q26: How does FastAPI auto-generate documentation?

FastAPI uses Python type hints + Pydantic models to generate an OpenAPI 3.0 schema at runtime. This schema is served at /openapi.json. Swagger UI (/docs) and ReDoc (/redoc) consume this schema to render interactive docs.

•

Q27: What are status_code best practices in FastAPI?

OperationCodeConstant
GET success200status.HTTP_200_OK
POST created201status.HTTP_201_CREATED
DELETE no content204status.HTTP_204_NO_CONTENT
Bad request400status.HTTP_400_BAD_REQUEST
Unauthorized401status.HTTP_401_UNAUTHORIZED
Not found404status.HTTP_404_NOT_FOUND
Validation error422status.HTTP_422_UNPROCESSABLE_ENTITY
•

Q28: How do you handle environment-specific configuration?

Use pydantic-settings with .env files:

from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings

class Settings(BaseSettings):
    database_url: str
    debug: bool = False

    class Config:
        env_file = ".env"

settings = Settings()
•

Q29: What are some performance optimization tips for FastAPI?

  1. Use async def for I/O-bound endpoints
  2. Use connection pooling for databases (SQLAlchemy pool_size)
  3. Add caching (Redis / cachetools)
  4. Use response_model_exclude_unset to reduce payload size
  5. Enable GZip middleware for large responses
  6. Use multiple Uvicorn workers (--workers 4)
  7. Profile with middleware (timing headers)
•

Q30: How do you handle graceful shutdown in FastAPI?

Use lifespan events to close DB connections, flush caches, and complete pending background tasks:

@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app: FastAPI):
    # Startup
    await database.connect()
    yield
    # Shutdown
    await database.disconnect()

app = FastAPI(lifespan=lifespan)

Rate Limiting & Pagination Interview Questions

•

Q31: What is rate limiting and why is it important?

Rate limiting restricts the number of API requests a client can make within a time window. It prevents abuse, DDoS attacks, resource exhaustion, and ensures fair usage. Common implementations use the Token Bucket or Sliding Window algorithm.

•

Q32: What are the common rate limiting algorithms?

Fixed WindowSliding WindowToken BucketLeaky Bucket
AlgorithmDescription
Fixed WindowCounts requests in fixed time slots. Simple but allows bursts at window edges.
Sliding WindowRolling time window. Smooth and accurate.
Token BucketTokens refill at a steady rate. Allows controlled bursts. Used by AWS, Stripe.
Leaky BucketRequests processed at constant rate. Smooths traffic. Used by Nginx.
•

Q33: How do you implement distributed rate limiting?

Use a shared store like Redis with atomic INCR + EXPIRE commands. Each API instance checks/updates the same counter. This ensures consistent limits across multiple server instances.

•

Q34: What HTTP headers should a rate-limited API return?

X-RateLimit-Limit: 100          # Max requests allowed
X-RateLimit-Remaining: 42       # Remaining requests in window
X-RateLimit-Reset: 1625478900   # When the window resets (Unix timestamp)
Retry-After: 30                 # Seconds to wait (on 429 response)
•

Q35: Offset pagination vs cursor pagination — when to use which?

OffsetCursor
  • Offset (?page=5&size=20): Use when users need to jump to arbitrary pages (e.g., admin dashboard). Becomes slow with large offsets (OFFSET 100000 scans 100K rows).
  • Cursor (?cursor=abc&size=20): Use for infinite scroll / large datasets. Always fast (uses indexed WHERE clause). Can't jump to arbitrary page.
•

Q36: What is gRPC and when should you use it over REST?

gRPC is a high-performance RPC framework using Protocol Buffers (binary) over HTTP/2. Use it for: - Internal microservice communication (7-10x faster than REST) - Real-time bidirectional streaming - Polyglot environments (auto-generates client/server code for 10+ languages)

Use REST for public APIs, browser clients, and quick prototyping.

•

Q37: What are the four gRPC communication patterns?

UnaryServer StreamingClient StreamingBidirectional StreamingEnd of FastAPI Notes
  1. UnarySingle request → single response (like REST)
  2. Server StreamingSingle request → stream of responses
  3. Client StreamingStream of requests → single response
  4. Bidirectional StreamingStream in both directions simultaneously

End of FastAPI Notes — Covers installation → deployment → rate limiting → pagination → gRPC → interview prep.

Pydantic15 sections

Pydantic — Complete Reference

Scope: Pydantic v2 BaseModel, field types & constraints with Field(), field/model validators, computed fields, ConfigDict, serialization (model_dump/model_dump_json), parsing (model_validate), generic & discriminated-union models, custom & annotated validators, settings management (pydantic-settings), v1→v2 migration, comparison with dataclasses/attrs/msgspec, and FastAPI integration. Pydantic v2 (pydantic-core, Rust-backed).

•

1. BaseModel Basics

A BaseModel declares typed fields; Pydantic validates and coerces input at construction time and rejects bad data with a ValidationError.

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from typing import Optional
from datetime import datetime

class Experiment(BaseModel):
    name: str
    learning_rate: float = Field(gt=0, le=1.0, description="LR for optimizer")
    epochs: int = Field(default=10, ge=1)
    tags: list[str] = Field(default_factory=list)
    created_at: datetime = Field(default_factory=datetime.now)
    description: Optional[str] = None

exp = Experiment(name="bert-finetune", learning_rate=0.001)
print(exp.model_dump())        # {'name': 'bert-finetune', 'learning_rate': 0.001, 'epochs': 10, ...}
print(exp.model_dump_json())   # '{"name":"bert-finetune","learning_rate":0.001,...}'
print(exp.model_fields.keys()) # dict_keys(['name', 'learning_rate', 'epochs', 'tags', ...])

Validation Errors

from pydantic import ValidationError

try:
    Experiment(name="x", learning_rate=5.0)   # > 1.0 violates le=1.0
except ValidationError as e:
    print(e.error_count())   # 1
    print(e.errors()[0]["type"], e.errors()[0]["loc"])
    # less_than_equal ('learning_rate',)

Coercion vs Strict

By default Pydantic coerces compatible types ("10" → 10). Coercion can be disabled per-field or per-model (see ConfigDict).

class M(BaseModel):
    n: int

print(M(n="10").n)   # 10   (str coerced to int)
print(M(n=3.0).n)    # 3    (float -> int when lossless)
•

2. Field — Constraints & Metadata

Field() attaches constraints, defaults, aliases, and documentation to a field.

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

class FeatureConfig(BaseModel):
    name: str = Field(min_length=1, max_length=100, pattern=r"^[a-z_]+$")
    dim: int = Field(ge=1, le=4096, alias="dimension")
    dropout: float = Field(ge=0.0, le=1.0, default=0.1)
    values: list[float] = Field(min_length=1, max_length=10000)

cfg = FeatureConfig(name="embedding", dimension=768, values=[1.0, 2.0])
print(cfg.dim)                          # 768  (populated via alias)
print(cfg.model_dump(by_alias=True))    # {'name': 'embedding', 'dimension': 768, 'dropout': 0.1, 'values': [...]}

Common Constraints

ConstraintApplies toMeaning
gt, ge, lt, lenumbersgreater/less than (or equal)
multiple_ofnumbersvalue must be a multiple
min_length, max_lengthstr / collectionslength bounds
patternstrregex the value must match
default / default_factoryanystatic default / callable default
alias / validation_alias / serialization_aliasanyexternal field name(s)
frozenanyfield is read-only after init
excludeanyomit from serialization by default

Use default_factory (not default=[]) for mutable defaults to avoid shared-state bugs.

•

3. field_validator

beforeafter

@field_validator validates or transforms one (or more) named fields. It must be a @classmethod.

from pydantic import BaseModel, field_validator

class TrainingConfig(BaseModel):
    model_name: str
    batch_size: int
    gpus: list[int]

    @field_validator("model_name")
    @classmethod
    def validate_model_name(cls, v: str) -> str:
        allowed = {"bert", "gpt2", "t5", "llama"}
        if v.lower() not in allowed:
            raise ValueError(f"Model must be one of {allowed}")
        return v.lower()                # transform: normalize to lowercase

    @field_validator("batch_size")
    @classmethod
    def must_be_power_of_two(cls, v: int) -> int:
        if v & (v - 1) != 0:
            raise ValueError("batch_size must be a power of 2")
        return v

    @field_validator("gpus", mode="before")
    @classmethod
    def parse_gpus(cls, v):
        """`mode='before'` runs prior to type coercion — accept a CSV string."""
        if isinstance(v, str):
            return [int(x.strip()) for x in v.split(",")]
        return v

cfg = TrainingConfig(model_name="BERT", batch_size=32, gpus="0, 1, 2")
print(cfg.model_name, cfg.gpus)   # bert [0, 1, 2]

mode="before" vs mode="after"

  • beforeruns on the raw input before Pydantic coerces to the declared type (use to reshape/normalize input).
  • after (default) — runs on the already-coerced, type-correct value (use to enforce business rules).

You can validate multiple fields at once: @field_validator("a", "b"). Use @field_validator("*") to apply to all fields.

•

4. model_validator

mode="before"mode="after"

@model_validator validates the whole model — used for cross-field rules and input reshaping.

from pydantic import BaseModel, model_validator

class OptimizerConfig(BaseModel):
    optimizer: str
    learning_rate: float
    weight_decay: float = 0.0
    warmup_steps: int = 0
    total_steps: int = 1000

    @model_validator(mode="after")
    def check_warmup(self):
        if self.warmup_steps >= self.total_steps:
            raise ValueError("warmup_steps must be < total_steps")
        if self.optimizer == "sgd" and self.weight_decay > 0:
            raise ValueError("SGD with weight_decay is unusual — use AdamW")
        return self                      # `after` validators return self

    @model_validator(mode="before")
    @classmethod
    def normalize_keys(cls, data: dict):
        """`before` validators see the raw input dict — remap camelCase keys."""
        mapping = {"learningRate": "learning_rate", "weightDecay": "weight_decay"}
        return {mapping.get(k, k): v for k, v in data.items()}
  • mode="before" is a @classmethod receiving the raw input (dict); return the (possibly transformed) data.
  • mode="after" is an instance method receiving the validated model; validate cross-field invariants and return self.
•

5. Annotated Validators & Custom Types

Annotated Validators

Attach validators to a type via Annotated so they are reusable across models.

from typing import Annotated
from pydantic import BaseModel, AfterValidator, BeforeValidator

def clamp_01(v: float) -> float:
    return max(0.0, min(1.0, v))

def ensure_lowercase(v: str) -> str:
    return v.lower()

ClampedFloat = Annotated[float, AfterValidator(clamp_01)]
LowerStr = Annotated[str, AfterValidator(ensure_lowercase)]

class Config(BaseModel):
    name: LowerStr
    dropout: ClampedFloat

cfg = Config(name="MyModel", dropout=1.5)
print(cfg.name)     # mymodel
print(cfg.dropout)  # 1.0  (clamped)

BeforeValidator, AfterValidator, and PlainValidator map to validator modes. Pydantic also ships annotated constraint helpers (conint, constr, or Annotated[int, Field(gt=0)]).

Custom Types via __get_pydantic_core_schema__

from typing import Any
from pydantic import GetCoreSchemaHandler
from pydantic_core import CoreSchema, core_schema

class Probability:
    """Enforces 0 <= value <= 1."""
    def __init__(self, value: float):
        if not 0 <= value <= 1:
            raise ValueError(f"Probability must be in [0, 1], got {value}")
        self.value = value

    @classmethod
    def __get_pydantic_core_schema__(cls, source: Any, handler: GetCoreSchemaHandler) -> CoreSchema:
        return core_schema.no_info_after_validator_function(
            cls,
            core_schema.float_schema(ge=0, le=1),
            serialization=core_schema.plain_serializer_function_ser_schema(lambda v: v.value),
        )
•

6. Computed Fields & model_post_init

Computed Fields

@computed_field exposes a derived property in the serialized output.

from pydantic import BaseModel, computed_field

class TrainingRun(BaseModel):
    train_loss: float
    val_loss: float

    @computed_field
    @property
    def gap(self) -> float:
        return round(self.val_loss - self.train_loss, 4)

    @computed_field
    @property
    def is_overfitting(self) -> bool:
        return (self.val_loss - self.train_loss) > 0.5

run = TrainingRun(train_loss=0.1, val_loss=0.8)
print(run.model_dump())   # {'train_loss': 0.1, 'val_loss': 0.8, 'gap': 0.7, 'is_overfitting': True}

model_post_init

Runs after __init__ — for derived state and side effects (no extra validation).

from pydantic import BaseModel

class Pipeline(BaseModel):
    steps: list[str]
    _compiled: bool = False        # private attr (leading underscore), not validated

    def model_post_init(self, __context):
        if "normalize" in self.steps and "standardize" in self.steps:
            raise ValueError("Cannot use both normalize and standardize")
        object.__setattr__(self, "_compiled", True)
•

7. ConfigDict

model_config = ConfigDict(...) replaces v1's inner class Config.

from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict

class StrictModel(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(
        strict=True,               # no coercion: int won't accept "5"
        frozen=True,               # immutable + hashable after creation
        extra="forbid",            # reject unknown fields ("ignore" / "allow" also valid)
        str_strip_whitespace=True, # trim string fields
        validate_default=True,     # validate default values too
        populate_by_name=True,     # accept both field name and alias on input
        use_enum_values=True,      # store enum .value instead of the member
        from_attributes=True,      # read from object attributes (ORM mode)
        validate_assignment=True,  # re-validate when a field is set after init
        arbitrary_types_allowed=True,  # permit non-pydantic types (e.g., np.ndarray)
        ser_json_timedelta="float",    # serialize timedeltas as float seconds (vs "iso8601")
    )
    name: str
    value: int
OptionEffect
strictdisables type coercion
frozenmakes instances immutable & hashable
extra"ignore" (default), "forbid", or "allow" unknown fields
from_attributespopulate from object attributes (ORM/dataclass instances)
populate_by_nameaccept field name and alias as input
use_enum_valuesserialize enums as their underlying value
str_strip_whitespacestrip whitespace from string fields
arbitrary_types_allowedpermit non-pydantic types (e.g., np.ndarray)
•

8. Serialization & Parsing

Dumping (Serialization)

exp = Experiment(name="run1", learning_rate=0.01)

exp.model_dump()                      # -> dict
exp.model_dump(mode="json")           # -> dict with JSON-safe values (datetime -> str)
exp.model_dump_json()                 # -> JSON string
exp.model_dump(exclude={"tags"})      # drop fields
exp.model_dump(include={"name"})      # keep only these
exp.model_dump(exclude_unset=True)    # only fields the user explicitly set
exp.model_dump(exclude_none=True)     # drop None values
exp.model_dump(by_alias=True)         # use serialization aliases

Parsing (Validation)

data = {"name": "run1", "learning_rate": 0.01}
Experiment.model_validate(data)                      # from dict (was parse_obj)
Experiment.model_validate_json('{"name": "run1", "learning_rate": 0.01}')  # from JSON (was parse_raw)
Experiment.model_validate(obj, from_attributes=True) # from an ORM/attrs object

Custom Serializers

from pydantic import BaseModel, field_serializer, model_serializer, ConfigDict

class Embedding(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(arbitrary_types_allowed=True)
    vector: list[float]

    @field_serializer("vector")
    def serialize_vector(self, v: list[float], _info) -> list:
        return [round(x, 6) for x in v]

class CompactModel(BaseModel):
    name: str
    scores: list[float]

    @model_serializer
    def custom(self) -> dict:
        return {"n": self.name, "s": [round(s, 2) for s in self.scores]}
•

9. Generic & Discriminated-Union Models

Generic Models

from pydantic import BaseModel
from typing import TypeVar, Generic

T = TypeVar("T")

class APIResponse(BaseModel, Generic[T]):
    status: int
    data: T
    message: str = "ok"

class Prediction(BaseModel):
    label: str
    score: float

resp = APIResponse[Prediction](status=200, data=Prediction(label="cat", score=0.95))
batch = APIResponse[list[Prediction]](status=200, data=[Prediction(label="cat", score=0.9)])
print(resp.model_dump())

Discriminated Unions

A discriminator field selects which model in a Union to build — O(1) dispatch, clearer errors, and correct oneOf OpenAPI schema (vs trying each model in turn).

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from typing import Literal, Union, Annotated

class CNNConfig(BaseModel):
    arch: Literal["cnn"]
    num_filters: int = 64

class TransformerConfig(BaseModel):
    arch: Literal["transformer"]
    num_heads: int = 8
    d_model: int = 512

ModelConfig = Annotated[Union[CNNConfig, TransformerConfig], Field(discriminator="arch")]

class Experiment(BaseModel):
    name: str
    model: ModelConfig

exp = Experiment(name="t", model={"arch": "transformer", "num_heads": 12, "d_model": 768})
print(type(exp.model).__name__)   # TransformerConfig
•

10. Settings Management

pydantic-settings loads typed configuration from environment variables, .env files, and defaults.

# pip install pydantic-settings
from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsConfigDict
from typing import Optional

class MLSettings(BaseSettings):
    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(
        env_file=".env",
        env_file_encoding="utf-8",
        env_prefix="ML_",            # reads ML_MODEL_NAME, ML_BATCH_SIZE, ...
        env_nested_delimiter="__",   # ML_DB__HOST -> db.host
        case_sensitive=False,
    )
    model_name: str = "bert-base-uncased"
    batch_size: int = 32
    learning_rate: float = 3e-5
    wandb_api_key: Optional[str] = None

settings = MLSettings()   # auto-loads from env + .env

Resolution Priority (highest → lowest)

  1. Arguments to the constructor — MLSettings(batch_size=8)
  2. Environment variables (with optional env_prefix)
  3. .env file values
  4. Field defaults

Nested Settings

from pydantic import BaseModel
from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsConfigDict

class DatabaseConfig(BaseModel):
    host: str = "localhost"
    port: int = 5432

class AppSettings(BaseSettings):
    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(env_nested_delimiter="__")
    db: DatabaseConfig = DatabaseConfig()
    debug: bool = False

# Override via: APP env vars  ->  DB__HOST=10.0.0.1  DB__PORT=5433

Supports secrets from files via secrets_dir, and fully custom sources via settings_customise_sources.

•

11. v1 → v2 Migration

Pydantic v2 rewrote the validation core in Rust (pydantic-core), delivering ~5–50x speedups along with API changes.

Pydantic v1Pydantic v2
@validator@field_validator (with @classmethod)
@root_validator@model_validator(mode="before" \| "after")
inner class Configmodel_config = ConfigDict(...)
.dict().model_dump()
.json().model_dump_json()
.parse_obj().model_validate()
.parse_raw().model_validate_json()
Config.orm_mode = Truemodel_config = ConfigDict(from_attributes=True)
Config.allow_population_by_field_namepopulate_by_name=True
__fields__model_fields
Field(..., regex=...)Field(..., pattern=...)
copy()model_copy()

Other v2 notables: strict mode (strict=True disables coercion), computed_field, annotated validators (BeforeValidator/AfterValidator), and discriminated unions via Field(discriminator=...).

# v1
class M(BaseModel):
    name: str
    class Config:
        orm_mode = True
    @validator("name")
    def upper(cls, v): return v.upper()

# v2
class M(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(from_attributes=True)
    name: str
    @field_validator("name")
    @classmethod
    def upper(cls, v): return v.upper()
•

12. Comparison: dataclasses / attrs / msgspec

StdlibValidationPerformanceJSON serializationCoercionSchema generation
FeaturedataclassesPydantic v2attrsmsgspec
StdlibYesNoNoNo
ValidationNoneRichValidatorsConstraints
PerformanceFastGood (Rust core)FastFastest
JSON serializationManualBuilt-invia cattrsBuilt-in
CoercionNoYesConvertersNo
Schema generationNoJSON SchemaNoJSON Schema
Settings from envNopydantic-settingsNoNo
Best forSimple DTOsAPIs, configsLib internalsHigh-perf serde

attrs

import attr

@attr.define(frozen=True, slots=True)
class FeatureSpec:
    name: str
    dtype: str = attr.field(validator=attr.validators.in_(["float32", "int64", "string"]))
    dim: int = attr.field(validator=attr.validators.gt(0))
    nullable: bool = False

p1 = FeatureSpec(name="x", dtype="float32", dim=8)
# immutable update:
import attr as _a
# p2 = _a.evolve(p1, dim=16)

attrs also supports converters (coerce on assignment), evolve (immutable update), and per-attribute validators via the @<field>.validator decorator:

import attr

@attr.define
class Point:
    x: float = attr.field(converter=float)     # "1" -> 1.0 on construction
    y: float = attr.field(converter=float)
    label: str = "unknown"

    @x.validator
    def _check_x(self, attribute, value):
        if value < 0:
            raise ValueError("x must be non-negative")

p1 = Point(x="1", y=2)            # converters coerce -> Point(x=1.0, y=2.0)
p2 = attr.evolve(p1, x=10)        # immutable-style update -> new instance

msgspec (fastest)

import msgspec
from msgspec import Struct, field

class ModelConfig(Struct, frozen=True, gc=False):    # gc=False: skip cyclic GC, faster
    name: str
    layers: int = field(default=12, ge=1)
    dropout: float = field(default=0.1, ge=0.0, le=1.0)

cfg = ModelConfig(name="bert")
data = msgspec.json.encode(cfg)                       # bytes, extremely fast
cfg2 = msgspec.json.decode(data, type=ModelConfig)    # validated decode
packed = msgspec.msgpack.encode(cfg)                  # binary, even faster

msgspec Tagged Unions (Struct discriminator)

msgspec discriminates a Union by a tag field — its equivalent of Pydantic's discriminated union:

import msgspec
from typing import Union

class LinearLayer(msgspec.Struct, tag="linear"):
    in_features: int
    out_features: int

class Conv2dLayer(msgspec.Struct, tag="conv2d"):
    in_channels: int
    out_channels: int
    kernel_size: int = 3

Layer = Union[LinearLayer, Conv2dLayer]

data = b'{"type":"conv2d","in_channels":3,"out_channels":64}'
layer = msgspec.json.decode(data, type=Layer)   # -> Conv2dLayer (dispatched by "type")

Performance Benchmark (approximate, 1M roundtrips)

Library         Create    Validate    JSON Encode    JSON Decode
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
dataclasses     1x        N/A         N/A            N/A
msgspec         1.2x      1x          1x             1x
attrs           1.5x      2x          3x (cattrs)    3x (cattrs)
Pydantic v2     3x        3x          2x             2x
Pydantic v1     15x       15x         8x             8x

Guidance: use dataclasses for trivial internal DTOs; attrs for library internals needing lean validation without schema overhead; msgspec for high-throughput pipelines/brokers; Pydantic for API layers, configs, and anywhere you need JSON Schema/OpenAPI and rich coercion.

•

13. FastAPI Integration

FastAPI uses Pydantic models for request validation, response serialization, and OpenAPI schema generation.

Request / Response Models

from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

app = FastAPI()

class PredictRequest(BaseModel):
    text: str = Field(min_length=1, max_length=10000)
    top_k: int = Field(default=5, ge=1, le=100)
    temperature: float = Field(default=1.0, gt=0, le=2.0)

class PredictionResult(BaseModel):
    label: str
    score: float = Field(ge=0, le=1)

class PredictResponse(BaseModel):
    predictions: list[PredictionResult]
    latency_ms: float

@app.post("/predict", response_model=PredictResponse)
async def predict(req: PredictRequest):          # body validated against PredictRequest
    results = run_inference(req.text, req.top_k)
    return PredictResponse(predictions=results, latency_ms=12.3)

Settings as a Dependency

from functools import lru_cache
from fastapi import Depends
from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsConfigDict

class AppSettings(BaseSettings):
    model_path: str = "./models/bert"
    api_key: str
    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(env_file=".env")

@lru_cache
def get_settings() -> AppSettings:
    return AppSettings()

@app.get("/info")
async def info(settings: AppSettings = Depends(get_settings)):
    return {"model_path": settings.model_path}

Nested Models & Enums in a Request

An endpoint body can nest models and use a str-Enum for a constrained field; FastAPI validates the whole tree and documents the enum's allowed values in OpenAPI:

from enum import Enum
from typing import Optional

class TaskType(str, Enum):
    classification = "classification"
    regression = "regression"
    generation = "generation"

class DatasetConfig(BaseModel):
    path: str
    split: str = "train"
    max_samples: Optional[int] = None

class TrainRequest(BaseModel):
    task: TaskType
    dataset: DatasetConfig
    hyperparams: dict[str, float] = {}

@app.post("/train")
async def train(req: TrainRequest):
    # req.task is a TaskType member; req.dataset.path / req.dataset.split are typed
    ...

Returning ORM Objects

Set from_attributes=True so a response model can read SQLAlchemy/ORM instance attributes directly:

class ItemResponse(BaseModel):
    id: int
    name: str
    model_config = {"from_attributes": True}
•

14. Practical Examples

Hierarchical ML Experiment Config

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, model_validator
from typing import Literal, Optional
from pathlib import Path

class DataConfig(BaseModel):
    train_path: Path
    val_path: Path
    max_seq_length: int = Field(default=512, ge=16, le=8192)
    batch_size: int = Field(default=32, ge=1)

    @model_validator(mode="after")
    def check_paths_exist(self):
        for p in (self.train_path, self.val_path):
            if not p.exists():
                raise ValueError(f"path does not exist: {p}")
        return self

class ModelConfig(BaseModel):
    arch: Literal["bert", "roberta", "gpt2", "t5"]
    pretrained: str = "bert-base-uncased"
    num_labels: int = Field(ge=2)
    hidden_dropout: float = Field(default=0.1, ge=0, le=0.9)
    attention_dropout: float = Field(default=0.1, ge=0, le=0.9)

class TrainerConfig(BaseModel):
    optimizer: Literal["adam", "adamw", "sgd"] = "adamw"
    lr: float = Field(default=3e-5, gt=0)
    weight_decay: float = Field(default=0.01, ge=0)
    epochs: int = Field(default=3, ge=1)
    warmup_ratio: float = Field(default=0.1, ge=0, le=1)
    fp16: bool = True
    gradient_accumulation_steps: int = Field(default=1, ge=1)
    max_grad_norm: float = Field(default=1.0, gt=0)

class ExperimentConfig(BaseModel):
    name: str = Field(min_length=1, max_length=100)
    data: DataConfig
    model: ModelConfig
    trainer: TrainerConfig
    seed: int = 42
    output_dir: Path = Path("./outputs")

    def model_post_init(self, __context):
        self.output_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

# Load and validate from JSON/YAML, failing fast with all errors aggregated:
# config = ExperimentConfig.model_validate_json(Path("experiment.json").read_text())
# config = ExperimentConfig.model_validate(yaml.safe_load(Path("experiment.yaml").read_text()))

Feature Schema with Cross-Field Validation

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, model_validator
from typing import Literal, Any

class FeatureSchema(BaseModel):
    name: str = Field(pattern=r"^[a-z][a-z0-9_]*$")
    dtype: Literal["float32", "int64", "string", "bool", "category"]
    min_val: float | None = None
    max_val: float | None = None
    allowed_values: list[Any] | None = None

    @model_validator(mode="after")
    def validate_constraints(self):
        if self.min_val is not None and self.max_val is not None and self.min_val >= self.max_val:
            raise ValueError("min_val must be < max_val")
        if self.allowed_values and self.dtype != "category":
            raise ValueError("allowed_values only valid for category dtype")
        return self

class DatasetSchema(BaseModel):
    name: str
    version: str = "1.0"
    features: list[FeatureSchema]
    target: str   # must name one of the features

    @model_validator(mode="after")
    def target_exists(self):
        names = {f.name for f in self.features}
        if self.target not in names:
            raise ValueError(f"target '{self.target}' not in features: {names}")
        return self

Batch Inference Schema with UUID & Computed Field

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, computed_field
from uuid import UUID, uuid4

class InferenceItem(BaseModel):
    id: UUID = Field(default_factory=uuid4)
    text: str = Field(min_length=1)
    metadata: dict[str, str] = {}

class BatchRequest(BaseModel):
    items: list[InferenceItem] = Field(min_length=1, max_length=256)
    model_version: str = "latest"

    @computed_field
    @property
    def batch_size(self) -> int:
        return len(self.items)

15. Quick Reference Cheat Sheet

DEFINE                                VALIDATE / TRANSFORM
class M(BaseModel): ...               @field_validator("x")  one field
field: int = Field(ge=0)              @field_validator("x", mode="before")
field: list = Field(default_factory=list)  @model_validator(mode="after")   cross-field
field: int = Field(alias="X")         @model_validator(mode="before")  reshape input
                                      Annotated[int, AfterValidator(fn)]

PARSE                                 SERIALIZE
M.model_validate(dict)                m.model_dump()              -> dict
M.model_validate_json(json_str)       m.model_dump(mode="json")   -> JSON-safe dict
M(**kwargs)                           m.model_dump_json()         -> JSON string
M.model_validate(obj,                 m.model_dump(exclude_unset=True)
   from_attributes=True)              m.model_dump(by_alias=True)

CONFIG (ConfigDict)                   v1 -> v2 RENAMES
strict=True       no coercion         @validator      -> @field_validator
frozen=True       immutable           @root_validator -> @model_validator
extra="forbid"    reject unknown      .dict()         -> .model_dump()
from_attributes=True  ORM mode        .json()         -> .model_dump_json()
populate_by_name=True alias+name      .parse_obj()    -> .model_validate()
use_enum_values=True  enum -> value   orm_mode        -> from_attributes

EXTRAS
@computed_field @property  derived field in output
Field(discriminator="kind")  discriminated union
BaseModel, Generic[T]        generic model
pydantic-settings BaseSettings   env / .env config

14 — Pydantic & Data Validation in Python

Pro-level reference for ML engineers — Pydantic v2, attrs, msgspec, FastAPI integration, and practical patterns.

1. Pydantic v2 Fundamentals
•

1.1 BaseModel Basics

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from typing import Optional
from datetime import datetime

class Experiment(BaseModel):
    name: str
    learning_rate: float = Field(gt=0, le=1.0, description="LR for optimizer")
    epochs: int = Field(default=10, ge=1)
    tags: list[str] = Field(default_factory=list)
    created_at: datetime = Field(default_factory=datetime.now)
    description: Optional[str] = None

exp = Experiment(name="bert-finetune", learning_rate=0.001)
print(exp.model_dump())        # dict output
print(exp.model_dump_json())   # JSON string
print(exp.model_fields)        # field metadata
•

1.2 Field — Constraints and Metadata

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

class FeatureConfig(BaseModel):
    name: str = Field(min_length=1, max_length=100, pattern=r"^[a-z_]+$")
    dim: int = Field(ge=1, le=4096, alias="dimension")
    dropout: float = Field(ge=0.0, le=1.0, default=0.1)
    values: list[float] = Field(min_length=1, max_length=10000)

# Using alias
cfg = FeatureConfig(name="embedding", dimension=768, values=[1.0, 2.0])
print(cfg.model_dump(by_alias=True))  # {"name": ..., "dimension": 768, ...}
•

1.3 field_validator

from pydantic import BaseModel, field_validator

class TrainingConfig(BaseModel):
    model_name: str
    batch_size: int
    learning_rate: float
    gpus: list[int]

    @field_validator("model_name")
    @classmethod
    def validate_model_name(cls, v: str) -> str:
        allowed = {"bert", "gpt2", "t5", "llama"}
        if v.lower() not in allowed:
            raise ValueError(f"Model must be one of {allowed}")
        return v.lower()

    @field_validator("batch_size")
    @classmethod
    def must_be_power_of_two(cls, v: int) -> int:
        if v & (v - 1) != 0:
            raise ValueError("batch_size must be a power of 2")
        return v

    @field_validator("gpus", mode="before")
    @classmethod
    def parse_gpus(cls, v):
        """Accept comma-separated string or list."""
        if isinstance(v, str):
            return [int(x.strip()) for x in v.split(",")]
        return v
•

1.4 model_validator

from pydantic import BaseModel, model_validator

class OptimizerConfig(BaseModel):
    optimizer: str
    learning_rate: float
    weight_decay: float = 0.0
    warmup_steps: int = 0
    total_steps: int = 1000

    @model_validator(mode="after")
    def check_warmup(self):
        if self.warmup_steps >= self.total_steps:
            raise ValueError("warmup_steps must be < total_steps")
        if self.optimizer == "sgd" and self.weight_decay > 0:
            raise ValueError("SGD with weight_decay is unusual — use AdamW")
        return self

    @model_validator(mode="before")
    @classmethod
    def normalize_keys(cls, data: dict):
        """Accept snake_case or camelCase keys."""
        mapping = {"learningRate": "learning_rate", "weightDecay": "weight_decay"}
        return {mapping.get(k, k): v for k, v in data.items()}

        strict=True,              # no coercion: int won't accept "5"
        frozen=True,              # immutable after creation
        extra="forbid",           # reject unknown fields
        str_strip_whitespace=True,
        validate_default=True,
        populate_by_name=True,    # accept both field name and alias
        use_enum_values=True,     # store enum value, not enum member
        ser_json_timedelta="float",
    )
    name: str
    value: int

1.6 model_post_init

from pydantic import BaseModel

class Pipeline(BaseModel):
    steps: list[str]
    _compiled: bool = False  # private attribute (not validated)

    def model_post_init(self, __context):
        """Called after __init__ — useful for derived state."""
        if "normalize" in self.steps and "standardize" in self.steps:
            raise ValueError("Cannot use both normalize and standardize")
        object.__setattr__(self, "_compiled", True)
2. Pydantic v2 Advanced
•

2.1 Generic Models

from pydantic import BaseModel
from typing import TypeVar, Generic

T = TypeVar("T")

class APIResponse(BaseModel, Generic[T]):
    status: int
    data: T
    message: str = "ok"

class Prediction(BaseModel):
    label: str
    score: float

# Concrete usage
response = APIResponse[Prediction](
    status=200,
    data=Prediction(label="cat", score=0.95)
)
print(response.model_dump())

# Works with lists too
batch = APIResponse[list[Prediction]](
    status=200,
    data=[Prediction(label="cat", score=0.95), Prediction(label="dog", score=0.05)]
)

2.2 Discriminated Unions

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from typing import Literal, Union, Annotated

class CNNConfig(BaseModel):
    arch: Literal["cnn"]
    num_filters: int = 64
    kernel_size: int = 3

class TransformerConfig(BaseModel):
    arch: Literal["transformer"]
    num_heads: int = 8
    d_model: int = 512

# Discriminated union — Pydantic uses 'arch' to pick the right model
ModelConfig = Annotated[
    Union[CNNConfig, TransformerConfig],
    Field(discriminator="arch")
]

class Experiment(BaseModel):
    name: str
    model: ModelConfig

# Automatically parses to the correct subtype
exp = Experiment(name="test", model={"arch": "transformer", "num_heads": 12, "d_model": 768})
print(type(exp.model))  # <class 'TransformerConfig'>
•

2.3 Custom Types

from pydantic import GetCoreSchemaHandler
from pydantic_core import CoreSchema, core_schema
from typing import Any

class Probability:
    """Custom type that enforces 0 <= value <= 1."""
    def __init__(self, value: float):
        if not 0 <= value <= 1:
            raise ValueError(f"Probability must be in [0, 1], got {value}")
        self.value = value

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"Probability({self.value})"

    @classmethod
    def __get_pydantic_core_schema__(
        cls, source_type: Any, handler: GetCoreSchemaHandler
    ) -> CoreSchema:
        return core_schema.no_info_after_validator_function(
            cls,
            core_schema.float_schema(ge=0, le=1),
            serialization=core_schema.plain_serializer_function_ser_schema(
                lambda v: v.value
            ),
        )

2.4 Computed Fields

from pydantic import BaseModel, computed_field

class TrainingRun(BaseModel):
    train_loss: float
    val_loss: float
    train_acc: float
    val_acc: float

    @computed_field
    @property
    def is_overfitting(self) -> bool:
        return (self.val_loss - self.train_loss) > 0.5

    @computed_field
    @property
    def gap(self) -> float:
        return round(self.val_loss - self.train_loss, 4)

run = TrainingRun(train_loss=0.1, val_loss=0.8, train_acc=0.95, val_acc=0.7)
print(run.model_dump())  # includes is_overfitting=True, gap=0.7

2.5 Annotated Validators

from typing import Annotated
from pydantic import BaseModel, BeforeValidator, AfterValidator, PlainValidator

def clamp_01(v: float) -> float:
    return max(0.0, min(1.0, v))

def ensure_lowercase(v: str) -> str:
    return v.lower()

ClampedFloat = Annotated[float, AfterValidator(clamp_01)]
LowerStr = Annotated[str, AfterValidator(ensure_lowercase)]

class Config(BaseModel):
    name: LowerStr
    dropout: ClampedFloat

cfg = Config(name="MyModel", dropout=1.5)
print(cfg.name)     # "mymodel"
print(cfg.dropout)  # 1.0 (clamped)
•

2.6 JSON Serialization Control

from pydantic import BaseModel, field_serializer, model_serializer
import numpy as np

class Embedding(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(arbitrary_types_allowed=True)
    vector: list[float]
    metadata: dict

    @field_serializer("vector")
    def serialize_vector(self, v: list[float], _info) -> list:
        return [round(x, 6) for x in v]

# model_serializer for full control
class CompactModel(BaseModel):
    name: str
    scores: list[float]

    @model_serializer
    def custom_serialize(self) -> dict:
        return {
            "n": self.name,
            "s": [round(s, 2) for s in self.scores],
        }

4. attrs — Lean Alternative
import attr
from attr import validators

@attr.s(auto_attribs=True, frozen=True, slots=True)
class FeatureSpec:
    name: str = attr.ib(validator=validators.instance_of(str))
    dtype: str = attr.ib(validator=validators.in_(["float32", "int64", "string"]))
    dim: int = attr.ib(validator=[validators.instance_of(int), validators.gt(0)])
    nullable: bool = attr.ib(default=False)

# Modern attrs API (preferred)
@attr.define(frozen=True, slots=True)
class FeatureSpecV2:
    name: str
    dtype: str = attr.field(validator=attr.validators.in_(["float32", "int64", "string"]))
    dim: int = attr.field(validator=attr.validators.gt(0))
    nullable: bool = False

    @name.validator
    def _check_name(self, attribute, value):
        if not value.isidentifier():
            raise ValueError(f"name must be a valid identifier, got {value!r}")
•

attrs vs dataclasses

# dataclasses — stdlib, minimal
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)  # slots requires 3.10+
class Point:
    x: float
    y: float
    label: str = "unknown"

# attrs — richer validation, converters, evolve
@attr.define
class Point:
    x: float = attr.field(converter=float)
    y: float = attr.field(converter=float)
    label: str = "unknown"

# attrs evolve (immutable update)
p1 = Point(x=1, y=2)
p2 = attr.evolve(p1, x=10)  # Point(x=10, y=2, label="unknown")
5. msgspec — Fastest Validation
import msgspec
from msgspec import Struct, field
from typing import Optional

class ModelConfig(Struct, frozen=True, gc=False):
    """gc=False: excluded from cyclic GC — faster for simple structs."""
    name: str
    layers: int = field(default=12, ge=1)
    hidden_dim: int = field(default=768, ge=1)
    dropout: float = field(default=0.1, ge=0.0, le=1.0)
    vocab_size: int = 30522
    tags: tuple[str, ...] = ()

# JSON encode/decode — extremely fast
encoder = msgspec.json.Encoder()
decoder = msgspec.json.Decoder(ModelConfig)

cfg = ModelConfig(name="bert")
data = encoder.encode(cfg)       # bytes
cfg2 = decoder.decode(data)      # ModelConfig

# msgpack (binary, even faster)
packed = msgspec.msgpack.encode(cfg)
unpacked = msgspec.msgpack.decode(packed, type=ModelConfig)

Struct Inheritance and Tagged Unions

import msgspec
from typing import Union

class LinearLayer(msgspec.Struct, tag="linear"):
    in_features: int
    out_features: int

class Conv2dLayer(msgspec.Struct, tag="conv2d"):
    in_channels: int
    out_channels: int
    kernel_size: int = 3

Layer = Union[LinearLayer, Conv2dLayer]

# Auto-discriminates by "type" field
data = b'{"type":"conv2d","in_channels":3,"out_channels":64}'
layer = msgspec.json.decode(data, type=Layer)
print(type(layer))  # Conv2dLayer

8.1 ML Experiment Config Validation

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, model_validator
from typing import Literal, Optional
from pathlib import Path

class DataConfig(BaseModel):
    train_path: Path
    val_path: Path
    test_path: Optional[Path] = None
    max_seq_length: int = Field(default=512, ge=16, le=8192)
    batch_size: int = Field(default=32, ge=1)
    num_workers: int = Field(default=4, ge=0)

    @model_validator(mode="after")
    def check_paths_exist(self):
        if not self.train_path.exists():
            raise ValueError(f"train_path does not exist: {self.train_path}")
        if not self.val_path.exists():
            raise ValueError(f"val_path does not exist: {self.val_path}")
        return self

class ModelConfig(BaseModel):
    arch: Literal["bert", "roberta", "gpt2", "t5"]
    pretrained: str = "bert-base-uncased"
    num_labels: int = Field(ge=2)
    hidden_dropout: float = Field(default=0.1, ge=0, le=0.9)
    attention_dropout: float = Field(default=0.1, ge=0, le=0.9)

class TrainerConfig(BaseModel):
    optimizer: Literal["adam", "adamw", "sgd"] = "adamw"
    lr: float = Field(default=3e-5, gt=0)
    weight_decay: float = Field(default=0.01, ge=0)
    epochs: int = Field(default=3, ge=1)
    warmup_ratio: float = Field(default=0.1, ge=0, le=1)
    fp16: bool = True
    gradient_accumulation_steps: int = Field(default=1, ge=1)
    max_grad_norm: float = Field(default=1.0, gt=0)

class ExperimentConfig(BaseModel):
    """Top-level config — compose sub-configs."""
    name: str = Field(min_length=1, max_length=100)
    data: DataConfig
    model: ModelConfig
    trainer: TrainerConfig
    seed: int = 42
    output_dir: Path = Path("./outputs")

    def model_post_init(self, __context):
        self.output_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

# Load from YAML/JSON
import json
with open("experiment.json") as f:
    config = ExperimentConfig.model_validate_json(f.read())
•

8.2 Feature Schema for Data Pipelines

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from typing import Literal, Any

class FeatureSchema(BaseModel):
    name: str = Field(pattern=r"^[a-z][a-z0-9_]*$")
    dtype: Literal["float32", "float64", "int64", "string", "bool", "category"]
    nullable: bool = False
    default: Any = None
    min_val: float | None = None
    max_val: float | None = None
    allowed_values: list[Any] | None = None
    description: str = ""

    @model_validator(mode="after")
    def validate_constraints(self):
        if self.min_val is not None and self.max_val is not None:
            if self.min_val >= self.max_val:
                raise ValueError("min_val must be < max_val")
        if self.allowed_values and self.dtype != "category":
            raise ValueError("allowed_values only valid for category dtype")
        return self

class DatasetSchema(BaseModel):
    name: str
    version: str = "1.0"
    features: list[FeatureSchema]
    target: str  # must be one of the feature names

    @model_validator(mode="after")
    def target_exists(self):
        names = {f.name for f in self.features}
        if self.target not in names:
            raise ValueError(f"target '{self.target}' not in features: {names}")
        return self

9. Interview Questions
•

Q1: What changed from Pydantic v1 to v2, and why?

A: Pydantic v2 rewrote the core validation engine in Rust (pydantic-core), yielding 5–50x speedups. Key API changes: - @validator → @field_validator (with @classmethod) - @root_validator → @model_validator(mode="before"|"after") - Config inner class → model_config = ConfigDict(...) - .dict() → .model_dump(), .json() → .model_dump_json() - .parse_obj() → .model_validate(), .parse_raw() → .model_validate_json() - Strict mode added (strict=True prevents coercion) - computed_field added for serialized properties

•

Q2: When would you choose attrs or msgspec over Pydantic?

attrsmsgspecPydantic

A: - attrs: Best for library internals where you need lean, fast classes with optional validation. No JSON schema overhead. Pairs with cattrs for serialization. Preferred when you don't need API schema generation. - msgspec: Best for high-throughput data pipelines, message brokers, or real-time systems. 2–10x faster than Pydantic for JSON/msgpack encoding. Choose it when validation is needed but FastAPI integration is not. - Pydantic: Best for API layers (FastAPI), config management, and anywhere you need JSON Schema, OpenAPI docs, or rich coercion.

•

Q3: How do discriminated unions work in Pydantic, and why use them?

A: Discriminated unions use a literal field (the discriminator) to determine which model in a Union to instantiate. Instead of trying each model until one validates (slow, ambiguous errors), Pydantic reads the discriminator field first and directly validates against the matching model.

ModelConfig = Annotated[Union[CNNConfig, TransformerConfig], Field(discriminator="arch")]

Benefits: O(1) dispatch instead of O(n), clearer error messages, correct OpenAPI schema generation with oneOf.

•

Q4: How does pydantic-settings resolve configuration values?

A: Priority order (highest to lowest): 1. Arguments passed to the constructor (Settings(debug=True)) 2. Environment variables (optionally with env_prefix) 3. .env file values 4. Field defaults in the model

Supports nested settings with env_nested_delimiter (e.g., APP__DB__HOST), secrets from files (secrets_dir), and custom sources via settings_customise_sources.

•

Q5: How would you validate a complex ML training config at startup?

A: Use a hierarchical Pydantic model: 1. Define sub-configs (DataConfig, ModelConfig, TrainerConfig) with typed fields and constraints (Field(ge=0, le=1)) 2. Compose them into an ExperimentConfig parent model 3. Use model_validator(mode="after") for cross-field validation (e.g., warmup_steps < total_steps) 4. Use model_post_init for side effects (creating directories, logging) 5. Load from YAML/JSON with ExperimentConfig.model_validate(yaml.safe_load(f)) 6. Fail fast at startup — if validation fails, Pydantic raises ValidationError with all errors aggregated, preventing silent misconfigurations during long training runs.

Backend Web Development Concepts

Rate Limiting vs Throttling
•

Rate Limiting

DefinitionPurposeImplementationTypes

Definition: Control mechanism that restricts the number of requests a client can make within a specific time window.

Purpose: - Prevent abuse and DDoS attacks - Protect server resources - Ensure fair usage

Implementation:

from fastapi import FastAPI
from slowapi import Limiter
from slowapi.util import get_remote_address

app = FastAPI()
limiter = Limiter(key_func=get_remote_address)

@app.get("/api/data")
@limiter.limit("5/minute")
async def get_data(request: Request):
    return {"data": "example"}

Types: - Token Bucket Algorithm - Sliding Window Counter - Fixed Window Counter

•

Throttling

DefinitionPurposeKey Differences

Definition: Technique to delay or reduce the rate of processing requests to match server capacity.

Purpose: - Graceful degradation - Resource management - Prevent system overload

Key Differences:

FeatureRate LimitingThrottling
ResponseReturns 429 (Too Many Requests)Delays requests
User ExperienceBlocks requestsQueues/delays requests
Use CaseSecurityPerformance
ImplementationPer clientGlobal/queue-based
Hashing vs Encryption
•

Hashing

DefinitionCharacteristicsUse CasesCommon AlgorithmsSecurity Best Practices

Definition: One-way function that converts input data to fixed-size output.

Characteristics: - Irreversible (cannot decrypt) - Deterministic (same input = same output) - Fixed output size - Avalanche effect (tiny change → completely different hash)

Use Cases: - Password storage - Data integrity verification - Checksums

Common Algorithms:

import hashlib

# SHA-256
hash_obj = hashlib.sha256(b"password")
print(hash_obj.hexdigest())

# For passwords: use bcrypt
import bcrypt
hashed = bcrypt.hashpw(b"password", bcrypt.gensalt())
bcrypt.checkpw(b"password", hashed)  # True

Security Best Practices: - Always use salt - Use modern algorithms (SHA-256+, bcrypt, argon2) - Never store plaintext passwords

•

Encryption

DefinitionCharacteristicsTypesSymmetric EncryptionAsymmetric EncryptionUse Cases

Definition: Two-way process that converts plaintext to ciphertext (reversible).

Characteristics: - Reversible (can decrypt with key) - Requires encryption key - Variable output size - Only authorized parties can decrypt

Types: 1. Symmetric Encryption (same key for encryption/decryption)

from cryptography.fernet import Fernet
key = Fernet.generate_key()
f = Fernet(key)
encrypted = f.encrypt(b"secret data")
decrypted = f.decrypt(encrypted)
  1. Asymmetric Encryption (public/private keys)
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives import serialization
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric import rsa

private_key = rsa.generate_private_key(
    public_exponent=65537,
    key_size=2048
)
public_key = private_key.public_key()

Use Cases: - Secure data transmission (HTTPS) - API secrets storage - Database encryption

•

Key Differences:

AspectHashingEncryption
ReversibleNoYes
Use CaseVerificationSecrecy
KeyNo key neededKey required
Output SizeFixedVariable
CORS
•

Definition

Cross-Origin Resource Sharing: Mechanism allowing restricted resources on web pages to be requested from another domain outside the domain from which the resource originated.

•

Problem It Solves

Browser Security Policy:
- Request from: http://frontend.com
- To resource: http://api.com
→ Browser blocks request (different origin)
•

Solution

from fastapi.middleware.cors import CORSMiddleware
from fastapi import FastAPI

app = FastAPI()

app.add_middleware(
    CORSMiddleware,
    allow_origins=["http://localhost:3000", "https://example.com"],
    allow_credentials=True,
    allow_methods=["*"],  # or ["GET", "POST"]
    allow_headers=["*"],
)
•

CORS Headers

Request Headers:
- Origin: http://frontend.com
- Access-Control-Request-Method: POST

Response Headers:
- Access-Control-Allow-Origin: http://frontend.com
- Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET, POST, PUT
- Access-Control-Allow-Headers: Content-Type
- Access-Control-Max-Age: 3600
•

Common Scenarios

Frontend on different domainSame domain (localhost)Public API
  1. Frontend on different domain: Use CORS middleware
  2. Same domain (localhost): May not need CORS
  3. Public API: Use wildcard carefully (allow_origins=["*"])
Middleware
•

Definition

Software component that processes requests before they reach the route handler and responses before they're sent to client.

•

Request/Response Flow

Request → Middleware 1 → Middleware 2 → Route Handler
↓                                              ↓
Response ← Middleware 1 ← Middleware 2 ← Response
•

FastAPI Middleware Examples

1. Custom Middleware2. Logging Middleware3. Authentication Middleware

1. Custom Middleware:

from starlette.middleware.base import BaseHTTPMiddleware
from starlette.requests import Request

class CustomMiddleware(BaseHTTPMiddleware):
    async def dispatch(self, request: Request, call_next):
        # Pre-request processing
        print(f"Incoming request: {request.method} {request.url.path}")
        
        response = await call_next(request)
        
        # Post-response processing
        response.headers["X-Custom-Header"] = "value"
        return response

app.add_middleware(CustomMiddleware)

2. Logging Middleware:

@app.middleware("http")
async def log_requests(request: Request, call_next):
    start_time = time.time()
    response = await call_next(request)
    process_time = time.time() - start_time
    response.headers["X-Process-Time"] = str(process_time)
    return response

3. Authentication Middleware:

@app.middleware("http")
async def auth_middleware(request: Request, call_next):
    token = request.headers.get("Authorization")
    if not token:
        return JSONResponse({"error": "Unauthorized"}, status_code=401)
    response = await call_next(request)
    return response
•

Common Middleware Types

CORS MiddlewareAuthenticationLoggingError HandlingRate LimitingCompression
  • CORS Middleware: Cross-origin requests
  • Authentication: Token validation
  • Logging: Request/response tracking
  • Error Handling: Exception catching
  • Rate Limiting: Request throttling
  • Compression: Response compression (gzip)
Caching
•

Types of Caching

1. HTTP Caching (Browser/CDN)2. Server-Side Caching (Redis)3. Application Caching

1. HTTP Caching (Browser/CDN)

from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.responses import Response

@app.get("/data")
async def get_data():
    return Response(
        content={"data": "example"},
        headers={
            "Cache-Control": "public, max-age=3600",
            "ETag": "123abc",
        }
    )

2. Server-Side Caching (Redis)

import redis
from fastapi import FastAPI

cache = redis.Redis(host='localhost', port=6379, db=0)

@app.get("/data")
async def get_data():
    # Try to get from cache
    cached = cache.get("data_key")
    if cached:
        return json.loads(cached)
    
    # If not cached, compute and store
    data = {"result": "expensive computation"}
    cache.setex("data_key", 3600, json.dumps(data))
    return data

3. Application Caching

from functools import lru_cache

@lru_cache(maxsize=128)
def expensive_function(param):
    # Computation happens only once per unique param
    return param * 2
•

Cache Strategies

Time-To-Live (TTL)InvalidationLRU (Least Recently Used)Write-ThroughWrite-Behind
  • Time-To-Live (TTL): Automatic expiry
  • Invalidation: Manual cache clearing
  • LRU (Least Recently Used): Remove least used entries
  • Write-Through: Update cache and DB simultaneously
  • Write-Behind: Update cache first, then DB
•

Cache Invalidation Problem

# Problem: Stale data
user_cache["user_1"] = {"name": "John", "age": 30}

# User updates age to 31, but cache still has 30
# Solution: Invalidate cache on update
def update_user(user_id, data):
    db.update(user_id, data)
    cache.delete(f"user_{user_id}")  # Invalidate
WebSocket
•

Definition

Protocol providing full-duplex communication over single TCP connection.

•

HTTP vs WebSocket

HTTP (Request-Response):
Client → Request → Server
Client ← Response ← Server
(Connection closes after each response)

WebSocket (Persistent Connection):
Client ↔↔↔↔↔ Server
(Bidirectional, persistent)
•

FastAPI WebSocket Implementation

from fastapi import WebSocket

@app.websocket("/ws/chat/{room_id}")
async def websocket_endpoint(websocket: WebSocket, room_id: str):
    await websocket.accept()
    
    try:
        while True:
            # Receive message from client
            data = await websocket.receive_text()
            
            # Broadcast to all connected clients
            for client in connected_clients:
                await client.send_text(f"Message: {data}")
    
    except Exception as e:
        await websocket.close(code=1000)
•

Use Cases

Real-time chatLive notificationsCollaborative editingLive dashboardsGaming
  • Real-time chat: Low latency messaging
  • Live notifications: Instant updates
  • Collaborative editing: Live document collaboration
  • Live dashboards: Real-time data updates
  • Gaming: Multiplayer synchronization

Performance Considerations

Persistent connectionsScalingFallbacks
  • Persistent connections: More memory per client

When to Use ORM or Not
•

When to Use ORM ✅

AdvantagesGood Scenarios

Advantages: - SQL injection protection (parameterized queries) - Code reusability - Database abstraction - Automatic migrations - Built-in validation - Relationship management

Good Scenarios:

# Simple CRUD operations
from sqlalchemy import create_engine
from sqlalchemy.orm import Session
from app.models import User

def create_user(db: Session, user_data: dict):
    user = User(**user_data)
    db.add(user)
    db.commit()
    return user

# Relationships
class User(Base):
    __tablename__ = "users"
    posts = relationship("Post", back_populates="user")

class Post(Base):
    __tablename__ = "posts"
    user = relationship("User", back_populates="posts")
•

When NOT to Use ORM ❌

DisadvantagesGood Scenarios

Disadvantages: - Performance overhead for complex queries - Less control over SQL - Learning curve - Debugging difficulty

Good Scenarios:

# Complex analytical queries
import psycopg2

conn = psycopg2.connect("dbname=mydb")
cursor = conn.cursor()

# Optimized query with joins, aggregations
cursor.execute("""
    SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) as post_count, AVG(likes) as avg_likes
    FROM posts
    WHERE created_at > NOW() - INTERVAL '30 days'
    GROUP BY user_id
    HAVING COUNT(*) > 10
    ORDER BY post_count DESC
""")

results = cursor.fetchall()
•

Hybrid Approach (Best Practice)

from sqlalchemy import text

class UserService:
    # Use ORM for simple operations
    def get_user(self, user_id: int) -> User:
        return db.query(User).filter(User.id == user_id).first()
    
    # Use raw SQL for complex queries
    def get_user_analytics(self, user_id: int):
        query = text("""
            SELECT u.id, u.name, COUNT(p.id) as posts
            FROM users u
            LEFT JOIN posts p ON u.id = p.user_id
            WHERE u.id = :user_id
            GROUP BY u.id
        """)
        return db.execute(query, {"user_id": user_id}).fetchone()
Async/Await

Concepts

Blocking vs Non-Blocking:

# Blocking (slow)
def get_data():
    response = requests.get("https://api.example.com/data")  # Wait 2 seconds
    return response.json()

# Non-blocking (fast)
async def get_data():
    async with aiohttp.ClientSession() as session:
        async with session.get("https://api.example.com/data") as resp:
            return await resp.json()
