FastAPI with Async

from fastapi import FastAPI
import asyncio

app = FastAPI()

@app.get("/fast")
async def fast_endpoint():
    # Async operation
    await asyncio.sleep(1)
    return {"status": "done"}

@app.get("/parallel")
async def parallel_operations():
    # Execute multiple operations concurrently
    results = await asyncio.gather(
        fetch_user_data(),
        fetch_posts_data(),
        fetch_comments_data()
    )
    return {"user": results[0], "posts": results[1], "comments": results[2]}

async def fetch_user_data():
    await asyncio.sleep(2)
    return {"id": 1, "name": "John"}

async def fetch_posts_data():
    await asyncio.sleep(1)
    return [{"id": 1, "title": "Post 1"}]

async def fetch_comments_data():
    await asyncio.sleep(0.5)
    return [{"id": 1, "text": "Comment 1"}]

Event Loop

import asyncio

Best Practices

  1. Use async def for I/O-bound operations
  2. Use .gather() for concurrent operations
  3. Avoid blocking calls in async functions
  4. Use async libraries (aiohttp, asyncpg, motor)

API Design Scenarios

ProblemSolutionTradeoffsOffsetCursor

Scenario 1: Implementing Pagination for Large Datasets

Problem: Your API endpoint /posts returns 1M posts. Fetching all causes timeout and memory issues.

Solution:

from pydantic import BaseModel

class PaginationParams(BaseModel):
    skip: int = 0
    limit: int = 10
    max_limit: int = 100

@app.get("/posts")
async def list_posts(params: PaginationParams, db: Session):
    # Validate limit
    limit = min(params.limit, params.max_limit)
    
    # Query with pagination
    total = db.query(Post).count()
    posts = db.query(Post).offset(params.skip).limit(limit).all()
    
    return {
        "data": posts,
        "pagination": {
            "skip": params.skip,
            "limit": limit,
            "total": total,
            "has_more": (params.skip + limit) < total
        }
    }

# Alternative: Cursor-based pagination (better for large offsets)
@app.get("/posts/cursor")
async def list_posts_cursor(cursor: Optional[int] = None, limit: int = 10, db: Session = Depends()):
    posts = db.query(Post).filter(Post.id > cursor or True).limit(limit + 1).all()
    
    next_cursor = posts[-1].id if len(posts) > limit else None
    return {
        "data": posts[:limit],
        "next_cursor": next_cursor,
        "has_more": len(posts) > limit
    }

Tradeoffs: - Offset: Simple, but slow for large offsets - Cursor: Fast, but stateful

Scenario 2: Filtering with Multiple Optional Parameters

Problem: Users want to filter posts by status, author, date range, and tags.

Solution:

from typing import Optional, List
from datetime import datetime

class PostFilter(BaseModel):
    status: Optional[str] = None
    author_id: Optional[int] = None
    created_after: Optional[datetime] = None
    created_before: Optional[datetime] = None
    tags: Optional[List[str]] = None
    skip: int = 0
    limit: int = 10

@app.get("/posts/filter")
async def filter_posts(filter_params: PostFilter, db: Session):
    query = db.query(Post)
    
    # Apply filters dynamically
    if filter_params.status:
        query = query.filter(Post.status == filter_params.status)
    
    if filter_params.author_id:
        query = query.filter(Post.author_id == filter_params.author_id)
    
    if filter_params.created_after:
        query = query.filter(Post.created_at >= filter_params.created_after)
    
    if filter_params.created_before:
        query = query.filter(Post.created_at <= filter_params.created_before)
    
    # Tag filtering (many-to-many)
    if filter_params.tags:
        query = query.join(Tag).filter(Tag.name.in_(filter_params.tags))
    
    total = query.count()
    posts = query.offset(filter_params.skip).limit(filter_params.limit).all()
    
    return {
        "data": posts,
        "total": total,
        "skip": filter_params.skip,
        "limit": filter_params.limit
    }

Scenario 3: Versioning API Endpoints

Problem: You need to release a new API version with breaking changes.

Solution:

from fastapi import APIRouter

# Version 1
v1_router = APIRouter(prefix="/api/v1")

@v1_router.get("/users/{user_id}")
async def get_user_v1(user_id: int):
    return {"id": user_id, "name": "John"}

# Version 2 - Breaking change: user_id renamed to id
v2_router = APIRouter(prefix="/api/v2")

@v2_router.get("/users/{user_id}")
async def get_user_v2(user_id: int):
    return {"id": user_id, "name": "John", "email": "john@example.com"}

app.include_router(v1_router)
app.include_router(v2_router)

# Deprecation headers
@app.middleware("http")
async def deprecation_middleware(request: Request, call_next):
    response = await call_next(request)
    
    if "v1" in request.url.path:
        response.headers["Deprecation"] = "true"
        response.headers["Sunset"] = "Sun, 31 Dec 2024 23:59:59 GMT"
        response.headers["Link"] = "</api/v2/users>; rel=\"successor-version\""
    
    return response

Performance Optimization

ProblemBad ImplementationSolution - Eager LoadingSolution

Scenario 1: N+1 Query Problem

Problem: Getting user with all their posts causes N+1 queries.

Bad Implementation:

users = db.query(User).all()  # 1 query
for user in users:
    posts = db.query(Post).filter(Post.user_id == user.id).all()  # N queries
    user.posts = posts
# Total: N+1 queries

Solution - Eager Loading:

# Option 1: joinedload (single JOIN)
users = db.query(User).options(joinedload(User.posts)).all()

# Option 2: selectinload (2 queries, better for large datasets)
users = db.query(User).options(selectinload(User.posts)).all()

# Option 3: Manual join
from sqlalchemy import distinct
users = db.query(distinct(User)).join(Post).all()

Scenario 2: Slow Report Generation

Problem: Generating monthly reports takes 10 minutes and times out.

Solution:

from celery import Celery
from celery.result import AsyncResult

celery_app = Celery('reports', broker='redis://localhost')

@app.post("/reports/monthly")
async def generate_monthly_report(month: str):
    # Queue report generation
    task = generate_report.delay(month)
    return {"task_id": task.id, "status": "queued"}

@app.get("/reports/status/{task_id}")
async def get_report_status(task_id: str):
    result = AsyncResult(task_id)
    return {
        "status": result.status,
        "result": result.result if result.ready() else None
    }

@celery_app.task(bind=True)
def generate_report(self, month: str):
    # Generate report in chunks
    from sqlalchemy import text
    
    query = text("""
        SELECT DATE(created_at) as date, COUNT(*) as count, SUM(amount) as total
        FROM orders
        WHERE EXTRACT(MONTH FROM created_at) = :month
        GROUP BY DATE(created_at)
    """)
    
    results = []
    for row in db.execute(query, {"month": month}):
        results.append(dict(row))
        # Update task progress
        self.update_state(state='PROGRESS', meta={'current': len(results)})
    
    return {"data": results, "count": len(results)}

Scenario 3: Caching Frequently Accessed Data

Problem: Same data queried thousands of times per second.

Solution:

from functools import wraps
import redis
import json
from datetime import timedelta

redis_client = redis.Redis(host='localhost', port=6379, decode_responses=True)

def cache_result(ttl: int = 3600):
    def decorator(func):
        @wraps(func)
        async def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
            # Create cache key
            cache_key = f"{func.__name__}:{args}:{kwargs}"
            
            # Try cache
            cached = redis_client.get(cache_key)
            if cached:
                return json.loads(cached)
            
            # Execute function
            result = await func(*args, **kwargs)
            
            # Cache result
            redis_client.setex(cache_key, ttl, json.dumps(result))
            return result
        
        return wrapper
    return decorator

@cache_result(ttl=3600)
async def get_trending_posts(db: Session):
    return db.query(Post).filter(Post.likes > 100).all()

# Cache invalidation
def invalidate_cache(pattern: str = "*"):
    keys = redis_client.keys(pattern)
    for key in keys:
        redis_client.delete(key)

Error Handling & Recovery

ProblemSolution

Scenario 1: Handling External API Failures

Problem: Your API depends on external payment service that sometimes fails.

Solution - Retry with Exponential Backoff:

from tenacity import retry, stop_after_attempt, wait_exponential
import aiohttp

@retry(
    stop=stop_after_attempt(3),
    wait=wait_exponential(multiplier=1, min=2, max=10)
)
async def call_payment_api(order_id: int, amount: float):
    async with aiohttp.ClientSession() as session:
        async with session.post(
            "https://payment-service.com/charge",
            json={"order_id": order_id, "amount": amount}
        ) as resp:
            if resp.status == 500:
                raise Exception("Payment service error")
            return await resp.json()

@app.post("/pay")
async def process_payment(order_id: int, amount: float):
    try:
        result = await call_payment_api(order_id, amount)
        return {"status": "success", "transaction_id": result["id"]}
    except Exception as e:
        logger.error(f"Payment failed: {e}")
        return {"status": "failed", "error": "Payment processing failed"}

Scenario 2: Graceful Degradation

Problem: Cache goes down, but service should still work.

Solution:

from contextlib import contextmanager

@contextmanager
def get_data_with_fallback(user_id: int, db: Session):
    # Try cache first
    try:
        cached = redis_client.get(f"user:{user_id}")
        if cached:
            yield json.loads(cached)
            return
    except redis.ConnectionError:
        logger.warning("Redis unavailable, using database")
    
    # Fallback to database
    user = db.query(User).filter(User.id == user_id).first()
    yield user

@app.get("/users/{user_id}")
async def get_user(user_id: int, db: Session):
    with get_data_with_fallback(user_id, db) as user:
        if not user:
            raise HTTPException(status_code=404)
        return user

Concurrency Issues

ProblemBad CodeSolution - Database-Level LockSolution

Scenario 1: Race Condition in Stock Update

Problem: Two simultaneous requests try to buy the last item, both succeed.

Bad Code:

@app.post("/buy/{product_id}")
async def buy_product(product_id: int, db: Session):
    product = db.query(Product).filter(Product.id == product_id).first()
    
    if product.stock > 0:  # Check
        product.stock -= 1  # Update (race condition window)
        db.commit()
        return {"status": "success"}
    
    return {"status": "out of stock"}

Solution - Database-Level Lock:

from sqlalchemy import select, update

@app.post("/buy/{product_id}")
async def buy_product(product_id: int, db: Session):
    # Lock row for update
    product = db.query(Product).with_for_update().filter(
        Product.id == product_id
    ).first()
    
    if product.stock > 0:
        product.stock -= 1
        db.commit()
        return {"status": "success"}
    
    return {"status": "out of stock"}

# Or use atomic operation
@app.post("/buy2/{product_id}")
async def buy_product2(product_id: int, db: Session):
    result = db.execute(
        update(Product)
        .where((Product.id == product_id) & (Product.stock > 0))
        .values(stock=Product.stock - 1)
    )
    db.commit()
    
    return {"status": "success" if result.rowcount > 0 else "out of stock"}

Scenario 2: Handling Async Task Ordering

Problem: Task B depends on Task A, but B might execute first.

Solution:

from celery import chain, group

# Sequential task execution
@celery_app.task
def task_a():
    return "Result A"

@celery_app.task
def task_b(result_a):
    return f"Task B got {result_a}"

# Chain ensures order
workflow = chain(task_a.s(), task_b.s())
result = workflow.apply_async()

# Or: Callback approach
@celery_app.task
def process_image(image_id: int):
    # Process image
    process_image_api(image_id)
    
    # Chain next task
    send_notification.delay(image_id)

@celery_app.task
def send_notification(image_id: int):
    # Send notification
    pass

Database Scenarios

ProblemSolution

Scenario 1: Migration with Zero Downtime

Problem: Adding a NOT NULL column to large table blocks writes.

Solution:

# Step 1: Add column as nullable
# Migration 001:
class Migration:
    def upgrade(self):
        op.add_column('users', Column('email', String, nullable=True))

# Step 2: Backfill existing rows (done in background job)
# alembic/versions/002_backfill.py
def upgrade():
    # Backfill in batches to avoid locking
    import time
    batch_size = 1000
    
    conn = op.get_bind()
    while True:
        conn.execute("""
            UPDATE users 
            SET email = CONCAT(id, '@example.com')
            WHERE email IS NULL
            LIMIT :batch_size
        """, batch_size=batch_size)
        
        if conn.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users WHERE email IS NULL").scalar() == 0:
            break
        
        time.sleep(0.1)  # Let database catch up

# Step 3: Add NOT NULL constraint after backfill
# Migration 003:
op.alter_column('users', 'email', nullable=False)

Scenario 2: Detecting Slow Queries

Problem: Some endpoints are slow, but you don't know which queries.

Solution:

from sqlalchemy import event
from sqlalchemy.engine import Engine
import logging
import time

logger = logging.getLogger("slow_queries")

@event.listens_for(Engine, "before_cursor_execute")
def before_cursor_execute(conn, cursor, statement, parameters, context, executemany):
    conn.info.setdefault('query_start_time', []).append(time.time())

@event.listens_for(Engine, "after_cursor_execute")
def after_cursor_execute(conn, cursor, statement, parameters, context, executemany):
    total_time = time.time() - conn.info['query_start_time'].pop(-1)
    
    if total_time > 1.0:  # Log queries slower than 1 second
        logger.warning(f"SLOW QUERY ({total_time:.2f}s): {statement}")

Problem: Redis memory grows indefinitely.

Solution - TTL Management:

# Bad: No expiration
redis_client.set("user:1", json.dumps(user_data))

Security Scenarios

ProblemBad CodeSolution - Parameterized QueriesSolution

Scenario 1: SQL Injection Prevention

Problem: User input directly in SQL string.

Bad Code:

query = f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '{email}'"  # SQL injection!

Solution - Parameterized Queries:

# SQLAlchemy (safe)
user = db.query(User).filter(User.email == email).first()

# Raw SQL with parameters
query = text("SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = :email")
result = db.execute(query, {"email": email})

Scenario 2: JWT Token Expiration

Problem: Tokens never expire, increasing security risk.

Solution:

from datetime import datetime, timedelta
from jose import jwt

SECRET_KEY = "secret"
ALGORITHM = "HS256"
ACCESS_TOKEN_EXPIRE_HOURS = 24

def create_access_token(user_id: int):
    expire = datetime.utcnow() + timedelta(hours=ACCESS_TOKEN_EXPIRE_HOURS)
    payload = {
        "user_id": user_id,
        "exp": expire,  # Expiration time
        "iat": datetime.utcnow(),  # Issued at
    }
    return jwt.encode(payload, SECRET_KEY, algorithm=ALGORITHM)

def verify_token(token: str):
    try:
        payload = jwt.decode(token, SECRET_KEY, algorithms=[ALGORITHM])
        user_id = payload.get("user_id")
        exp = payload.get("exp")
        
        if datetime.fromtimestamp(exp) < datetime.utcnow():
            raise HTTPException(status_code=401, detail="Token expired")
        
        return user_id
    except jwt.ExpiredSignatureError:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=401, detail="Token expired")
    except jwt.InvalidTokenError:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=401, detail="Invalid token")

System Design Challenges

RequirementsSolutionProblem

Scenario 1: Designing Real-Time Notification System

Requirements: - Millions of users - Sub-second latency - Reliable delivery

Solution:

# Use WebSocket + Message Queue
from fastapi import WebSocket, WebSocketDisconnect

class NotificationManager:
    def __init__(self):
        self.active_connections: Dict[int, WebSocket] = {}
        self.message_queue = redis_client.pubsub()
    
    async def connect(self, user_id: int, websocket: WebSocket):
        await websocket.accept()
        self.active_connections[user_id] = websocket
    
    def disconnect(self, user_id: int):
        del self.active_connections[user_id]
    
    async def broadcast(self, message: dict):
        # Publish to Redis (fan-out)
        redis_client.publish("notifications", json.dumps(message))
    
    async def send_personal_notification(self, user_id: int, message: dict):
        if user_id in self.active_connections:
            await self.active_connections[user_id].send_json(message)
        else:
            # Store in queue for offline user
            redis_client.lpush(f"pending_notifications:{user_id}", json.dumps(message))

manager = NotificationManager()

@app.websocket("/ws/notifications/{user_id}")
async def websocket_endpoint(websocket: WebSocket, user_id: int):
    await manager.connect(user_id, websocket)
    try:
        # Listen for messages
        while True:
            message = await websocket.receive_json()
            await manager.broadcast(message)
    except WebSocketDisconnect:
        manager.disconnect(user_id)

Scenario 2: Rate Limiting per User

Problem: Premium users should have higher rate limits than free users.

Solution:

from slowapi import Limiter
from slowapi.util import get_remote_address

limiter = Limiter(key_func=get_remote_address)

def get_user_rate_limit(user_id: int) -> str:
    user = db.query(User).filter(User.id == user_id).first()
    if user.plan == "premium":
        return "1000/hour"
    elif user.plan == "basic":
        return "100/hour"
    else:
        return "10/hour"

@app.get("/api/data")
@limiter.limit("10/minute")
async def get_data(request: Request, db: Session = Depends()):
    user_id = get_current_user(request)
    limit = get_user_rate_limit(user_id)
    
    # Check custom rate limit
    key = f"rate_limit:{user_id}"
    count = redis_client.incr(key)
    redis_client.expire(key, 3600)
    
    if count > parse_limit(limit):
        raise HTTPException(status_code=429, detail="Rate limit exceeded")
    
    return {"data": "example"}

Python Backend System Design45 sections

Python Backend System Design

A backend-focused guide to designing scalable, reliable systems — with a repeatable interview framework, capacity math, distributed-systems trade-offs, and full worked examples implemented with Python (FastAPI, SQLAlchemy, Redis, Celery).

How to Approach a System Design Question

Don't jump to a diagram. Use a repeatable 6-step framework so you never freeze:

  1. REQUIREMENTS → Functional + Non-functional. Pin down scope. Ask questions.
  2. ESTIMATE → Traffic (QPS), storage, bandwidth. Read vs write ratio.
  3. API → Define the contract (endpoints, request/response, errors).
  4. DATA MODEL → Tables/entities, access patterns, which DB type and why.
  5. HIGH-LEVEL → Boxes & arrows: client → LB → API → cache → DB → queue.
  6. DEEP DIVE → Bottlenecks: scaling, sharding, consistency, failure modes.
•

1. Clarify Requirements (always do this first)

FunctionalNon-functionalTip
TypeExamples to ask about
FunctionalWhat operations? Who are the users? What's in/out of scope?
Non-functionalScale (DAU/QPS)? Latency target (p99)? Consistency vs availability? Read/write ratio? Durability?

Tip: State your assumptions out loud ("I'll assume 10M DAU, read-heavy 100:1"). The interviewer corrects you if wrong — that's a signal, not a failure.

•

2. Drive Non-Functional Requirements into the Design

RequirementDesign lever it pushes you toward
Low latency readsCaching (Redis/CDN), read replicas, denormalization
High write throughputSharding, async writes via queue, LSM-tree DBs (Cassandra)
Strong consistencySingle-leader DB, transactions, synchronous replication
High availabilityMulti-region, eventual consistency, graceful degradation
DurabilityReplication factor ≥ 3, WAL, backups
CostCache hit ratio, tiered storage, autoscaling
Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Estimation

Interviewers want to see you reason about scale, not exact numbers.

•

Numbers Every Engineer Should Know

1 thousand   = 10^3   = KB
1 million    = 10^6   = MB
1 billion    = 10^9   = GB
1 trillion   = 10^12  = TB

Latency (orders of magnitude):
  L1 cache ref ........ 0.5 ns
  Main memory ref ..... 100 ns
  SSD random read ..... 100 µs   (150,000 ns)
  Network within DC ... 0.5 ms
  Disk seek ........... 10 ms
  Network US→EU ....... 150 ms
•

Worked Estimate (Twitter-like service)

Assumptions:
  300M DAU, each user posts 2 tweets/day  → 600M writes/day
  Read:write ratio = 100:1                → 60B reads/day

QPS (writes):
  600M / 86,400 s ≈ 7,000 writes/sec  (avg)
  Peak ≈ 2× avg   ≈ 14,000 writes/sec

QPS (reads):
  100 × 7,000 ≈ 700,000 reads/sec (avg)  →  heavily cache this

Storage (5 years):
  Tweet ≈ 300 bytes (text + metadata)
  600M/day × 300 B × 365 × 5 ≈ 330 TB  (text only; media goes to object store/CDN)

Bandwidth:
  Writes: 7,000 × 300 B ≈ 2 MB/s
  Reads:  700,000 × 300 B ≈ 210 MB/s  →  CDN/cache offloads most of this

Takeaways that shape the design: read-heavy → cache aggressively + read replicas; 330 TB → must shard; media → object store + CDN, never in the DB.

# Quick estimation helper you can reason with live
def estimate(dau, actions_per_user_per_day, bytes_per_action, read_write_ratio=100):
    writes_per_day = dau * actions_per_user_per_day
    write_qps = writes_per_day / 86_400
    read_qps = write_qps * read_write_ratio
    daily_storage_gb = (writes_per_day * bytes_per_action) / 1e9
    return {
        "write_qps_avg": round(write_qps),
        "write_qps_peak": round(write_qps * 2),
        "read_qps_avg": round(read_qps),
        "storage_per_year_tb": round(daily_storage_gb * 365 / 1000, 1),
    }

print(estimate(dau=300_000_000, actions_per_user_per_day=2, bytes_per_action=300))
Architecture Patterns
•

Monolith vs Microservices (start here in interviews)

Best whenDeployScalingFailureComplexityData
MonolithMicroservices
Best whenSmall team, early stage, unclear domainMany teams, clear bounded contexts, independent scaling
DeployOne unitPer service
ScalingWhole app togetherScale hot services only
FailureOne bug can take down allIsolated (with bulkheads)
ComplexityLowHigh (network, observability, data consistency)
DataShared DB, easy transactionsDB-per-service, distributed transactions

Default advice: start with a modular monolith, extract microservices only when a clear scaling or team-autonomy reason appears. "Microservices first" is a common anti-pattern.

•

1. Layered Architecture

ImplementationWhy the separation matters
┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
│      Presentation Layer (Routes)        │  ← HTTP, validation (Pydantic)
├─────────────────────────────────────────┤
│      Business Logic Layer (Services)    │  ← pure logic, no framework deps
├─────────────────────────────────────────┤
│      Data Access Layer (Repositories)   │  ← DB queries, isolates ORM
├─────────────────────────────────────────┤
│      Database Layer                     │
└─────────────────────────────────────────┘

Implementation:

# routes.py (Presentation)
from fastapi import APIRouter, Depends

router = APIRouter()

@router.get("/users/{user_id}")
async def get_user(user_id: int, svc: UserService = Depends(get_user_service)):
    return await svc.get_user(user_id)

# services.py (Business Logic) — no FastAPI / SQLAlchemy imports leak in here
class UserService:
    def __init__(self, user_repo: "UserRepository"):
        self.user_repo = user_repo

    async def get_user(self, user_id: int):
        user = await self.user_repo.get_by_id(user_id)
        if not user:
            raise UserNotFoundError()
        return self._format_user(user)

    def _format_user(self, user):
        return {"id": user.id, "name": user.name, "email": user.email}

# repositories.py (Data Access) — the only layer that knows about SQLAlchemy
class UserRepository:
    def __init__(self, db):
        self.db = db

    async def get_by_id(self, user_id: int):
        return self.db.query(User).filter(User.id == user_id).first()

# models.py (Database)
class User(Base):
    __tablename__ = "users"
    id = Column(Integer, primary_key=True)
    name = Column(String)
    email = Column(String, unique=True)

Why the separation matters: you can unit-test UserService with a fake repo (no DB), and swap Postgres → another store by changing only the repository.

•

2. Hexagonal Architecture (Ports & Adapters)

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Driving Adapters (HTTP API, CLI, gRPC)              │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│            Ports (Interfaces / Protocols)            │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│            Core Business Logic (pure Python)         │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│            Ports (Interfaces / Protocols)            │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Driven Adapters (Postgres, Redis, Kafka, Stripe)    │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
from typing import Protocol

# Port (interface) — core depends on this, not on a concrete DB
class UserStore(Protocol):
    def get(self, user_id: int) -> "User | None": ...
    def save(self, user: "User") -> None: ...

# Core logic depends only on the port
class RegisterUser:
    def __init__(self, store: UserStore):
        self.store = store

    def execute(self, name: str, email: str) -> "User":
        # ...pure business rules, fully unit-testable with a fake UserStore...
        ...

Benefits: testable core, replaceable adapters, no framework/DB dependency inside business logic.

REST vs gRPC vs GraphQL

TransportBest forProsCons
RESTgRPCGraphQL
TransportHTTP/1.1 JSONHTTP/2 + Protobuf (binary)HTTP POST, JSON
Best forPublic APIs, CRUD, cachingInternal service-to-service, low latencyMobile/clients needing flexible fields
ProsSimple, cacheable, ubiquitousFast, typed contracts, streamingNo over/under-fetching, one round trip

RESTful Conventions

GET    /users          → list (paginated)
POST   /users          → create
GET    /users/{id}     → read one
PUT    /users/{id}     → full replace (idempotent)
PATCH  /users/{id}     → partial update
DELETE /users/{id}     → delete (idempotent)

Status codes: 200 OK · 201 Created · 204 No Content · 400 Bad Request ·
401 Unauthorized · 403 Forbidden · 404 Not Found · 409 Conflict ·
422 Unprocessable Entity · 429 Too Many Requests · 500 / 503
•

Idempotency (critical for payments, retries)

A request is idempotent if making it N times has the same effect as once. Clients retry on timeouts — without idempotency you double-charge a card.

# Client sends a unique Idempotency-Key header; server dedupes.
@app.post("/payments")
async def create_payment(body: PaymentIn, idempotency_key: str = Header(...)):
    cached = await redis.get(f"idem:{idempotency_key}")
    if cached:
        return json.loads(cached)  # return the original result, don't re-charge

    result = await charge_card(body)                       # do the side effect once
    await redis.set(f"idem:{idempotency_key}",
                    json.dumps(result), ex=86_400, nx=True)  # store for 24h
    return result
•

Pagination (offset vs cursor)

# Offset pagination — simple but slow at high offsets (DB scans + skips rows)
#   GET /posts?page=5000  → OFFSET 49990 LIMIT 10  (scans 50k rows)

# Cursor (keyset) pagination — O(1) regardless of depth, stable under inserts
@app.get("/posts")
async def list_posts(cursor: int | None = None, limit: int = 20):
    q = db.query(Post).order_by(Post.id.desc())
    if cursor:
        q = q.filter(Post.id < cursor)        # uses the index, no OFFSET
    rows = q.limit(limit + 1).all()
    next_cursor = rows[limit].id if len(rows) > limit else None
    return {"data": rows[:limit], "next_cursor": next_cursor}

Rule: use cursor pagination for infinite scroll / large datasets; offset is fine only for small, shallow page numbers.

•

API Versioning

# URL versioning (most explicit, most common)
app.include_router(v1_router, prefix="/api/v1")
app.include_router(v2_router, prefix="/api/v2")
# Alternatives: header (Accept: application/vnd.api+json;version=2) or query param.
Service-Oriented Design
•

Microservices Communication

1. Synchronous (REST/gRPC)use

1. Synchronous (REST/gRPC):

from httpx import AsyncClient

async def get_user_from_service(user_id: int):
    async with AsyncClient(timeout=2.0) as client:   # ALWAYS set a timeout
        response = await client.get(f"http://user-service:8000/users/{user_id}")
        response.raise_for_status()
    return response.json()

@app.get("/orders/{order_id}")
async def get_order(order_id: int):
    order = get_order_from_db(order_id)
    user = await get_user_from_service(order.user_id)
    return {**order, "user": user}

Challenges: network latency, cascading failures (wrap with timeout + circuit breaker + retry with jitter), tight runtime coupling.

2. Asynchronous (Message Queue):

from celery import Celery

celery_app = Celery('orders', broker='redis://localhost')

@app.post("/orders")
async def create_order(order: OrderCreate):
    order_id = save_order(order)
    send_notification_email.delay(order_id)   # fire-and-forget, decoupled
    return {"order_id": order_id}

@celery_app.task
def send_notification_email(order_id: int):
    order = get_order(order_id)
    send_email(order.user_email, f"Order {order_id} created")

Advantages: decoupling, fault tolerance (broker buffers), independent scaling, natural backpressure.

Sync vs async decision: use sync when the caller needs the result now to respond; use async for side effects (emails, analytics, derived data) the caller doesn't need to wait on.

API Gateway Pattern
from fastapi import FastAPI, Request
from fastapi.responses import Response, JSONResponse
import httpx

app = FastAPI()

SERVICES = {
    "users": "http://user-service:8000",
    "orders": "http://order-service:8000",
    "products": "http://product-service:8000",
}

@app.api_route("/{service}/{path:path}", methods=["GET", "POST", "PUT", "DELETE"])
async def gateway(service: str, path: str, request: Request):
    if service not in SERVICES:
        return JSONResponse({"error": "Service not found"}, status_code=404)
    service_url = f"{SERVICES[service]}/{path}"
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=5.0) as client:
        response = await client.request(
            method=request.method, url=service_url,
            content=await request.body(), headers=request.headers,
        )
    return Response(content=response.content, status_code=response.status_code,
                    headers=dict(response.headers))

# Cross-cutting concern handled once, at the edge, for every service
@app.middleware("http")
async def auth_middleware(request: Request, call_next):
    token = request.headers.get("Authorization")
    if not token or not validate_jwt(token):
        return JSONResponse({"error": "Unauthorized"}, status_code=401)
    return await call_next(request)

Responsibilities: routing, auth/authz, rate limiting, load balancing, request/response transformation, SSL termination, aggregation (BFF pattern).

See also: how the gateway relates to a plain reverse proxy and a load balancer — Forward Proxy vs Reverse Proxy vs Load Balancer vs API Gateway in the System Design notes.

Event-Driven Architecture
•

Event Sourcing

Store the sequence of events as the source of truth, not just current state. You can rebuild state by replaying events and get a full audit log for free.

from datetime import datetime, timezone
from enum import Enum
import json

class EventType(Enum):
    USER_CREATED = "user.created"
    ORDER_PLACED = "order.placed"
    PAYMENT_PROCESSED = "payment.processed"

class DomainEvent:
    def __init__(self, event_type: EventType, aggregate_id: str, data: dict, version: int):
        self.event_type = event_type
        self.aggregate_id = aggregate_id
        self.data = data
        self.timestamp = datetime.now(timezone.utc)
        self.version = version

class EventStore:
    def __init__(self, db):
        self.db = db

    def append(self, event: DomainEvent):
        self.db.add(EventRecord(
            aggregate_id=event.aggregate_id, event_type=event.event_type.value,
            data=json.dumps(event.data), timestamp=event.timestamp, version=event.version,
        ))
        self.db.commit()

    def get_events(self, aggregate_id: str):
        return (self.db.query(EventRecord)
                .filter(EventRecord.aggregate_id == aggregate_id)
                .order_by(EventRecord.version).all())

# Rebuild current state by folding events
def rebuild_order(events) -> dict:
    state = {}
    for e in events:
        if e.event_type == EventType.ORDER_PLACED.value:
            state = {"status": "placed", **json.loads(e.data)}
        elif e.event_type == EventType.PAYMENT_PROCESSED.value:
            state["status"] = "paid"
    return state
•

CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation)

write modelread modelWhen to useCost

Separate the write model (optimized for consistency) from the read model (optimized for queries, often denormalized). Pairs naturally with event sourcing.

# Command side (writes) — enforces invariants, emits events
class CreateUserCommandHandler:
    def __init__(self, db, event_bus):
        self.db, self.event_bus = db, event_bus

    def handle(self, name: str, email: str):
        user = User(name=name, email=email)
        self.db.add(user); self.db.commit()
        self.event_bus.publish(UserCreatedEvent(user.id, user.name, user.email))

# Query side (reads) — denormalized read model, possibly a different store
class GetUserQueryHandler:
    def __init__(self, read_db):
        self.read_db = read_db

    def handle(self, user_id: int):
        return self.read_db.query(UserReadModel).filter(UserReadModel.id == user_id).first()

When to use: read and write workloads differ wildly in shape/scale. Cost: eventual consistency between write and read models + more moving parts. Don't reach for CQRS/event sourcing by default — they add real complexity.

Message Queues
•

When you need one

Decoupling, smoothing traffic spikes (buffer), retries, async work (email/PDF/ML), and fan-out to multiple consumers.

•

Delivery semantics (know these cold)

At-least-oncemake consumers idempotent
GuaranteeMeaningCost
At-most-onceMay lose messages, never duplicateSimplest
At-least-onceNever lost, may duplicate → make consumers idempotentMost common default
Exactly-onceNo loss, no dupExpensive; often "effectively once" via dedup
•

RabbitMQ/Redis with Celery

from celery import Celery

celery_app = Celery('tasks', broker='amqp://guest:guest@localhost:5672/',
                    backend='redis://localhost:6379/')

@celery_app.task(bind=True, max_retries=3)
def process_payment(self, order_id: int):
    try:
        return process_payment_api(order_id)
    except Exception as exc:
        # exponential backoff: 2^retry seconds + jitter avoids thundering herd
        raise self.retry(exc=exc, countdown=2 ** self.request.retries)
•

Redis Streams (lightweight queue with consumer groups)

import redis, json
r = redis.Redis()

def publish(event_type: str, data: dict):
    r.xadd("events", {"msg": json.dumps({"type": event_type, "data": data})})

def consume(group="workers", consumer="w1"):
    try:
        r.xgroup_create("events", group, id="0", mkstream=True)
    except redis.ResponseError:
        pass  # group already exists
    while True:
        msgs = r.xreadgroup(group, consumer, {"events": ">"}, count=10, block=5000)
        for _stream, entries in msgs:
            for msg_id, fields in entries:
                process(json.loads(fields[b"msg"]))
                r.xack("events", group, msg_id)   # ack only after success

Dead Letter Queue (DLQ): after max retries, route the message to a DLQ for inspection instead of dropping it or blocking the queue forever.

Caching Strategy
•

Caching patterns

Cache-asideRead-throughWrite-throughWrite-behind
PatternHow it worksTrade-off
Cache-aside (lazy)App checks cache; on miss, reads DB and populates cacheMost common; first request slow, possible staleness
Read-throughCache library loads from DB on missCleaner app code, library coupling
Write-throughWrite to cache + DB synchronouslyConsistent, slower writes
Write-behindWrite to cache, async flush to DBFast writes, risk of loss on crash
•

Multi-Level Cache-Aside (in-process L1 → Redis L2 → DB)

import json, time, redis
r = redis.Redis()
CACHE_TTL = 3600
app_cache, app_expiry = {}, {}

def get_user(user_id: int):
    # L1: in-process (fastest, but per-instance, small)
    if user_id in app_cache and time.time() < app_expiry.get(user_id, 0):
        return app_cache[user_id]
    # L2: Redis (shared across instances)
    if cached := r.get(f"user:{user_id}"):
        user = json.loads(cached)
        app_cache[user_id], app_expiry[user_id] = user, time.time() + CACHE_TTL
        return user
    # L3: database
    user = db.query(User).filter(User.id == user_id).first()
    data = {"id": user.id, "name": user.name}
    r.setex(f"user:{user_id}", CACHE_TTL, json.dumps(data))
    app_cache[user_id], app_expiry[user_id] = data, time.time() + CACHE_TTL
    return data

def update_user(user_id: int, data: dict):
    db.query(User).filter(User.id == user_id).update(data); db.commit()
    app_cache.pop(user_id, None)        # invalidate every level on write
    r.delete(f"user:{user_id}")
•

Cache failure modes (interview favorites)

Thundering herd / stampedeCache penetrationCache avalancheStale data
ProblemCauseFix
Thundering herd / stampedeHot key expires, 1000s hit DB at onceLock/single-flight on rebuild; stale-while-revalidate; jittered TTL
Cache penetrationQueries for non-existent keys bypass cache → DBCache the "null" result briefly; Bloom filter of valid keys
Cache avalancheMany keys expire at the same instantAdd random jitter to TTLs
Stale dataDB updated, cache not invalidatedInvalidate on write; short TTL; versioned keys
# Single-flight: only one worker rebuilds a hot key; others wait briefly
def get_with_lock(key, loader, ttl=300):
    if (v := r.get(key)) is not None:
        return json.loads(v)
    if r.set(f"lock:{key}", "1", nx=True, ex=10):   # I won the rebuild
        try:
            value = loader()
            r.setex(key, ttl + random.randint(0, 60), json.dumps(value))  # jitter
            return value
        finally:
            r.delete(f"lock:{key}")
    time.sleep(0.05)                                 # someone else is rebuilding
    return get_with_lock(key, loader, ttl)

•

Replication: Read Replicas

from sqlalchemy import create_engine
from sqlalchemy.orm import Session
import random

primary = create_engine("postgresql://u:p@primary:5432/db")          # writes
replicas = [create_engine(f"postgresql://u:p@replica{i}:5432/db") for i in (1, 2)]

def write_session() -> Session:
    return Session(primary)

def read_session() -> Session:
    return Session(random.choice(replicas))   # spread heavy reads

# Caveat: replication lag → a read right after a write may see stale data.
# Fix: read-your-writes by routing that user's reads to the primary briefly.
•

Sharding (horizontal partitioning)

from hashlib import md5
from sqlalchemy import create_engine
from sqlalchemy.orm import Session

class ShardManager:
    def __init__(self, num_shards: int = 4):
        self.num_shards = num_shards
        self.engines = {i: create_engine(f"postgresql://u:p@shard{i}:5432/db")
                        for i in range(num_shards)}

    def shard_for(self, key: int) -> int:
        return int(md5(str(key).encode()).hexdigest(), 16) % self.num_shards

    def save_user(self, user_id: int, data: dict):
        s = Session(self.engines[self.shard_for(user_id)])
        s.add(User(**data)); s.commit()

Sharding trade-offs: cross-shard queries and joins become hard; transactions can't span shards easily; rebalancing when adding a shard reshuffles data — which is exactly what consistent hashing minimizes.

•

Consistent Hashing (minimal reshuffling on scale changes)

almost allUsed by

Plain hash(key) % N remaps almost all keys when N changes. Consistent hashing places nodes and keys on a ring; adding/removing a node only moves the keys between adjacent points (~1/N of keys).

import bisect
from hashlib import md5

class ConsistentHashRing:
    def __init__(self, nodes=None, vnodes=150):
        self.vnodes = vnodes        # virtual nodes smooth out distribution
        self.ring = {}              # hash position -> node
        self.sorted_keys = []
        for n in (nodes or []):
            self.add(n)

    def _hash(self, key: str) -> int:
        return int(md5(key.encode()).hexdigest(), 16)

    def add(self, node: str):
        for i in range(self.vnodes):
            h = self._hash(f"{node}:{i}")
            self.ring[h] = node
            bisect.insort(self.sorted_keys, h)

    def remove(self, node: str):
        for i in range(self.vnodes):
            h = self._hash(f"{node}:{i}")
            self.ring.pop(h, None)
            self.sorted_keys.remove(h)

    def get_node(self, key: str) -> str:
        if not self.ring:
            return None
        h = self._hash(key)
        idx = bisect.bisect(self.sorted_keys, h) % len(self.sorted_keys)
        return self.ring[self.sorted_keys[idx]]

ring = ConsistentHashRing(["cache-1", "cache-2", "cache-3"])
print(ring.get_node("user:42"))   # deterministic; stable when nodes change

Used by: Cassandra, DynamoDB, Redis Cluster, memcached client libraries, CDNs.

Consistency, CAP & Distributed Transactions
•

CAP Theorem

partition (P)Consistency (C)Availability (A)will

In a network partition (P), you must choose between Consistency (C) and Availability (A) — you can't have both.

CP (consistent, sacrifices availability under partition):
   e.g. traditional RDBMS w/ sync replication, ZooKeeper, etcd, HBase
   → banking, inventory: better to error than serve wrong data

AP (available, sacrifices strong consistency under partition):
   e.g. Cassandra, DynamoDB, Riak
   → social feed, shopping cart: better to serve slightly stale than 500

Networks will partition, so "drop P" isn't an option in a distributed system. Single-node systems aren't subject to CAP.

•

Consistency models (spectrum)

StrongEventualRead-your-writes
Strong  ─────────────────────────────────────────────►  Weak
Linearizable   Sequential   Causal   Read-your-writes   Eventual
(always latest) ............................ (converges "eventually")
  • Strong: every read sees the latest write (costly, needs coordination).
  • Eventual: replicas converge given no new writes (fast, available).
  • Read-your-writes: a user always sees their own updates (common UX compromise).
•

Distributed Transactions: the Saga Pattern

sagacompensatingOrchestrationChoreography

You can't run an ACID transaction across microservices. A saga is a sequence of local transactions; if a step fails, run compensating actions to undo prior steps.

# Orchestration-based saga: a coordinator drives steps and rollbacks.
class OrderSaga:
    async def execute(self, order):
        completed = []
        try:
            await payment_service.charge(order);    completed.append("payment")
            await inventory_service.reserve(order);  completed.append("inventory")
            await shipping_service.schedule(order);  completed.append("shipping")
            return {"status": "confirmed"}
        except Exception as e:
            # Compensate in reverse order — undo what already succeeded
            if "shipping" in completed:  await shipping_service.cancel(order)
            if "inventory" in completed: await inventory_service.release(order)
            if "payment" in completed:   await payment_service.refund(order)
            return {"status": "failed", "reason": str(e)}
  • Orchestration: central coordinator (above) — easier to reason about/monitor.
  • Choreography: services react to each other's events — looser coupling, harder to trace.
•

Two-Phase Commit (2PC) — and why sagas usually win

2PC (prepare → commit) gives atomicity but is blocking: if the coordinator dies after "prepare," participants hold locks indefinitely. It hurts availability and throughput, so high-scale systems prefer sagas + idempotency + eventual consistency.

•

Outbox Pattern (reliable "update DB + publish event")

Writing to the DB and publishing to a broker isn't atomic — a crash between them loses the event. Write the event to an outbox table in the same transaction, then a relay publishes it.

def place_order(db, order, event):
    with db.begin():                     # single local ACID transaction
        db.add(order)
        db.add(OutboxEvent(type="order.placed", payload=json.dumps(event)))
    # A separate poller reads unpublished OutboxEvents and pushes to Kafka,
    # marking them sent. Guarantees at-least-once delivery; consumers dedupe.
Concurrency Control
•

Optimistic vs Pessimistic Locking

AssumesMechanismBest forFailure mode
OptimisticPessimistic
AssumesConflicts are rareConflicts are common
MechanismVersion column, check on writeSELECT ... FOR UPDATE row lock
Best forRead-heavy, low contentionWrite-heavy, hot rows (inventory, balance)
Failure modeRetry on version mismatchLock waits / deadlocks
# Optimistic locking — version column; update fails if someone changed it first
class Account(Base):
    __tablename__ = "accounts"
    id = Column(Integer, primary_key=True)
    balance = Column(Integer)
    version = Column(Integer, nullable=False, default=0)

def withdraw_optimistic(db, account_id, amount):
    acct = db.query(Account).get(account_id)
    if acct.balance < amount:
        raise ValueError("insufficient funds")
    rows = (db.query(Account)
            .filter(Account.id == account_id, Account.version == acct.version)
            .update({"balance": acct.balance - amount, "version": acct.version + 1}))
    db.commit()
    if rows == 0:                       # another txn won the race
        raise ConflictError("retry")    # caller retries the whole operation
# Pessimistic locking — lock the row so concurrent writers block until commit
def withdraw_pessimistic(db, account_id, amount):
    acct = (db.query(Account)
            .filter(Account.id == account_id)
            .with_for_update()          # SELECT ... FOR UPDATE
            .one())
    if acct.balance < amount:
        raise ValueError("insufficient funds")
    acct.balance -= amount
    db.commit()                         # lock released here
•

Distributed Lock (across multiple app instances)

import uuid

def acquire_lock(r, name, ttl=10):
    token = str(uuid.uuid4())
    # SET NX EX is atomic: only one instance gets the lock; TTL prevents deadlock
    return token if r.set(f"lock:{name}", token, nx=True, ex=ttl) else None

def release_lock(r, name, token):
    # Release only if we still own it (compare token), atomically via Lua
    lua = "if redis.call('get', KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then return redis.call('del', KEYS[1]) else return 0 end"
    r.eval(lua, 1, f"lock:{name}", token)

For correctness-critical locking across nodes, know the trade-offs of Redlock vs a consensus store (etcd/ZooKeeper). For most app needs, a single-Redis lock with TTL + ownership token is fine.

Scalability & Resilience Patterns
•

Load Balancing

AlgorithmsL4 (TCP)
upstream api_backend {
    least_conn;                 # route to the instance with fewest active conns
    server api1:8000 weight=2;
    server api2:8000;
    server api3:8000;
}
server {
    listen 80;
    location / {
        proxy_pass http://api_backend;
        proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
    }
}

Algorithms: round-robin, least-connections, weighted, IP-hash (sticky). L4 (TCP) vs L7 (HTTP, can route by path/header).

•

Circuit Breaker (stop hammering a failing dependency)

from enum import Enum
from datetime import datetime, timedelta

class State(Enum):
    CLOSED = "closed"; OPEN = "open"; HALF_OPEN = "half_open"

class CircuitBreaker:
    def __init__(self, failure_threshold=5, timeout=60):
        self.failure_threshold, self.timeout = failure_threshold, timeout
        self.state, self.failures, self.last_failure = State.CLOSED, 0, None

    def call(self, func, *args, **kwargs):
        if self.state == State.OPEN:
            if datetime.now() > self.last_failure + timedelta(seconds=self.timeout):
                self.state = State.HALF_OPEN          # probe with one request
            else:
                raise Exception("Circuit OPEN — failing fast")
        try:
            result = func(*args, **kwargs)
            if self.state == State.HALF_OPEN:
                self.state, self.failures = State.CLOSED, 0   # recovered
            return result
        except Exception:
            self.failures += 1
            self.last_failure = datetime.now()
            if self.failures >= self.failure_threshold:
                self.state = State.OPEN
            raise
•

Retry with Exponential Backoff + Jitter

import random, time

def retry(func, max_attempts=5, base=0.1):
    for attempt in range(max_attempts):
        try:
            return func()
        except TransientError:
            if attempt == max_attempts - 1:
                raise
            # jitter prevents synchronized retries (thundering herd)
            time.sleep(base * (2 ** attempt) + random.uniform(0, 0.1))
•

Other resilience patterns

BulkheadTimeout everywhereBackpressureGraceful degradationIdempotency + DLQ
  • Bulkhead: isolate resources (separate thread/conn pools per dependency) so one slow service can't exhaust everything.
  • Timeout everywhere: every network call needs a deadline; no infinite waits.
  • Backpressure: bounded queues + reject/429 when overloaded instead of OOM.
  • Graceful degradation: serve cached/partial data when a dependency is down.
  • Idempotency + DLQ: safe retries and a place for poison messages.

Structured logging + correlation/request IDs

import logging, json, uuid
from fastapi import Request

logger = logging.getLogger("app")

@app.middleware("http")
async def add_request_id(request: Request, call_next):
    rid = request.headers.get("X-Request-ID", str(uuid.uuid4()))
    response = await call_next(request)
    response.headers["X-Request-ID"] = rid           # propagate to client + downstream
    logger.info(json.dumps({"request_id": rid, "path": request.url.path,
                            "method": request.method, "status": response.status_code}))
    return response
•

Metrics (the four golden signals)

Latency, Traffic, Errors, Saturation. Track p50/p95/p99 latency, not just averages — averages hide tail latency that real users feel.

from prometheus_client import Counter, Histogram

REQUESTS = Counter("http_requests_total", "Total requests", ["method", "endpoint", "status"])
LATENCY = Histogram("http_request_duration_seconds", "Latency", ["endpoint"])

@app.middleware("http")
async def metrics_mw(request, call_next):
    with LATENCY.labels(request.url.path).time():
        resp = await call_next(request)
    REQUESTS.labels(request.method, request.url.path, resp.status_code).inc()
    return resp

Worked Examples
•

Example 1: URL Shortener

RequirementsScaleCapacityCounter + base62 encodeScale-out

Requirements: shorten a long URL → short code; redirect; ~100:1 read:write; analytics optional. Scale: 100M new URLs/month.

Capacity: 100M/month ≈ 40 writes/s; reads ≈ 4,000/s → cache redirects. 5 years ≈ 6B URLs → need 7-char base62 code (62^7 ≈ 3.5 trillion combos).

Key design choice — how to generate the short code:

ApproachProsCons
Hash(url) + truncateStatelessCollisions → must check & retry
Random base62SimpleCollision check on insert
Counter + base62 encodeNo collisions, short codesNeeds a global counter (sequence / Redis INCR / range-allocated per host)
import string
ALPHABET = string.digits + string.ascii_letters   # base62

def encode_base62(num: int) -> str:
    if num == 0:
        return ALPHABET[0]
    s = []
    while num:
        num, rem = divmod(num, 62)
        s.append(ALPHABET[rem])
    return "".join(reversed(s))

@app.post("/shorten")
async def shorten(url: str):
    # Atomic global counter avoids collisions entirely
    seq = await redis.incr("url:counter")     # in prod: pre-allocate ranges per host
    code = encode_base62(seq)
    await db_insert(code=code, long_url=url)
    await redis.setex(f"url:{code}", 86_400, url)   # warm the redirect cache
    return {"short_url": f"https://sho.rt/{code}"}

@app.get("/{code}")
async def redirect(code: str):
    if (url := await redis.get(f"url:{code}")) is None:   # cache-aside
        url = await db_lookup(code)
        if not url:
            raise HTTPException(404)
        await redis.setex(f"url:{code}", 86_400, url)
    return RedirectResponse(url, status_code=301)

Scale-out: read replicas + Redis for redirects (99%+ cache hit), shard the URL table by code, CDN in front for hot links, async analytics via queue.

•

Example 2: Distributed Rate Limiter

RequirementmanyAlgorithm choices

Requirement: limit each user to N requests/window across many API instances (so in-memory counters won't work — must be shared).

# Token bucket in Redis via an atomic Lua script (no race between instances).
RATE_LIMIT_LUA = """
local key = KEYS[1]
local rate = tonumber(ARGV[1])         -- tokens added per second
local capacity = tonumber(ARGV[2])     -- max burst
local now = tonumber(ARGV[3])
local requested = tonumber(ARGV[4])
local bucket = redis.call('HMGET', key, 'tokens', 'ts')
local tokens = tonumber(bucket[1]) or capacity
local ts = tonumber(bucket[2]) or now
tokens = math.min(capacity, tokens + (now - ts) * rate)   -- refill
local allowed = tokens >= requested
if allowed then tokens = tokens - requested end
redis.call('HMSET', key, 'tokens', tokens, 'ts', now)
redis.call('EXPIRE', key, math.ceil(capacity / rate) * 2)
return allowed and 1 or 0
"""

async def is_allowed(user_id: str, rate=10, capacity=20) -> bool:
    allowed = await redis.eval(RATE_LIMIT_LUA, 1, f"rl:{user_id}",
                               rate, capacity, time.time(), 1)
    return bool(allowed)

@app.middleware("http")
async def rate_limit(request, call_next):
    user = request.headers.get("X-User-Id", request.client.host)
    if not await is_allowed(user):
        return JSONResponse({"error": "rate limited"}, status_code=429,
                            headers={"Retry-After": "1"})
    return await call_next(request)

Algorithm choices: fixed window (simple, boundary bursts), sliding window log (accurate, memory-heavy), sliding window counter (good middle ground), token bucket (allows bursts, smooth — used above), leaky bucket (smooths output rate).

•

Example 3: Real-Time Notification System

RequirementWhy this scales

Requirement: deliver notifications to online users instantly (WebSocket) and to offline users via push/email; must scale across multiple servers.

# Per-instance connection registry + Redis Pub/Sub to fan out across instances.
class ConnectionManager:
    def __init__(self):
        self.active: dict[str, WebSocket] = {}    # local connections only

    async def connect(self, user_id: str, ws: WebSocket):
        await ws.accept()
        self.active[user_id] = ws

    def disconnect(self, user_id: str):
        self.active.pop(user_id, None)

    async def deliver_local(self, user_id: str, message: dict):
        if ws := self.active.get(user_id):
            await ws.send_json(message)
            return True
        return False

manager = ConnectionManager()

@app.websocket("/ws/{user_id}")
async def ws_endpoint(ws: WebSocket, user_id: str):
    await manager.connect(user_id, ws)
    try:
        while True:
            await ws.receive_text()           # keepalive / client messages
    except WebSocketDisconnect:
        manager.disconnect(user_id)

# Any instance publishes; the instance holding the user's socket delivers it.
async def notify(user_id: str, message: dict):
    if not await manager.deliver_local(user_id, message):
        # Not connected here → publish so the right instance picks it up
        await redis.publish("notifications", json.dumps({"user": user_id, "msg": message}))
        # Still not online anywhere → fall back to push/email and store as unread
        await queue_push_or_email.delay(user_id, message)

Why this scales: WebSocket state is per-instance, so use Redis Pub/Sub (or Kafka) to route a message to whichever instance holds the connection. Offline users fall back to a durable queue (push/email) and an "unread" table they sync on login.

•

Example 4: News Feed / Timeline

On postOn readBest forProblemHybrid (what real systems do)don't

The core question: fan-out on write vs fan-out on read.

Fan-out on WRITE (push)Fan-out on READ (pull)
On postWrite post into every follower's feed cacheJust store the post
On readRead pre-computed feed (fast)Merge recent posts from all followees (slow)
Best forMost users (few followers)Celebrities (millions of followers)
Problem"Celebrity" post → millions of writesRead latency grows with #followees

Hybrid (what real systems do): fan-out on write for normal users; for celebrity accounts, don't fan out — pull their posts at read time and merge. Best of both.

async def publish_post(author_id: str, post: dict):
    await save_post(post)
    follower_count = await get_follower_count(author_id)
    if follower_count < 10_000:                       # normal user → push
        for follower_id in await get_followers(author_id):
            await redis.lpush(f"feed:{follower_id}", post["id"])
            await redis.ltrim(f"feed:{follower_id}", 0, 999)   # cap feed size
    # else: celebrity → skip fan-out; merged in at read time

async def get_feed(user_id: str):
    post_ids = await redis.lrange(f"feed:{user_id}", 0, 50)    # pushed posts
    posts = await load_posts(post_ids)
    # Merge in fresh posts from celebrity accounts this user follows (pull)
    for celeb in await get_followed_celebrities(user_id):
        posts += await get_recent_posts(celeb, limit=10)
    return sorted(posts, key=lambda p: p["created_at"], reverse=True)[:50]
