1. Async event loop blocked by sync work

TopicsSymptomDiagnosisblockingFix — match the tool to the workTakeaway

Topics: FastAPI · Multithreading · Python (GIL)

Symptom: Latency on every endpoint spikes whenever one report endpoint is hit. Health checks time out even though CPU isn't saturated.

Diagnosis: An async def endpoint called a blocking function (requests.get, a sync DB driver, time.sleep, heavy pandas). FastAPI runs async def handlers directly on the single event loop thread — any blocking call there stalls all concurrent requests on that worker. (A plain def handler is different: Starlette offloads it to a threadpool, so it doesn't block the loop — but that pool is finite, ~40 threads by default.)

# ❌ Blocks the event loop for everyone
@app.get("/report")
async def report():
    data = requests.get("https://slow-api/data").json()   # sync I/O on the loop
    return heavy_pandas_crunch(data)                       # CPU on the loop

Fix — match the tool to the work:

import asyncio, httpx

@app.get("/report")
async def report():
    # I/O-bound: use an async client so the loop stays free during the wait
    async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:
        data = (await client.get("https://slow-api/data")).json()

    # CPU-bound: push OFF the loop. to_thread only helps if the work releases the
    # GIL (numpy/pandas C code do); for pure-Python CPU work use a process pool.
    return await asyncio.to_thread(heavy_pandas_crunch, data)

# Pure-Python CPU work → process pool (bypasses the GIL)
from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor
pool = ProcessPoolExecutor()

@app.get("/primes")
async def primes(n: int):
    loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()
    return await loop.run_in_executor(pool, count_primes, n)

Takeaway: In async def, everything you call must be non-blocking. Offload I/O to async libs, GIL-releasing CPU to to_thread, and pure-Python CPU to a process pool. If a route is unavoidably sync, declare it def (not async def) and let Starlette's threadpool handle it.

•

2. Sharing one SQLAlchemy Session across threads/requests

TopicsSymptomDiagnosisSession is not thread-safeTakeaway

Topics: SQL ORM · Multithreading · Backend

Symptom: Intermittent, impossible-to-reproduce errors: This session is provisioning a new connection; concurrent operations are not permitted, garbled results, objects from one request appearing in another.

Diagnosis: A single Session (or a module-level global session) was shared across requests or handed to worker threads. Session is not thread-safe — it manages a unit of work and an identity map that assume one logical owner. Concurrency corrupts its internal state.

Fix — one Session per request/thread, via a factory:

from sqlalchemy.orm import sessionmaker, scoped_session

SessionLocal = sessionmaker(bind=engine, autoflush=False, expire_on_commit=False)

# FastAPI: one session per request through a dependency (see Scenario 13)
def get_db():
    db = SessionLocal()
    try:
        yield db
    finally:
        db.close()

# Background threads: each thread makes its OWN session
def worker(item_id: int):
    with SessionLocal() as db:          # fresh session, scoped to this thread
        item = db.get(Item, item_id)
        ...
        db.commit()

# If you must use a global handle in threaded code, scoped_session gives
# each thread its own underlying Session keyed by thread id:
Session = scoped_session(SessionLocal)

Takeaway: The engine (and its connection pool) is global and thread-safe; the Session is not. Rule of thumb: one Session per request, per thread, per task — never shared.

•

3. Connection pool exhaustion ("QueuePool limit reached")

TopicsSymptomDiagnosisAlwaysPgBouncerTakeaway

Topics: SQL ORM · Backend · Multithreading

Symptom: Under load, requests hang for ~30s then fail with TimeoutError: QueuePool limit of size 5 overflow 10 reached.

Diagnosis: Connections are checked out but never returned — usually a session that isn't closed on an error path, a long-running transaction, or spawning more worker threads than the pool can serve. Each Session holds a connection from first query until commit()/close().

Fix — size the pool and guarantee return:

from sqlalchemy import create_engine

engine = create_engine(
    DB_URL,
    pool_size=20,          # steady-state connections
    max_overflow=10,       # burst headroom (total cap = 30)
    pool_timeout=30,       # wait before giving up on a free conn
    pool_recycle=1800,     # recycle conns older than 30 min (avoid stale)
    pool_pre_ping=True,    # validate conn before use (survives DB restarts/timeouts)
)
  • Always close sessions (with SessionLocal() as db: or the Depends finally).
  • Keep transactions short — don't hold a connection across a slow external API call.
  • Size the pool to the DB, not the app: (pool_size + max_overflow) × num_workers must stay under Postgres max_connections. With 4 Uvicorn workers and pool 30 that's 120 connections — if max_connections=100 you'll exhaust the server. Use a proxy like PgBouncer when worker/replica counts are high.

Takeaway: Pool exhaustion is almost always a leak (unclosed session / over-long txn), not a too-small pool. Fix the lifecycle first, then size deliberately against the DB's own limit.

•

4. Lazy-loading blows up in async SQLAlchemy (MissingGreenlet)

TopicsSymptomDiagnosislazyTakeaway

Topics: SQL ORM · FastAPI (async) · Python

Symptom: With async SQLAlchemy, serializing a response raises MissingGreenlet: greenlet_spawn has not been called or sqlalchemy.exc.InvalidRequestError, often only when a relationship is accessed.

Diagnosis: A relationship (user.posts) is lazy by default. In async, touching it after the awaited query triggers implicit I/O outside an await — which the async engine forbids. The same access pattern in sync code silently fires the N+1 queries instead.

Fix — eager-load explicitly; never rely on lazy in async:

from sqlalchemy import select
from sqlalchemy.orm import selectinload

@app.get("/users/{uid}")
async def get_user(uid: int, db: AsyncSession = Depends(get_async_db)):
    result = await db.execute(
        select(User)
        .where(User.id == uid)
        .options(selectinload(User.posts))   # second SELECT ... WHERE post.user_id IN (...)
    )
    return result.scalar_one()
  • selectinload → 2 queries, no JOIN row-multiplication (best for collections / one-to-many).
  • joinedload → single JOIN (best for many-to-one / one-to-one).
  • Or set expire_on_commit=False so attributes already loaded aren't re-fetched after commit.

Takeaway: Async ORM removes the "lazy load just works" safety net. Decide your loading strategy per query; eager-load anything you'll serialize. (In sync code lazy loading "works" but hands you the N+1 problem — also fix it there.)

•

5. Oversold inventory: threads + DB race condition

TopicsSymptomDiagnosischeck-then-actTakeawaydatabase

Topics: Multithreading · SQL ORM · Backend

Symptom: A flash sale of 100 units sells 118. Two requests read stock = 1 at the same time and both decrement.

Diagnosis: Classic check-then-act race. Reading, deciding, and writing are three steps; concurrent workers interleave between the check and the write. An app-level threading.Lock only guards a single process — with multiple Uvicorn workers / pods it doesn't help. The invariant must be enforced where the data lives: the database.

Fix — make the DB do the atomic check-and-decrement:

from sqlalchemy import update

# Option A: atomic conditional UPDATE — no row pre-read, no lock held by app
@app.post("/buy/{pid}")
async def buy(pid: int, db: Session = Depends(get_db)):
    res = db.execute(
        update(Product)
        .where(Product.id == pid, Product.stock > 0)   # condition in the WHERE
        .values(stock=Product.stock - 1)               # decrement server-side
    )
    db.commit()
    if res.rowcount == 0:
        raise HTTPException(409, "Out of stock")
    return {"status": "ok"}

# Option B: pessimistic row lock when you must read-modify-write across several columns
def buy_locked(pid: int, db: Session):
    product = db.execute(
        select(Product).where(Product.id == pid).with_for_update()  # SELECT ... FOR UPDATE
    ).scalar_one()
    if product.stock <= 0:
        raise HTTPException(409, "Out of stock")
    product.stock -= 1
    db.commit()

Add a defense-in-depth CHECK (stock >= 0) constraint so the DB rejects oversell even if logic slips.

Takeaway: Correctness for shared mutable state across processes belongs in the database (atomic UPDATE ... WHERE, SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, or a constraint) — not an in-process lock. In-process locks only coordinate threads within one process.

•

6. CPU-bound endpoint freezes the whole server

TopicsSymptomDiagnosisGILtask queue (Celery/RQ)Takeaway

Topics: Python (GIL) · Multithreading · FastAPI

Symptom: One /resize-image or /parse-pdf request makes the whole worker unresponsive; adding threads doesn't help.

Diagnosis: The GIL lets only one thread execute Python bytecode at a time, so threads give no speedup for pure-Python CPU work — they just time-slice. On the event loop it's worse: the loop is frozen until the function returns.

Fix — separate processes for CPU parallelism:

from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor
import asyncio

cpu_pool = ProcessPoolExecutor(max_workers=4)   # 4 real cores → ~4x

@app.post("/resize")
async def resize(file: UploadFile):
    data = await file.read()
    loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()
    out = await loop.run_in_executor(cpu_pool, resize_image, data)  # runs in another process
    return Response(out, media_type="image/jpeg")
  • Libraries that drop the GIL in C (NumPy, Pillow, Pandas, bcrypt) can parallelize with threads / asyncio.to_thread — measure before assuming.
  • For heavy or bursty CPU jobs, prefer a task queue (Celery/RQ) over an in-process pool so the web worker stays lean and the work survives a restart (see Scenario 7).
  • Python 3.13's free-threaded ("no-GIL") build changes this calculus, but assume the GIL on standard CPython in interviews unless told otherwise.

Takeaway: Threads → concurrency for I/O. Processes → parallelism for CPU. The GIL is the dividing line.

•

7. BackgroundTasks lost work on deploy

TopicsSymptomDiagnosisDecision ruleTakeaway

Topics: FastAPI · Backend · Multithreading

Symptom: "Send welcome email" tasks silently vanish during deploys; long jobs started via BackgroundTasks sometimes never finish.

Diagnosis: FastAPI BackgroundTasks run in the same process, after the response is sent. They are not durable — a restart, crash, or scale-down kills them. They also share the worker's event loop / threadpool, so heavy ones steal capacity from request handling.

Fix — pick by durability requirement:

# OK for cheap, fire-and-forget, loss-tolerant work (e.g. access logging)
@app.post("/signup")
async def signup(user: UserIn, bg: BackgroundTasks):
    u = create_user(user)
    bg.add_task(write_audit_log, u.id)   # fine if occasionally lost
    return u

# Durable / retryable / heavy work → real queue with a separate worker
@app.post("/signup")
async def signup(user: UserIn):
    u = create_user(user)
    send_welcome_email.delay(u.id)       # Celery: persisted in broker, retried, survives deploys
    return u

Decision rule:

Use BackgroundTasksUse Celery / RQ
Cheap, fast, loss-tolerantMust not be lost; needs retries
No retry neededScheduled / periodic
Tied to this request's lifetimeHeavy CPU, fan-out, multi-step workflows

Takeaway: BackgroundTasks = "after this response, same process, best-effort." Anything that must survive a restart or be retried needs a broker-backed queue.

•

8. Duplicate charges from client retries (idempotency)

TopicsSymptomDiagnosisnot idempotentTakeaway

Topics: Backend · SQL ORM · FastAPI

Symptom: A mobile client times out, retries POST /payments, and the customer is charged twice. The original request actually succeeded.

Diagnosis: POST is not idempotent by default. Network retries, double-clicks, and proxy re-sends create duplicate side effects. The server must dedupe explicitly.

Fix — idempotency key + unique constraint:

# Client sends a stable key per logical operation: header "Idempotency-Key: <uuid>"
# Table: idempotency_keys(key PK, response_json, created_at)

@app.post("/payments")
def create_payment(body: PaymentIn, idem_key: str = Header(...), db: Session = Depends(get_db)):
    existing = db.get(IdempotencyKey, idem_key)
    if existing:
        return existing.response_json          # replay the original result, no new charge

    try:
        charge = process_charge(body)          # the real side effect
        rec = IdempotencyKey(key=idem_key, response_json=charge.dict())
        db.add(rec)
        db.commit()                            # UNIQUE(key) makes the insert the dedupe point
    except IntegrityError:                      # concurrent duplicate raced us
        db.rollback()
        return db.get(IdempotencyKey, idem_key).response_json
    return charge.dict()

Takeaway: Make write endpoints idempotent with a caller-supplied key enforced by a unique constraint — the DB is the source of truth for "did this already happen," so it works even across concurrent retries and multiple app instances.

•

9. Fan-out to a slow upstream API without melting it

TopicsSymptomDiagnosisboundedasync + semaphoretimeouts

Topics: Multithreading / async · Backend · FastAPI

Symptom: An endpoint enriches 500 records by calling a partner API. Either it's painfully sequential, or a naive gather opens 500 connections and the partner rate-limits / you exhaust sockets.

Diagnosis: Two failure modes: serial (too slow) and unbounded concurrency (too aggressive). You want bounded concurrency — many in flight, but capped.

Fix — semaphore-bounded async fan-out with a shared client:

import asyncio, httpx

async def enrich_all(ids: list[int]) -> list[dict]:
    sem = asyncio.Semaphore(10)                       # at most 10 concurrent upstream calls
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=5) as client:   # reuse connection pool
        async def one(i):
            async with sem:
                r = await client.get(f"https://partner/api/{i}")
                r.raise_for_status()
                return r.json()
        # return_exceptions so one failure doesn't cancel the batch
        results = await asyncio.gather(*(one(i) for i in ids), return_exceptions=True)
    return [r for r in results if not isinstance(r, Exception)]
  • I/O-bound and lots of calls → async + semaphore (this).
  • Library is sync-only (no async client) → ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=10) instead.
  • Add per-call timeouts and retry with backoff (tenacity) for resilience, and a circuit breaker if the partner flaps.

Takeaway: The goal is never "max concurrency" — it's bounded concurrency: a semaphore (async) or a fixed-size thread pool (sync), plus timeouts, retries, and a reused client.

•

10. Database deadlocks under concurrent updates

TopicsSymptomDiagnosisin opposite ordershortTakeaway

Topics: SQL ORM · Backend · Multithreading

Symptom: Intermittent DeadlockDetected / Deadlock found when trying to get lock; one of two concurrent transactions is aborted by the DB.

Diagnosis: Two transactions lock the same rows in opposite order (txn A locks row 1 then 2; txn B locks 2 then 1) and wait on each other. The DB breaks the cycle by killing a victim.

Fix — consistent lock ordering + retry the victim:

# 1) Always acquire locks in a deterministic order (e.g. ascending primary key)
def transfer(db, from_id, to_id, amount):
    a, b = sorted([from_id, to_id])                 # same order for everyone
    accounts = db.execute(
        select(Account).where(Account.id.in_([a, b])).with_for_update().order_by(Account.id)
    ).scalars().all()
    ...
    db.commit()

# 2) Deadlocks are expected under contention — retry the loser with backoff
from tenacity import retry, retry_if_exception_type, wait_exponential, stop_after_attempt
from sqlalchemy.exc import OperationalError

@retry(retry=retry_if_exception_type(OperationalError),
       wait=wait_exponential(min=0.05, max=1), stop=stop_after_attempt(3))
def do_transfer(...):
    ...
  • Keep transactions short (don't do external I/O while holding row locks).
  • Consider lower-contention designs: a single atomic UPDATE, or a queue serializing hot rows.

Takeaway: Prevent deadlocks with consistent lock ordering and short transactions; survive the unavoidable ones with idempotent retries.

•

11. Lost updates: optimistic vs pessimistic locking

TopicsSymptomDiagnosisFix — choose by contention levelTakeawayOptimistic

Topics: SQL ORM · Backend

Symptom: Two editors open the same document, both save; the second silently overwrites the first's changes.

Diagnosis: Read-modify-write with a gap. No lock or version check means the last writer wins and the first edit is lost.

Fix — choose by contention level:

# Optimistic (low contention, web edit forms): version column, check-on-write
class Document(Base):
    __tablename__ = "documents"
    id = Column(Integer, primary_key=True)
    body = Column(Text)
    version = Column(Integer, nullable=False, default=0)

@app.put("/docs/{doc_id}")
def update_doc(doc_id: int, body: str, expected_version: int, db: Session = Depends(get_db)):
    res = db.execute(
        update(Document)
        .where(Document.id == doc_id, Document.version == expected_version)
        .values(body=body, version=Document.version + 1)
    )
    db.commit()
    if res.rowcount == 0:
        raise HTTPException(409, "Document changed since you loaded it — reload and retry")

SQLAlchemy can automate this via __mapper_args__ = {"version_id_col": version}.

# Pessimistic (high contention, money): lock the row up front
row = db.execute(select(Account).where(Account.id == aid).with_for_update()).scalar_one()

Takeaway: Optimistic locking (version column, 409 on conflict) scales for rare conflicts; pessimistic (FOR UPDATE) is for hot, high-stakes rows where retrying is costly.

•

12. Thread-safe in-process cache that doesn't leak memory

TopicsSymptomDiagnosisunboundedTakeawaytwo

Topics: Multithreading · Python · Backend

Symptom: A hand-rolled dict cache shared across request threads occasionally KeyErrors on pop, and memory climbs until OOM.

Diagnosis: Two bugs: (1) compound operations on a plain dict (check-then-pop) aren't atomic across threads, and (2) an unbounded cache never evicts.

Fix — bound it and guard compound ops:

from functools import lru_cache

# Simplest: bounded + thread-safe for pure functions of their args
@lru_cache(maxsize=10_000)
def get_country(code: str) -> str:
    return db_lookup(code)            # lru_cache is internally locked; eviction is automatic

# When you need TTL / manual control, guard compound operations with a lock
import threading, time
class TTLCache:
    def __init__(self, ttl=60):
        self._d, self._ttl, self._lock = {}, ttl, threading.Lock()
    def get(self, key):
        with self._lock:                              # atomic read+expiry check
            v = self._d.get(key)
            if v and time.monotonic() - v[1] < self._ttl:
                return v[0]
            self._d.pop(key, None)
            return None
    def set(self, key, val):
        with self._lock:
            self._d[key] = (val, time.monotonic())

Takeaway: Caches need two properties: thread-safety for compound ops (a Lock, or lru_cache which is already locked) and a bound (maxsize/TTL) so they can't grow forever. For multi-process/multi-pod sharing, move the cache to Redis.

•

13. Session left dirty: commit/rollback lifecycle in Depends

TopicsSymptomDiagnosisroll back on exceptioncloseone transaction per request

Topics: SQL ORM · FastAPI · Backend

Symptom: After one request errors mid-write, later requests on the same connection see partial data or raise PendingRollbackError.

Diagnosis: The session dependency yielded a session but didn't roll back on exception or close reliably, so a half-finished transaction leaked onto a pooled connection.

Fix — a dependency that commits on success, rolls back on error, always closes:

def get_db():
    db = SessionLocal()
    try:
        yield db
        db.commit()                 # commit only if the handler returned cleanly
    except Exception:
        db.rollback()               # undo partial work on any error
        raise
    finally:
        db.close()                  # always return the connection to the pool
  • Prefer one transaction per request committed here over scattering db.commit() through business logic — it keeps the unit of work atomic.
  • expire_on_commit=False avoids a surprise re-query when you read attributes after commit (e.g. while building the response).

Takeaway: The request-scoped session must always resolve its transaction: commit on success, rollback on failure, close in finally. Leaking an open transaction poisons the next user of that pooled connection.

•

14. Streaming a huge query without OOM

TopicsSymptomDiagnosisTakeawaystreaming both ends

Topics: SQL ORM · FastAPI · Python (generators)

Symptom: GET /export on a 5M-row table spikes memory and the worker gets OOM-killed.

Diagnosis: .all() materializes every row (and ORM objects) into memory at once, and building one giant response body holds it all again before sending.

Fix — stream rows with a server-side cursor + a generator response:

from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse
import csv, io

@app.get("/export")
def export(db: Session = Depends(get_db)):
    def rows():
        # yield_per → fetch in batches via a server-side cursor, not all at once
        q = db.execute(select(Order).execution_options(yield_per=1000)).scalars()
        buf = io.StringIO(); w = csv.writer(buf)
        w.writerow(["id", "total"]); yield buf.getvalue(); buf.seek(0); buf.truncate()
        for o in q:                              # one batch in memory at a time
            w.writerow([o.id, o.total])
            yield buf.getvalue(); buf.seek(0); buf.truncate()
    return StreamingResponse(rows(), media_type="text/csv")
  • For pure throughput, query only needed columns (select(Order.id, Order.total)) to skip ORM object overhead entirely.
  • Truly large exports are often better as an async job that writes to S3 and returns a link (see Scenario 7).

Takeaway: Constant memory comes from streaming both ends — yield_per (server-side cursor) on the DB side and a generator StreamingResponse on the HTTP side. Never .all() an unbounded result set.

•

15. Graceful shutdown that drains in-flight work

TopicsSymptomDiagnosisgraceful timeoutTakeawaydrain-then-die

Topics: Backend · FastAPI · Multithreading

Symptom: Deploys cause sporadic 502s and a few half-written DB rows. In-flight requests and background workers are killed mid-flight.

Diagnosis: On SIGTERM the process exits immediately instead of (a) stopping new traffic, (b) letting in-flight requests finish, and (c) cleanly shutting pools/executors.

Fix — lifespan to set up/tear down; let the server drain:

from contextlib import asynccontextmanager

@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app: FastAPI):
    app.state.http = httpx.AsyncClient()         # startup: shared resources
    app.state.pool = ProcessPoolExecutor()
    yield
    # shutdown: runs after the server stops accepting new requests and drains
    await app.state.http.aclose()
    app.state.pool.shutdown(wait=True)           # let CPU jobs finish
    engine.dispose()                             # close DB connections

app = FastAPI(lifespan=lifespan)
  • Run Uvicorn/Gunicorn with a graceful timeout so it stops accepting connections and waits for active requests (--timeout-graceful-shutdown).
  • In Kubernetes, set terminationGracePeriodSeconds ≥ that timeout, and a preStop sleep so the load balancer deregisters the pod before SIGTERM.

Takeaway: Zero-downtime deploys need drain-then-die: stop new work, finish in-flight work, then close pools/connections in lifespan. Coordinate the app timeout with the orchestrator's grace period.

•

16. Choosing threads vs processes vs async (decision)

TopicsSymptom (interview framing)Takeawayclassify each unit of work

Topics: Python (GIL) · Multithreading · FastAPI · Backend

Symptom (interview framing): "An endpoint must call 3 microservices, hash a password, and resize an image. How do you run each part?"

Diagnosis & fix — classify each piece of work, then pick the model:

Work in the requestNatureRight toolWhy
Call 3 microservicesI/O-boundasync + httpx, asyncio.gatherLoop stays free during waits; run the 3 concurrently
Hash password (bcrypt)CPU but releases GIL in Cawait asyncio.to_thread(...)A thread can run the C code in parallel without blocking the loop
Resize image (pure-Python heavy)CPU-bound, holds GILProcessPoolExecutor via run_in_executorOnly a separate process gives real CPU parallelism
@app.post("/onboard")
async def onboard(req: OnboardIn):
    loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()
    async with httpx.AsyncClient() as c:
        svc = await asyncio.gather(c.get(A), c.get(B), c.get(C))      # I/O: concurrent
    pw  = await asyncio.to_thread(bcrypt.hashpw, req.pw, salt)        # GIL-releasing CPU
    img = await loop.run_in_executor(cpu_pool, resize, req.image)     # pure-Python CPU
    return assemble(svc, pw, img)

Takeaway: Don't pick one model for the whole endpoint — classify each unit of work (I/O vs GIL-releasing CPU vs pure-Python CPU) and route each to the matching executor. That single mental model (the GIL is released during I/O and inside many C extensions) explains every choice above.

•

17. Quick-reference decision tables

Concurrency modelSQLAlchemy session rulesnotare

Concurrency model

WorkloadModelFastAPI mechanism
Network / disk / DB waitsasync (cooperative)async def + async libs
Many sync I/O calls (no async lib)Threadsdef route, or ThreadPoolExecutor

Scope of contentionMechanism

RuleReason

•

Summary — the five recurring lessons

The GIL draws the lineBound everythingPlan for failure & restarts
  1. The GIL draws the line: threads for I/O, processes for pure-Python CPU; never block the event loop (Scenarios 1, 6, 16).
  2. Sessions are per-request, engines are global: never share a Session across threads, always commit/rollback/close (Scenarios 2, 3, 13).
  3. Invariants belong where the data lives: enforce uniqueness, stock, and balances in the DB with atomic updates, row locks, and constraints — not in-process locks (Scenarios 5, 8, 10, 11).
  4. Bound everything: concurrency (semaphore/pool), caches (maxsize/TTL), pools (size vs DB), transactions (keep short) (Scenarios 9, 12, 3, 10).
  5. Plan for failure & restarts: idempotency keys, retries with backoff, durable queues, and graceful drain-then-die shutdowns (Scenarios 7, 8, 10, 15).
Database and ORM66 sections

Database and ORM Topics

Fundamentals & Definitions

Before the performance material below, here are the core terms this topic assumes.

•

What is a Database?

databaseDBMSRelational (SQL) databasestablesschemasSQL

A database is an organized, persistent store of data managed by a DBMS (Database Management System) that handles storage, retrieval, concurrency, and integrity. Two broad families:

  • Relational (SQL) databasesdata in tables of rows and columns with enforced schemas and relationships (PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite). Queried with SQL.
  • NoSQL databasesnon-tabular models for flexibility/scale: document (MongoDB), key-value (Redis), wide-column (Cassandra), graph (Neo4j).
SQL (Relational)NoSQL
SchemaFixed, enforcedFlexible / schema-less
ScalingVertical (mostly)Horizontal-friendly
JoinsNativeLimited / app-side
Best forStructured data, transactions, integrityHigh volume, evolving/unstructured data
•

What is SQL?

SQL (Structured Query Language)DDLDMLDCL / TCL

SQL (Structured Query Language) is the standard language for relational databases, grouped into: - DDL (Data Definition): CREATE, ALTER, DROP — define schema. - DML (Data Manipulation): SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE — work with rows. - DCL / TCL: permissions (GRANT) and transactions (COMMIT, ROLLBACK).

•

What is a Transaction? (ACID)

transactionACIDAtomicityConsistencyIsolationDurability

A transaction is a unit of work that either fully completes or fully rolls back. Relational databases guarantee ACID:

  • Atomicityall statements succeed or none do.
  • Consistencythe database moves from one valid state to another (constraints hold).
  • Isolationconcurrent transactions don't corrupt each other (tuned via isolation levels).
  • Durabilityonce committed, data survives crashes.
try:
    db.add(order)
    db.add(payment)
    db.commit()        # both persisted atomically
except Exception:
    db.rollback()      # neither persisted

Deep dive: for how transactions work internally (WAL, MVCC, isolation levels, savepoints, distributed/outbox) and per-role guidance, see the Database Transactions (Deep Dive) section below.

•

What is an Index?

indexB-treewithout scanning the whole table

An index is an auxiliary data structure (usually a B-tree) that lets the database find rows by a column's value without scanning the whole table — turning an O(n) scan into roughly O(log n) lookup. Indexes speed up reads but slow down writes and use disk, so you add them deliberately (see the next section).

•

What is an ORM?

ORM (Object-Relational Mapper)tables to Python classesrows to objectsSQLAlchemyDjango ORMTortoise ORM

An ORM (Object-Relational Mapper) is a library that maps database tables to Python classes and rows to objects, so you read/write data with Python instead of hand-writing SQL. SQLAlchemy is the de-facto Python ORM; Django ORM and Tortoise ORM (async) are alternatives.

# Without ORM (raw SQL)
cur.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = %s", (1,))

# With ORM (SQLAlchemy)
user = db.query(User).get(1)   # returns a User object

Why use one: less boilerplate, database-agnostic code, automatic escaping (SQL-injection safety), and Python-native relationships. Cost: an abstraction layer that can hide expensive queries (see the N+1 problem).

•

SQLAlchemy: Engine, Session, and Models

Engineconnection poolSessionDeclarative model
  • Enginethe entry point that manages the DBAPI connection and a connection pool (reused TCP connections; opening a fresh DB connection per request is expensive).
  • Sessionthe ORM "workspace" / unit of work: it tracks object changes in memory and flushes them as SQL on commit(). Roughly one Session per request.
  • Declarative modela Python class inheriting from Base that maps to a table via __tablename__ and Column definitions.
from sqlalchemy import create_engine, Column, Integer, String
from sqlalchemy.orm import declarative_base, sessionmaker

engine = create_engine("postgresql://user:pass@localhost/mydb", pool_size=10)
Session = sessionmaker(bind=engine)
Base = declarative_base()

class User(Base):
    __tablename__ = "users"
    id = Column(Integer, primary_key=True)
    email = Column(String, unique=True, index=True)

with Session() as db:          # session per unit of work
    db.add(User(email="a@b.com"))
    db.commit()
•

Key terms used later in this topic

Primary keyForeign keyNormalizationdenormalizationMigrationAlembic
  • Primary keycolumn(s) uniquely identifying a row.
  • Foreign keycolumn referencing another table's primary key (defines relationships).
  • Normalizationstructuring tables to remove redundancy; denormalization trades redundancy for read speed.
  • Migrationa versioned, repeatable change to the database schema (managed by Alembic for SQLAlchemy).
  • Connection poola cache of open DB connections reused across requests to avoid reconnect overhead.
When to Use Indexes
•

Index Selection Rules

✅ Use Indexes ForWHERE Clause ColumnsForeign Key ColumnsORDER BY and GROUP BY ColumnsJOIN ColumnsDISTINCT Columns

✅ Use Indexes For:

  1. WHERE Clause Columns
# This query benefits from indexing 'email'
SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'user@example.com'

class User(Base):
    __tablename__ = "users"
    email = Column(String, index=True)  # Add index
  1. Foreign Key Columns
class Post(Base):
    __tablename__ = "posts"
    user_id = Column(Integer, ForeignKey('users.id'), index=True)
  1. ORDER BY and GROUP BY Columns
-- Benefits from index on 'created_at'
SELECT * FROM posts ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 10

-- Benefits from index on 'status'
SELECT status, COUNT(*) FROM posts GROUP BY status
  1. JOIN Columns
-- Index both sides of join
SELECT * FROM users 
JOIN posts ON users.id = posts.user_id

# Index both:
users.id (primary key - already indexed)
posts.user_id
  1. DISTINCT Columns
SELECT DISTINCT category FROM products
-- Index on 'category' speeds this up
  1. Unique Constraints
class User(Base):
    email = Column(String, unique=True)  # Index created automatically
    username = Column(String, unique=True)

❌ Don't Index:

  1. Low Cardinality Columns
# Bad: Only 2-3 unique values
class User(Base):
    is_active = Column(Boolean, index=True)  # Don't index!
    gender = Column(String(1), index=True)   # Don't index!
  1. Columns with Frequent Updates
# Bad: Constantly updated indexes cause overhead
class Product(Base):
    stock_count = Column(Integer, index=True)  # Don't index!
    last_updated = Column(DateTime, index=True)  # Avoid
  1. Small Tables
# For tables < 1000 rows, full table scan might be faster
class Config(Base):
    __tablename__ = "config"  # Don't index
  1. Text Columns (Large)
# Bad: Indexes on large text are expensive
class Article(Base):
    content = Column(Text, index=True)  # Don't index!
•

Index Selectivity

# High selectivity (good for indexing) - returns few rows
SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'john@example.com'  # 1 row

# Low selectivity (poor for indexing) - returns many rows
SELECT * FROM users WHERE is_active = True  # 50% of rows

# Check selectivity in PostgreSQL:
SELECT column_name, 
       COUNT(DISTINCT column_name) as distinct_values,
       COUNT(*) as total_rows
FROM users
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 2 DESC;
Index Types
•

1. B-Tree Index (Default)

from sqlalchemy import Index

class User(Base):
    __tablename__ = "users"
    email = Column(String, index=True)  # B-Tree by default
    
    # Explicit B-Tree
    __table_args__ = (
        Index('idx_email', 'email', mysql_length={'email': 255}),
    )

Use For: - Range queries (>, <, BETWEEN) - Equality (=) - ORDER BY - LIKE patterns (starting with known prefix)

•

2. Hash Index

Use ForAvoid
# PostgreSQL specific
class User(Base):
    __tablename__ = "users"
    
    __table_args__ = (
        Index('idx_user_id', 'user_id', postgresql_using='hash'),
    )

Use For: - Only equality comparisons - High cardinality columns

Avoid: - Range queries - Not suitable for most use cases

•

3. Composite Index

class Post(Base):
    __tablename__ = "posts"
    user_id = Column(Integer, ForeignKey('users.id'))
    created_at = Column(DateTime)
    is_published = Column(Boolean)
    
    # Multi-column index (order matters!)
    __table_args__ = (
        Index('idx_user_published_created', 'user_id', 'is_published', 'created_at'),
    )

# Queries that benefit:
# SELECT * FROM posts WHERE user_id = 1
# SELECT * FROM posts WHERE user_id = 1 AND is_published = True
# SELECT * FROM posts WHERE user_id = 1 AND is_published = True AND created_at > '2023-01-01'

# Queries that DON'T benefit:
# SELECT * FROM posts WHERE is_published = True  (doesn't start with user_id)
# SELECT * FROM posts WHERE created_at > '2023-01-01'  (doesn't start with user_id)

Index Column Order Rules: - Equality columns first - Range columns second - ORDER BY columns last

•

4. Partial Index

from sqlalchemy import Index, text

class Order(Base):
    __tablename__ = "orders"
    status = Column(String)
    created_at = Column(DateTime)
    
    # Only index active orders (saves space)
    __table_args__ = (
        Index('idx_active_orders', 'created_at', 
              postgresql_where=text('status = "active"')),
    )

# Benefits this query:
# SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = 'active' ORDER BY created_at DESC
•

5. GiST (Generalized Search Tree) Index

from sqlalchemy import Index
from geoalchemy2 import Geometry

class Location(Base):
    __tablename__ = "locations"
    geom = Column(Geometry('POINT'))
    
    __table_args__ = (
        Index('idx_location_geom', 'geom', postgresql_using='gist'),
    )

# For geographic/spatial queries:
# SELECT * FROM locations WHERE ST_DWithin(geom, POINT(0 0), 10)
Query Optimization
•

1. N+1 Query Problem

Bad ExampleSolution - Eager Loading

Bad Example:

# Runs N+1 queries: 1 for users + N queries for each user's posts
users = db.query(User).all()
for user in users:
    posts = db.query(Post).filter(Post.user_id == user.id).all()
    print(user.name, len(posts))

Solution - Eager Loading:

from sqlalchemy.orm import joinedload, selectinload

# Option 1: joinedload (single JOIN query)
users = db.query(User).options(joinedload(User.posts)).all()

# Option 2: selectinload (two queries, better for large datasets)
users = db.query(User).options(selectinload(User.posts)).all()

# Option 3: Manual JOIN
users = db.query(User).join(Post).filter(...).all()
•

2. Use Projection (Select Specific Columns)

# Bad: Fetch entire row
users = db.query(User).all()  # Returns all columns

# Good: Fetch only needed columns
user_names = db.query(User.id, User.name).all()
# Returns: [(1, 'John'), (2, 'Jane')]

# Projection with aggregation
post_counts = db.query(
    User.id,
    User.name,
    func.count(Post.id).label('post_count')
).join(Post).group_by(User.id, User.name).all()
•

3. Batch Operations

# Bad: Individual inserts (slow)
for user_data in users_list:
    user = User(**user_data)
    db.add(user)
    db.commit()

# Good: Bulk insert (fast)
db.bulk_insert_mappings(User, users_list)
db.commit()

# Good: Add multiple, single commit
for user_data in users_list:
    user = User(**user_data)
    db.add(user)
db.commit()

# Bulk update
db.query(User).filter(User.status == 'inactive').update(
    {User.status: 'active'},
    synchronize_session=False
)
db.commit()
•

4. Limit Result Sets

# Bad: Fetch all records
all_users = db.query(User).all()

# Good: Paginate
page = 1
page_size = 10
users = db.query(User).offset((page - 1) * page_size).limit(page_size).all()

# Count total for pagination
total = db.query(User).count()
pages = (total + page_size - 1) // page_size
•

5. Use Indexes in Query Planning

# View query plan (PostgreSQL)
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'test@example.com'

# If index isn't being used:
# - Check column data type matches
# - Ensure statistics are up to date (ANALYZE)
# - Check selectivity (not worth indexing if too many matches)

# Force index usage (last resort)
EXPLAIN ANALYZE 
SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'test@example.com' 
AND email IS NOT NULL  # Make query more selective
ORM vs Raw SQL Decision Tree
•

Use ORM When:

# ✅ Simple CRUD operations
user = db.query(User).filter(User.id == 1).first()

# ✅ Relationships needed
posts = user.posts  # Auto-loaded if defined in model

# ✅ Validation required
user = User(email="test@example.com")  # Validation happens

# ✅ Auto-generated IDs
db.add(user)
db.commit()
print(user.id)  # Auto-generated
•

Use Raw SQL When:

from sqlalchemy import text

# ✅ Complex analytical queries
result = db.execute(text("""
    SELECT u.id, u.name, COUNT(p.id) as post_count,
           AVG(p.likes) as avg_likes
    FROM users u
    LEFT JOIN posts p ON u.id = p.user_id
    WHERE u.created_at > :created_date
    GROUP BY u.id
    HAVING COUNT(p.id) > :min_posts
    ORDER BY avg_likes DESC
"""), {"created_date": "2023-01-01", "min_posts": 5})

# ✅ Performance-critical queries
result = db.execute(text("""
    SELECT * FROM posts 
    WHERE user_id = :user_id 
    AND is_published = true
    ORDER BY created_at DESC
    LIMIT :limit
"""), {"user_id": 1, "limit": 10})

# ✅ Complex joins
result = db.execute(text("""
    SELECT * FROM users u
    INNER JOIN posts p ON u.id = p.user_id
    INNER JOIN comments c ON p.id = c.post_id
    WHERE u.status = 'active'
    GROUP BY u.id
"""))
•

Hybrid Approach (Best Practice):

class UserRepository:
    def __init__(self, db: Session):
        self.db = db
    
    # Simple operations: ORM
    def get_user_by_id(self, user_id: int):
        return self.db.query(User).filter(User.id == user_id).first()
    
    # Complex queries: Raw SQL
    def get_user_engagement_stats(self, user_id: int):
        return self.db.execute(text("""
            SELECT u.name, COUNT(p.id) as posts, SUM(p.likes) as total_likes
            FROM users u
            LEFT JOIN posts p ON u.id = p.user_id
            WHERE u.id = :user_id
            GROUP BY u.id
        """), {"user_id": user_id}).fetchone()
Relationships in ORM
•

1. One-to-Many

class User(Base):
    __tablename__ = "users"
    id = Column(Integer, primary_key=True)
    name = Column(String)
    posts = relationship("Post", back_populates="user")

class Post(Base):
    __tablename__ = "posts"
    id = Column(Integer, primary_key=True)
    title = Column(String)
    user_id = Column(Integer, ForeignKey('users.id'))
    user = relationship("User", back_populates="posts")

# Usage
user = db.query(User).filter(User.id == 1).first()
posts = user.posts  # Auto-loaded
•

2. Many-to-Many

# Association table
post_tags = Table(
    'post_tags',
    Base.metadata,
    Column('post_id', Integer, ForeignKey('posts.id'), primary_key=True),
    Column('tag_id', Integer, ForeignKey('tags.id'), primary_key=True)
)

class Post(Base):
    __tablename__ = "posts"
    id = Column(Integer, primary_key=True)
    title = Column(String)
    tags = relationship("Tag", secondary=post_tags, back_populates="posts")

class Tag(Base):
    __tablename__ = "tags"
    id = Column(Integer, primary_key=True)
    name = Column(String)
    posts = relationship("Post", secondary=post_tags, back_populates="tags")

# Usage
post = db.query(Post).first()
post.tags.append(tag)  # Many-to-many relationship
db.commit()
•

3. Cascade Options

class User(Base):
    posts = relationship(
        "Post",
        cascade="all, delete-orphan",  # Delete posts when user deleted
        back_populates="user"
    )

class Post(Base):
    user_id = Column(Integer, ForeignKey('users.id', ondelete='CASCADE'))
    user = relationship("User", back_populates="posts")
Database Performance Tips
•

1. Connection Management

from sqlalchemy.pool import QueuePool, NullPool

# Production: Use connection pooling
engine = create_engine(
    "postgresql://user:password@localhost/db",
    poolclass=QueuePool,
    pool_size=20,
    max_overflow=40,
    pool_recycle=3600,  # Recycle old connections
    pool_pre_ping=True,  # Check connection health
)

# Development: No pooling
engine = create_engine(
    "sqlite:///test.db",
    poolclass=NullPool,
)
•

2. Lazy Loading vs Eager Loading

# Lazy loading (default) - loads when accessed
class User(Base):
    posts = relationship("Post")  # Loads when user.posts is accessed

# Eager loading - loads immediately
class User(Base):
    posts = relationship("Post", lazy='joined')  # Loads with user

# Control at query time
db.query(User).options(joinedload(User.posts)).all()
•

3. Database Maintenance

# PostgreSQL maintenance
VACUUM ANALYZE;  # Clean up and update statistics

# MySQL maintenance
OPTIMIZE TABLE users;
ANALYZE TABLE users;
•

4. Monitor Query Performance

from sqlalchemy import event
from sqlalchemy.engine import Engine

@event.listens_for(Engine, "before_cursor_execute")
def before_cursor_execute(conn, cursor, statement, parameters, context, executemany):
    print(f"Executing: {statement}")

# Or use logging
import logging
logging.basicConfig()
logging.getLogger('sqlalchemy.engine').setLevel(logging.INFO)

Alembic Setup

# Initialize
alembic init alembic

# Create migration
alembic revision --autogenerate -m "Add user email"

# Apply
