•

Best Practices

# alembic/env.py
from alembic import context
from sqlalchemy import engine_from_config, pool

# Always handle schema changes safely
def run_migrations_online() -> None:
    configuration = config.get_section(config.config_ini_section)
    configuration["sqlalchemy.url"] = os.environ.get("DATABASE_URL")
    
    connectable = engine_from_config(
        configuration,
        prefix="sqlalchemy.",
        poolclass=pool.NullPool,
    )
    
    with connectable.connect() as connection:
        context.configure(
            connection=connection, 
            target_metadata=target_metadata
        )
        
        with context.begin_transaction():
            context.run_migrations()
Normalization & Denormalization

These are two opposing ways to organize the columns and tables of a relational schema. Normalization removes redundancy for correctness; denormalization adds redundancy for read speed. Almost every real schema lives somewhere on the spectrum between them.

•

What is Normalization?

Normalizationeliminate data redundancyavoid update anomaliesnormal forms

Normalization is the process of structuring tables to eliminate data redundancy and avoid update anomalies by splitting data into related tables linked by foreign keys. You apply a series of rules called normal forms (1NF → 2NF → 3NF → BCNF), each stricter than the last.

The anomalies normalization prevents (illustrated with one bad "everything in one table" design):

   ❌ UNNORMALIZED "orders" table (redundant):
   ┌──────────┬───────────┬──────────────────┬──────────┬─────────┐
   │ order_id │ cust_name │ cust_email       │ product  │ price   │
   ├──────────┼───────────┼──────────────────┼──────────┼─────────┤
   │ 1        │ Alice     │ alice@mail.com   │ Keyboard │ 50      │
   │ 2        │ Alice     │ alice@mail.com   │ Mouse    │ 25      │   ← Alice repeated
   │ 3        │ Bob       │ bob@mail.com     │ Monitor  │ 200     │
   └──────────┴───────────┴──────────────────┴──────────┴─────────┘

   Problems:
   • UPDATE anomaly  → Alice changes email → must update MANY rows (miss one → inconsistent).
   • INSERT anomaly  → can't add a customer who hasn't ordered yet (no place to put them).
   • DELETE anomaly  → deleting Alice's only order erases her email entirely.
•

The Normal Forms (1NF → BCNF)

1NF2NF3NFBCNFPractical rule of thumbJOIN
FormRule (plain English)Fixes
1NFAtomic values only — no repeating groups or arrays in a cell; each row unique"comma-separated phone numbers in one column"
2NF1NF + every non-key column depends on the whole primary key (no partial dependency)columns that depend on only part of a composite key
3NF2NF + no non-key column depends on another non-key column (no transitive dependency)e.g., zip → city stored in an orders table
BCNFStronger 3NF — every determinant is a candidate keyrare edge cases 3NF misses

Practical rule of thumb: "normalize until it hurts, denormalize until it works." 3NF is the default target for transactional (OLTP) systems — it removes the dangerous anomalies without over-fragmenting your schema.

Normalized version of the example above (3NF — split into two tables):

class Customer(Base):
    __tablename__ = "customers"
    id    = Column(Integer, primary_key=True)
    name  = Column(String)
    email = Column(String, unique=True)          # stored ONCE — single source of truth
    orders = relationship("Order", back_populates="customer")

class Order(Base):
    __tablename__ = "orders"
    id          = Column(Integer, primary_key=True)
    customer_id = Column(Integer, ForeignKey("customers.id"), index=True)  # link, no duplication
    product     = Column(String)
    price       = Column(Numeric)
    customer    = relationship("Customer", back_populates="orders")

Now Alice's email exists in exactly one place — update it once, no anomalies. The cost: reading "orders with customer name" requires a JOIN.

•

What is Denormalization?

Denormalizationreintroduces redundancyCommon denormalization techniquesPre-joined / wide tablesMaterialized viewsComputed/aggregate columns

Denormalization deliberately reintroduces redundancy — copying or pre-joining data — to avoid expensive JOINs and speed up reads. You trade storage space and write complexity for read performance.

   NORMALIZED (read needs a JOIN)              DENORMALIZED (read is a single-table scan)
   customers ──┐                               ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   orders   ───┘ JOIN on customer_id           │ order_id │ customer_name │ product │ price  │
                                               │  (customer_name copied into each order row) │
                                               └─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
   ✅ no duplication, easy writes               ✅ fast reads, no JOIN
   ❌ JOIN cost on every read                   ❌ duplication; name change → update many rows

Common denormalization techniques: - Pre-joined / wide tables — store the joined result (a read model). - Materialized views — DB-maintained cached query results (REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW). - Computed/aggregate columns — store comment_count on posts instead of COUNT(*) every read. - Duplicated reference data — copy customer_name into orders so order lists need no JOIN.

# Example: denormalized counter to avoid COUNT(*) on every page load
class Post(Base):
    __tablename__ = "posts"
    id            = Column(Integer, primary_key=True)
    title         = Column(String)
    comment_count = Column(Integer, default=0)   # denormalized; updated when a comment is added

# Keep it in sync on write (the cost of denormalization moves to write time):
def add_comment(db, post, body):
    db.add(Comment(post_id=post.id, body=body))
    post.comment_count += 1          # must remember to maintain this everywhere comments change
    db.commit()
•

Normalization vs Denormalization — Trade-offs

The mature patternnormalized source of truthCQRS
Normalized (3NF)Denormalized
RedundancyNoneIntentional duplication
StorageMinimalMore
ReadsSlower (JOINs)Fast (single table)
WritesSimple, update onceComplex, update many copies
Data integrityHigh (single source of truth)Risk of drift / inconsistency
Best forOLTP, write-heavy, integrity-criticalOLAP, read-heavy, latency-critical

The mature pattern: keep a normalized source of truth for writes, and build denormalized read models / materialized views for fast reads. This is the core idea behind CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation). See ../../11_System_Design/01_The_Scaling_Blueprint_Zero_to_Millions.md.

Partitioning (Vertical & Horizontal)

Partitioning = splitting a large table into smaller pieces so queries touch less data and the system scales. There are two directions, and they're often confused:

   A SINGLE LARGE TABLE
   ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │ id │ name │ email │ bio(big) │ created_at         │
   │ r1 ...                                            │
   │ r2 ...                                              │   VERTICAL split → by COLUMNS
   │ r3 ...                                              │   ─────────────────────────────▶
   │ ...                                               │
   └───────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
            │
            ▼  HORIZONTAL split → by ROWS
Vertical PartitioningHorizontal Partitioning (→ Sharding)
Splits byColumnsRows
Each piece hasA subset of columns, same rowsAll columns, a subset of rows
GoalSeparate hot vs cold columns; reduce I/ODistribute volume/load across storage or servers
Linked byShared primary keyIndependent — each partition is self-contained
•

Vertical Partitioning

WhyTOAST

Split a wide table by columns based on access patterns — keep frequently-read ("hot") columns in one narrow table, and large or rarely-used ("cold") columns in another. Both tables share the same primary key.

   users (wide, slow)                  SPLIT into:

   ┌──────────────────────────┐   user_core (HOT — read constantly)   user_extra (COLD — rarely)
   │ id │ name │ email │ bio   │   ┌────┬──────┬───────┐               ┌────┬───────────┬─────────┐
   │    │      │       │(10 KB)│   │ id │ name │ email │               │ id │ bio       │ settings│
   └──────────────────────────┘   └────┴──────┴───────┘               └────┴───────────┴──────────┘
                                        same id  ◀───── shared primary key ─────▶  same id

Why: a query like SELECT id, name, email FROM users no longer drags the 10 KB bio column off disk for every row → less I/O, more rows per page, better cache hit rates.

class UserCore(Base):                 # hot columns, read on every request
    __tablename__ = "user_core"
    id    = Column(Integer, primary_key=True)
    name  = Column(String)
    email = Column(String, unique=True, index=True)
    extra = relationship("UserExtra", uselist=False, back_populates="core")

class UserExtra(Base):                 # cold/bulky columns, fetched only when needed
    __tablename__ = "user_extra"
    id       = Column(Integer, ForeignKey("user_core.id"), primary_key=True)
    bio      = Column(Text)
    settings = Column(JSON)
    core     = relationship("UserCore", back_populates="extra")

Note: vertical partitioning into separate tables is an app-level design choice. Postgres/MySQL also do this physically (e.g., Postgres TOAST automatically stores large values out-of-line).

•

Horizontal Partitioning

Split a table by rowspartition keyWithin one databasetable partitioningAcross multiple serverssharding

Split a table by rows — each partition holds the same columns but a different subset of rows, chosen by a partition key.

  • Within one database this is table partitioning (Postgres declarative partitioning, MySQL PARTITION BY). Great for time-series: partition by month, drop old partitions instantly, and let the planner prune irrelevant partitions.
  • Across multiple servers this becomes sharding (next section).
-- PostgreSQL: range-partition orders by month (single DB, many partitions)
CREATE TABLE orders (id BIGINT, created_at DATE, amount NUMERIC)
    PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at);

CREATE TABLE orders_2024_01 PARTITION OF orders
    FOR VALUES FROM ('2024-01-01') TO ('2024-02-01');
CREATE TABLE orders_2024_02 PARTITION OF orders
    FOR VALUES FROM ('2024-02-01') TO ('2024-03-01');

-- A query with WHERE created_at >= '2024-02-01' only scans orders_2024_02 (partition pruning).
-- Deleting old data is instant: DROP TABLE orders_2024_01;  (vs a slow bulk DELETE)
Sharding — How It Works

Sharding = horizontal partitioning across multiple independent database servers. Each server (a shard) holds a slice of the rows and handles only that slice's reads and writes. This is the main tool for scaling writes and total dataset size beyond a single machine — the one thing replication alone can't do.

   ┌─────────────────────── ALL USERS (too big for one server) ────────────────────────┐
   │  user_id 1–1M   │   user_id 1M–2M   │   user_id 2M–3M   │   ...                   │
   └────────┬────────────────────┬─────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┘
            ▼                     ▼                     ▼
      ┌───────────┐         ┌───────────┐         ┌───────────┐
      │  SHARD A  │         │  SHARD B  │         │  SHARD C  │     ← separate DB servers
      │ (server1) │         │ (server2) │         │ (server3) │       each holds ~1/3 of data
      └───────────┘         └───────────┘         └───────────┘       & ~1/3 of the traffic
•

How a sharded query is routed

  1. App receives request for user_id = 1_500_000
  2. Shard router applies the shard function: shard = route(shard_key)
  3. Router connects to the correct shard (Shard B) and runs the query there
  4. Result returned — other shards were never touched
•

Sharding Strategies (how to pick the shard for a key)

1. Range-basedrange scansHotspots2. Hash-basedEven distributionevery

1. Range-based — assign contiguous key ranges to shards.

def route(user_id):
    if user_id < 1_000_000:   return "shard_a"
    if user_id < 2_000_000:   return "shard_b"
    return "shard_c"
  • ✅ Simple; efficient range scans (e.g., "users 1M–1.1M" hit one shard).
  • ❌ Hotspots — if new users (high IDs) are the most active, the newest shard gets hammered.

2. Hash-based — hash the key and mod by shard count for even spread.

def route(user_id, num_shards=3):
    return f"shard_{hash(user_id) % num_shards}"
  • ✅ Even distribution, avoids hotspots.
  • ❌ Range queries now hit every shard; resharding (changing num_shards) remaps almost all keys → massive data movement.

3. Consistent hashing — map keys and shards onto a hash ring; a key belongs to the next shard clockwise. Adding/removing a shard only moves the keys in one segment, not all of them. - ✅ Minimal data movement on rebalancing — used by Cassandra, DynamoDB, Riak. - ❌ More complex; needs virtual nodes to keep the ring balanced.

4. Directory / lookup-based — a lookup service maps each key (or key range) → shard. - ✅ Most flexible; can move individual keys, supports uneven shards. - ❌ The lookup table is an extra hop and a potential single point of failure (must be HA + cached).

•

Choosing the Shard Key (the most important decision)

Spreads load evenlyMatches the most common queryAvoids hotspots

A good shard key: 1. Spreads load evenly (high cardinality, no single dominant value). 2. Matches the most common query so requests hit a single shard (avoid scatter-gather). 3. Avoids hotspots (don't shard a global app by country if one country is 80% of traffic).

   ❌ Bad: shard by `status` (only a few values) → all "active" rows pile onto one shard.
   ❌ Bad: shard by `created_at` → all *new* writes hit the newest shard (write hotspot).
   ✅ Good: shard by `user_id` (hashed) for a per-user workload → even spread, single-shard reads.
   ✅ Good: shard by `tenant_id` for multi-tenant SaaS → each customer isolated to one shard.
•

The Hard Parts of Sharding (why it's a last resort)

Cross-shard joins/queriesCross-shard transactionsRebalancing / reshardingHotspotsOperational complexityindexes
ChallengeWhat goes wrongMitigation
Cross-shard joins/queriesData for a query lives on multiple shardsDenormalize; query each shard and merge in app (scatter-gather); avoid by good key choice
Cross-shard transactionsACID across servers is hardKeep transactions within one shard; else use sagas / 2PC
Rebalancing / reshardingAdding a shard moves huge amounts of dataConsistent hashing; over-provision shards up front
HotspotsOne shard overloaded (celebrity user, bad key)Better key; split the hot shard; add caching
Operational complexityBackups, migrations, monitoring × N shardsAutomation; managed sharded DBs (Vitess, Citus, MongoDB)
Unique constraints / auto-incrementIDs can collide across shardsUse UUIDs or a distributed ID generator (Snowflake)

Order of operations for scaling a DB: ① add indexes & optimize queries → ② add a cache → ③ add read replicas → ④ vertically partition hot/cold columns → ⑤ shard only when writes/size truly exceed one machine. Sharding adds permanent complexity, so exhaust the cheaper options first.

Replication & Scaling Reads

Replication = keeping copies of the database on multiple servers. Unlike sharding (which splits data), replication copies the whole dataset. It scales reads and provides high availability, but does not increase write capacity or total storage (every replica holds everything).

                        WRITES
                          │
                          ▼
                  ┌────────────────┐
                  │ PRIMARY (R/W)  │  ── all writes go here
                  └───────┬────────┘
        replicate ┌───────┼───────┐ replicate
                  ▼       ▼       ▼
            ┌─────────┐┌─────────┐┌─────────┐
            │ REPLICA ││ REPLICA ││ REPLICA │  ── serve READS only
            └─────────┘└─────────┘└─────────┘

Key concepts: - Read/write split — point writes at the primary, reads at replicas. Most apps are read-heavy (~90% reads), so this is a big, cheap win. - Replication lag — replicas trail the primary by milliseconds to seconds. A user who writes then immediately reads from a replica may not see their own change → route critical "read-your-writes" queries to the primary. - Sync vs async — synchronous = primary waits for replicas (no data loss, slower writes); asynchronous = primary doesn't wait (fast, small risk of loss on failover). - Failover — if the primary dies, a replica is promoted to primary (automatic with managed DBs / Patroni / orchestrators).

# Route reads to a replica engine, writes to the primary (app-level read/write split)
write_engine = create_engine("postgresql://user:pass@primary/db")
read_engine  = create_engine("postgresql://user:pass@replica/db")

WriteSession = sessionmaker(bind=write_engine)
ReadSession  = sessionmaker(bind=read_engine)

def get_user(user_id):            # read → replica
    with ReadSession() as db:
        return db.query(User).get(user_id)

def create_user(data):            # write → primary
    with WriteSession() as db:
        db.add(User(**data)); db.commit()

Replication and sharding are complementary, not alternatives: large systems shard for write scale, then replicate each shard for read scale and availability. See ../../11_System_Design/01_The_Scaling_Blueprint_Zero_to_Millions.md and ../../11_System_Design/09_Data_Systems_Internals.md.

Scaling Decision Guide

When the database is the bottleneck, apply these in order — each step is cheaper and less complex than the next:

   PROBLEM                                  →  FIX (in order of preference)
   ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   Slow specific queries                    →  1. Add/refine INDEXES, optimize SQL (EXPLAIN)
   Repeated identical reads                  →  2. Add a CACHE (Redis) — serve from RAM
   Too many reads for one server            →  3. Add READ REPLICAS (read/write split)
   Wide table, hot+cold columns mixed       →  4. VERTICAL PARTITIONING (split columns)
   One server can't hold the data / writes  →  5. SHARDING (horizontal partition across servers)
   Read-heavy with expensive JOINs          →  +  DENORMALIZE into read models / materialized views
TechniqueScalesAddsComplexity
IndexingRead speed—Low
CachingRead throughputStaleness/invalidationLow–Med
ReplicationReads + availabilityReplication lagMedium
Vertical partitioningI/O efficiencyAn extra table/joinLow–Med
ShardingWrites + total sizeCross-shard painHigh
DenormalizationRead latencyDuplication/write costMedium
Summary Table
DecisionUse CaseProsCons
Index WHERE columnFilteringFaster queriesSlower writes
No index on booleanLow cardinalityReduces overheadNo benefit
Composite indexMulti-column queriesEfficientComplex
Eager loadingAccess relationshipsNo N+1More data
ORMSimple CRUDSafe, easySlower
Raw SQLComplex queriesFast, flexibleError-prone
Normalization (3NF)OLTP, integrity-criticalNo anomalies, single source of truthJOINs on read
DenormalizationRead-heavy, low-latencyFast reads, no JOINsDuplication, harder writes
Vertical partitioningWide tables, hot+cold columnsLess I/O, better cacheExtra join for cold data
Sharding (horizontal)Write/size beyond one serverScales writes & storageCross-shard joins, ops complexity
Read replicasRead-heavy workloadsScales reads, HAReplication lag, stale reads
Database Transactions (Deep Dive)

How transactions actually work inside the database (WAL, MVCC, isolation levels, savepoints, distributed/outbox) plus the Python/SQLAlchemy patterns, with a lens for each role.

•

1. Definitions (precise)

Transactionsingle, indivisible unit of workCommitpermanentRollbackall
TermDefinition
TransactionA sequence of one or more SQL statements executed as a single, indivisible unit of work that either fully commits or fully rolls back.
CommitMake all of a transaction's changes permanent and visible to other transactions.
RollbackDiscard all of a transaction's uncommitted changes, returning the DB to its pre-transaction state.
Atomic"All-or-nothing": a transaction's statements cannot partially apply.
Isolation levelA setting that controls what one transaction can see of another's in-flight changes, trading consistency for concurrency.
Concurrency anomalyAn incorrect result caused by interleaved transactions (dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom, lost update, write skew).
LockA reservation on a row/table that blocks conflicting access until the holding transaction ends.
MVCCMulti-Version Concurrency Control — the DB keeps multiple versions of a row so readers don't block writers and each transaction sees a consistent snapshot.
WALWrite-Ahead Log — changes are written to an append-only log before the data files, so a crash can be recovered. This is what makes commits durable.
SavepointA named marker inside a transaction you can partially roll back to without aborting the whole transaction.
DeadlockTwo transactions each holding a lock the other needs → neither can proceed; the DB kills one.
AutocommitA mode where each statement is its own transaction, committed immediately.
2PCTwo-Phase Commit — a protocol to commit a transaction atomically across multiple databases/resources.
•

2. What a transaction is — and why it exists

A transaction groups several operations so the database guarantees they behave as one. The canonical example is a bank transfer:

BEGIN;
  UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 1;   -- debit
  UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 100 WHERE id = 2;   -- credit
COMMIT;

Without a transaction, a crash between the two updates would destroy ₹100 — money leaves account 1 and never arrives in account 2. The transaction makes both happen or neither. Any time two or more writes must be consistent together, you need a transaction. The same applies to "create order + decrement inventory + write payment record," "insert prediction + update job status," or "write document row + write its embedding metadata."

•

3. The transaction lifecycle

BEGIN / START TRANSACTIONDo worknotCOMMITROLLBACKKey idea
BEGIN ──► [ statements: SELECT / INSERT / UPDATE / DELETE ] ──► COMMIT   (changes permanent)
                                  │
                                  └──────────────────────────► ROLLBACK (changes discarded)
  1. BEGIN / START TRANSACTIONopens the transaction. (Many drivers do this implicitly on the first statement.)
  2. Do workrun statements. Changes are visible to this transaction but, depending on isolation, not to others yet.
  3. COMMITdurably persist everything; release locks; make changes visible.
  4. ROLLBACKthrow away all changes (triggered explicitly, by an error, or by a crash).

Key idea: until COMMIT, your changes are provisional. A connection that opens a transaction and never commits/rolls back holds locks and a snapshot open — a frequent source of production pain (bloat, lock waits, pool exhaustion).

•

4. ACID, properly explained

AtomicityConsistencyvalidIsolationDurabilityrules
PropertyWhat it guaranteesWhat enforces itIf it were missing
AtomicityAll statements apply, or none doRollback + the undo/WAL logHalf-finished transfers, orphaned rows
ConsistencyThe DB moves from one valid state to another (constraints, FKs, triggers hold)Constraints + your transaction logicNegative stock, dangling foreign keys
IsolationConcurrent transactions don't corrupt each other's viewIsolation levels (locks/MVCC)Dirty/phantom reads, lost updates
DurabilityOnce committed, data survives a crash/power lossWAL flushed to disk (fsync) before commit returns"Committed" data vanishing on reboot

Consistency vs Isolation (a common mix-up): Consistency is about rules (a transaction never leaves the DB violating a constraint). Isolation is about concurrency (how much of an in-flight transaction others can see). They're different guarantees.

•

5. How the database makes it work (internals)

WALreplaysreversesnapshot

You don't need to implement these, but understanding them explains every behavior above.

Durability via the Write-Ahead Log (WAL)

Before changing the actual data files, the DB appends the change to a sequential WAL and fsyncs it to disk. Only then does COMMIT return success. If the server crashes, on restart it replays the WAL to recover committed transactions and discards uncommitted ones. Sequential log writes are far faster than random data-file writes, so this is both safe and fast.

Atomicity via undo information

The DB records enough to reverse each change (PostgreSQL keeps old row versions; others use an undo log). ROLLBACK — or crash recovery — uses it to erase a partial transaction.

Visibility

Each transaction gets a notion of "what counts as committed for me." In an MVCC database (PostgreSQL, Oracle, MySQL/InnoDB) that's a snapshot: reads see a consistent point-in-time view, unaffected by concurrent uncommitted writes.

•

6. Isolation levels & the anomalies they prevent

Read UncommittedRead CommittedRepeatable ReadSerializableThe anomalies, concretelyDirty read

Stronger isolation = fewer anomalies but more contention. The SQL standard defines four levels by which anomalies they forbid:

Isolation levelDirty readNon-repeatable readPhantom read
Read Uncommittedpossiblepossiblepossible
Read Committed (PostgreSQL default)preventedpossiblepossible
Repeatable Read (MySQL/InnoDB default)preventedpreventedpossible*
Serializablepreventedpreventedprevented

* PostgreSQL's Repeatable Read (snapshot isolation) also prevents phantoms.

The anomalies, concretely:

  • Dirty readyou read another transaction's uncommitted change; it then rolls back and you acted on data that never existed.
  • Non-repeatable readyou read a row twice in one transaction and get different values because another transaction committed an update in between.
  • Phantom readyou run the same WHERE query twice and the set of rows changes (someone inserted/deleted matching rows).
  • Lost updatetwo transactions read the same row, both write; the second silently overwrites the first. (See optimistic/pessimistic locking below.)
  • Write skewtwo transactions each read a shared invariant, then write disjoint rows that together violate it (e.g. both doctors go off-call because each saw the other on-call). Only Serializable prevents this.
# Set isolation per transaction in SQLAlchemy
with engine.connect().execution_options(isolation_level="SERIALIZABLE") as conn:
    with conn.begin():
        ...

Rule of thumb: use the lowest level that prevents the anomalies your use case can't tolerate. Read Committed is fine for most CRUD; use Repeatable Read for a consistent multi-query report; use Serializable (with retries) for invariants like booking/inventory where write skew is possible.

•

7. Locking vs MVCC

Lockingshared (read)exclusive (write)MVCCnew versionexplicit

Two strategies databases use to enforce isolation:

  • Lockinga transaction takes a shared (read) or exclusive (write) lock on rows; others wait. Simple but readers and writers can block each other.
  • MVCCwriters create a new version of a row instead of overwriting; readers see the version valid for their snapshot. Readers never block writers and writers never block readers. PostgreSQL, Oracle, and MySQL/InnoDB use MVCC for normal reads.

You still take explicit locks when you must serialize a read-modify-write:

-- Pessimistic lock: nobody else can modify this row until I commit
SELECT * FROM accounts WHERE id = 1 FOR UPDATE;
# SQLAlchemy: with_for_update()  → SELECT ... FOR UPDATE
acct = db.execute(select(Account).where(Account.id == 1).with_for_update()).scalar_one()
acct.balance -= 100
db.commit()                          # lock released here

Optimistic vs pessimistic for the lost update problem: - Pessimistic — lock the row up front (FOR UPDATE). Good for high contention / money. - Optimistic — add a version column; on write check it hasn't changed and bump it; a mismatch → retry (or 409). Good for low contention. (Worked examples in Python_FastAPI_Threading_ORM_Scenarios.)

•

8. Savepoints & nested transactions

A savepoint lets you roll back part of a transaction without aborting all of it.

BEGIN;
  INSERT INTO orders ...;
  SAVEPOINT before_items;
  INSERT INTO order_items ...;     -- this fails
  ROLLBACK TO before_items;        -- undo just the items, keep the order
  INSERT INTO order_items ...;     -- retry
COMMIT;

In SQLAlchemy, begin_nested() issues a SAVEPOINT — useful to attempt a risky sub-step and recover:

with Session() as db:
    db.add(order)
    try:
        with db.begin_nested():          # SAVEPOINT
            db.add(risky_child)
            db.flush()
    except IntegrityError:
        pass                              # rolled back to the savepoint; order survives
    db.commit()
•

9. Transactions in Python

already in a transactionKeep transactions short

9.1 Raw DBAPI (PEP 249)

A DBAPI connection is already in a transaction; you must commit() or it rolls back on close.

import psycopg2
conn = psycopg2.connect(DSN)
try:
    cur = conn.cursor()
    cur.execute("UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = %s", (1,))
    cur.execute("UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 100 WHERE id = %s", (2,))
    conn.commit()                # both or neither
except Exception:
    conn.rollback()
    raise
finally:
    conn.close()

9.2 SQLAlchemy Core — engine.begin()

A context manager that commits on success, rolls back on exception:

with engine.begin() as conn:                      # BEGIN
    conn.execute(update(Account).where(Account.id == 1).values(balance=Account.balance - 100))
    conn.execute(update(Account).where(Account.id == 2).values(balance=Account.balance + 100))
# COMMIT here automatically; ROLLBACK if the block raised

9.3 SQLAlchemy ORM — Session as unit of work

The Session batches your object changes and emits them in one transaction at commit().

with Session() as db:                  # opens a transaction lazily
    db.add(Order(...))
    db.add(Payment(...))
    db.commit()                        # flush + COMMIT atomically
    # any exception before commit → context manager rolls back

9.4 FastAPI: one transaction per request

The request-scoped dependency commits on success, rolls back on error, always closes — so a failed handler can't leak a half-finished transaction onto a pooled connection:

def get_db():
    db = SessionLocal()
    try:
        yield db
        db.commit()
    except Exception:
        db.rollback()
        raise
    finally:
        db.close()

Keep transactions short. Never hold one open across a slow external API call or user think-time — it pins a connection and (in MVCC DBs) blocks vacuum/cleanup, causing bloat.

•

10. Distributed transactions & the dual-write problem

two different systemsanddual-write problemTwo-Phase Commit (2PC)Transactional OutboxSaga

A single DB transaction can't span two different systems (e.g. Postgres and a vector DB, and a message broker). The "dual-write problem": you write to system A, then system B — and a crash in between leaves them inconsistent.

Options:

  • Two-Phase Commit (2PC)a coordinator asks all resources to prepare, then commit. Strong but slow, fragile, and poorly supported across modern stores — usually avoided.
  • Transactional Outboxwithin the same DB transaction, write your business row and an outbox row describing the event; a separate poller reads the outbox and publishes to Kafka/the vector DB/etc. Now the two writes are one atomic DB commit. The standard, robust pattern.
  • Sagamodel a multi-service workflow as a series of local transactions, each with a compensating action to undo it if a later step fails (e.g. "refund" compensates "charge").
  • Idempotency + retriesmake each step safe to repeat, then retry until consistent (eventual consistency).
# Transactional outbox: business write + event are ONE transaction
with Session() as db:
    db.add(Document(id=doc_id, text=text))
    db.add(Outbox(topic="embed", payload={"doc_id": doc_id}))   # same commit
    db.commit()
# A separate worker later reads Outbox and writes to the vector DB / publishes the event.
•

11. Common failure modes & how to handle them

SymptomCauseFix
could not serialize access (SQLSTATE 40001)Serializable/Repeatable-Read conflictRetry the whole transaction (expected under Serializable)
Deadlock detectedLocks acquired in opposite ordersConsistent lock ordering, short txns, retry the victim
idle in transaction connectionsA transaction opened but never committedCommit/rollback promptly; never await external I/O mid-txn
Lost update (silent overwrite)Read-modify-write raceOptimistic version column or FOR UPDATE
Table bloat / slow VACUUM (Postgres)Long-running transactions hold old snapshotsKeep transactions short; move analytics to a replica
Pool exhaustionSessions/connections not returnedwith/finally close; size pool vs DB limit
# Retry pattern for serialization failures (and deadlocks)
from sqlalchemy.exc import OperationalError
from tenacity import retry, retry_if_exception_type, stop_after_attempt, wait_random_exponential

@retry(retry=retry_if_exception_type(OperationalError),
       wait=wait_random_exponential(min=0.05, max=1), stop=stop_after_attempt(3))
def run_txn():
    with Session.begin() as db:
        ...
•

12. Role lenses: Backend · AI · ML · Data Science

Why it mattersone transactionoversell/double-chargeidempotency keysOne transaction per requestoutbox

Same mechanics, different stakes. Here's why transactions matter to each role and the patterns each should reach for.

🐍 Python Backend Engineer

Why it matters: correctness of money, orders, inventory, and user state under concurrency. - Wrap multi-write operations (order + payment + inventory) in one transaction. - Prevent oversell/double-charge with FOR UPDATE or atomic UPDATE ... WHERE, plus idempotency keys for retried POSTs. - One transaction per request (the FastAPI dependency in §9.4); keep it short. - Use the outbox pattern to emit events/webhooks consistently with the DB write.

Interview line: "For anything touching money I use an explicit transaction with row locking or an atomic conditional update, and an idempotency key so client retries can't double-apply."

🤖 AI Engineer (LLM apps / RAG / agents)

Why it matters: keeping a relational store, a vector DB, conversation history, and usage metering consistent — classic dual-write territory. - When you persist a document and its embedding metadata, you can't span Postgres + the vector store in one DB transaction → use the transactional outbox (§10) so the relational write and the "go embed this" event commit together. - Make webhook/event and tool-call handlers idempotent (LLM pipelines retry); dedupe on an event/request id — same at-least-once model as 34_API_Consumption and 25_FastAPI task queues. - Billing/token metering must be exact — increment usage inside the same transaction that records the request, or you'll under/over-bill. - Persist conversation turns atomically so a crash mid-response doesn't leave half a message.

Interview line: "The vector DB and Postgres can't share a transaction, so I commit the row plus an outbox event atomically and let a worker propagate to the index — no dual-write inconsistency."

📈 ML Engineer (pipelines / feature stores / serving)

Why it matters: reproducibility and avoiding partial writes in training/serving pipelines. - Point-in-time correctness in feature stores: read features as of a snapshot so training labels aren't contaminated by future data — isolation/snapshots make reads reproducible. - Make each pipeline step idempotent and atomic — a re-run (Airflow retry) must not double-write predictions or features. Use INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (UPSERT) inside a transaction, or write-to-staging-then-atomic-swap. - Model registry updates (new version + metrics + "is_production" flag) must be one transaction so a half-promoted model never serves. - For big batch writes, prefer bulk inserts / COPY in a single transaction over per-row commits (see the Database & ORM interview drills, Q20).

Interview line: "Pipeline steps are idempotent UPSERTs inside a transaction, so an Airflow retry re-runs safely and never leaves partial feature rows."

📊 Data Scientist / Analyst

Why it matters: consistent, reproducible reads — and not hurting the production DB. - For a multi-query report that must be internally consistent, run it in a Repeatable Read transaction so every query sees the same snapshot (no rows shifting mid-report). - Don't leave transactions open in a notebook — an idle-in-transaction connection blocks cleanup and holds locks. Read, then commit/close (pandas.read_sql with a context-managed connection). - Run heavy analytical queries against a read replica, not the primary, so long scans don't contend with production writes (and so a long snapshot doesn't bloat the primary). - Understand that on a replica you may read slightly stale data (replication lag) — fine for analytics, not for read-after-write checks.

Interview line: "For a consistent dashboard query I use a single Repeatable-Read snapshot on a read replica, and I never hold the transaction open past the read."

•

13. Checklist & interview soundbites

Checklistoneshortlowest isolation levelretryoutbox / saga + idempotency

Checklist - ✅ Group co-dependent writes into one transaction; commit on success, rollback on error. - ✅ Keep transactions short — no external I/O or user wait-time inside them. - ✅ Pick the lowest isolation level that blocks the anomalies you can't tolerate; retry serialization failures and deadlocks. - ✅ Serialize read-modify-write with FOR UPDATE (pessimistic) or a version column (optimistic). - ✅ Can't span two systems in one DB transaction → outbox / saga + idempotency, not 2PC. - ✅ One transaction per request (backend); idempotent atomic steps (ML/AI pipelines); snapshot reads on a replica (data science).

Soundbites - "A transaction is an all-or-nothing unit of work guaranteed by ACID." - "Durability comes from the write-ahead log; atomicity from undo/rollback." - "Isolation levels trade consistency for concurrency — Read Committed by default, Serializable (with retries) when write skew is possible." - "MVCC means readers don't block writers; take explicit FOR UPDATE locks only when you must." - "You can't put a relational write and a vector-DB/Kafka write in one transaction — use the transactional outbox."

See also: the earlier sections of this document (indexes, query tuning, ORM), and the Database & ORM interview drills (Q3 ACID, Q5 isolation, Q14 deadlock, Q18 locking), and the cross-cutting Python_FastAPI_Threading_ORM_Scenarios.md.

ORM Internals & Prisma

A deeper look at what an ORM is (patterns, trade-offs, the Python landscape) and a tour of Prisma, the schema-first ORM, compared with SQLAlchemy.

•

1. What is an ORM?

ORM (Object-Relational Mapper)database tables ↔ classes/objectstablemodel/classrowobject/record

An ORM (Object-Relational Mapper) is a library that maps database tables ↔ classes/objects, letting you read and write data using your programming language instead of hand-writing SQL strings.

  • A table maps to a model/class.
  • A row maps to an object/record.
  • A column maps to an attribute/field.
  • A foreign-key relationship maps to an object reference (user.posts).
# Raw SQL — you write the query, parse rows, handle escaping yourself
cur.execute("SELECT id, email FROM users WHERE id = %s", (1,))
row = cur.fetchone()          # a tuple: (1, "a@b.com")

# ORM — you work with objects; the ORM generates parameterized SQL
user = db.query(User).get(1)  # a User object: user.id, user.email

The name comes from the object-relational impedance mismatch: object-oriented code thinks in objects, graphs, and inheritance; relational databases think in tables, rows, and joins. The ORM is the translation layer between those two worlds.

•

2. The problem an ORM solves

automatic mappingrelationship navigationchange trackingdatabase portability

Without an ORM you repeatedly write boilerplate that is tedious and error-prone:

# Manual data-access layer
sql = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '" + email + "'"   # ❌ SQL injection!
cur.execute(sql)
rows = cur.fetchall()
users = [User(id=r[0], email=r[1]) for r in rows]            # manual row→object mapping

Problems: SQL-injection risk from string building, brittle index-based row unpacking, duplicated mapping code, and database-specific SQL dialects. An ORM removes all of that: parameterized queries (injection-safe), automatic mapping, relationship navigation, change tracking, and often database portability.

•

3. ORM patterns: Active Record vs Data Mapper

Active RecordDjango ORMData MapperSessionSQLAlchemyWhere does Prisma fit?

Two classic designs (Martin Fowler's patterns) — knowing which an ORM uses explains its API:

PatternIdeaThe object…Examples
Active RecordThe model object is the row and knows how to persist itself…has .save(), .delete() on itDjango ORM, Rails, Tortoise ORM
Data MapperA separate layer (a session) moves data between objects and the DB…is a plain object; a Session persists itSQLAlchemy (ORM), Hibernate
# Active Record (Django): the object persists itself
user = User(email="a@b.com")
user.save()

# Data Mapper (SQLAlchemy): a session is the unit of work
user = User(email="a@b.com")
db.add(user)        # session tracks it
db.commit()         # session flushes the SQL

Where does Prisma fit? Prisma is neither classic Active Record nor classic Data Mapper. It generates a type-safe query-builder client from a schema: you call methods on the client (prisma.user.create(...), prisma.user.find_many(...)) rather than on model instances or a session. Think "generated, typed data-access client" over a query engine.

•

4. What an ORM gives you (and costs you)

BenefitsSafetyProductivityPortabilityChange tracking / migrationsMaintainability

Benefits - Safety — parameterized queries prevent SQL injection by default. - Productivity — no boilerplate row-mapping; relationships as attributes. - Portability — often the same code runs on Postgres, MySQL, SQLite. - Change tracking / migrations — unit-of-work and schema-versioning tooling. - Maintainability — queries live in typed code, not scattered SQL strings.

Costs - Hidden expense — an innocent attribute access can fire the N+1 problem (see Query Optimization above). - Leaky abstraction — for complex analytics you still need to understand SQL and sometimes drop to raw queries. - Learning curve — sessions, lazy vs eager loading, identity map. - Overhead — object hydration is slower than raw rows for huge bulk operations.

Rule: use the ORM for application/business logic; drop to Core/raw SQL for bulk loads and heavy analytical queries.

•

5. The Python ORM landscape

SQLAlchemyDjango ORMTortoise ORMSQLModelPeeweePrisma (Client Python)
ORMPatternAsyncNotes
SQLAlchemyData Mapper (+ Core)✅ (2.0)The de-facto standard; most powerful & flexible
Django ORMActive RecordpartialTightly integrated with Django
Tortoise ORMActive Record✅Async-first, Django-like API
SQLModelData Mapper✅SQLAlchemy + Pydantic, by the FastAPI author

•

6. Prisma — overview

PrismaNode.js/TypeScriptPython clientPrisma ClientgeneratedPrisma Migrate

Prisma is an open-source, schema-first ORM that became hugely popular in the Node.js/TypeScript ecosystem and offers a Python client (prisma-client-py). Its hallmark is type safety driven by a single schema file: you declare your models once, run a generator, and get a fully-typed client — autocompletion and compile/lint-time checks for your queries.

Prisma has three main pieces:

ComponentRole
Prisma ClientAuto-generated, type-safe query builder/client used in your code
Prisma MigrateDeclarative schema migrations generated from your schema file
Prisma StudioA GUI to browse/edit your data

Supported databases: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server, CockroachDB, MongoDB.

How it works under the hood: Prisma reads your schema.prisma, and the generated client talks to a query engine (historically a Rust binary) that builds and runs the actual SQL and maps results back to typed objects. You never write the SQL; you compose queries through the client API.

Python status note: the Python client (prisma, a.k.a. Prisma Client Python) is a community-maintained port that brings Prisma's workflow to Python with both async and sync clients. Prisma's first-class, officially-supported target remains TypeScript/JavaScript — keep that in mind for production Python: SQLAlchemy has the larger Python ecosystem and support.

•

7. The Prisma Schema (PSL)

Prisma Schema Languagesingle source of truth

Everything starts from one declarative file, schema.prisma, written in Prisma Schema Language. It defines the datasource, the generator, and your models — this is the single source of truth for both the client and migrations.

// schema.prisma
datasource db {
  provider = "postgresql"
  url      = env("DATABASE_URL")     // read from environment — never hard-code
}

generator client {
  provider             = "prisma-client-py"   // generate the Python client
  interface            = "asyncio"            // or "sync"
  recursive_type_depth = 5
}

model User {
  id        Int      @id @default(autoincrement())
  email     String   @unique
  name      String?                      // ? = nullable/optional
  posts     Post[]                       // one-to-many relation
  createdAt DateTime @default(now())
}

model Post {
  id        Int     @id @default(autoincrement())
  title     String
  published Boolean @default(false)
  author    User    @relation(fields: [authorId], references: [id])
  authorId  Int
}

Then generate the typed client:

prisma generate        # reads schema.prisma → generates the typed Python client
•

8. Prisma Client in Python

The generated client gives you typed CRUD per model. With the asyncio interface:

import asyncio
from prisma import Prisma            # generated client

async def main():
    db = Prisma()
    await db.connect()

    # CREATE
    user = await db.user.create(data={"email": "ada@example.com", "name": "Ada"})

    # READ (filtering, ordering, pagination)
    users = await db.user.find_many(
        where={"name": {"contains": "Ada"}},
        order={"createdAt": "desc"},
        take=10, skip=0,
    )

    # READ with relations (eager include — avoids N+1)
    user_with_posts = await db.user.find_unique(
        where={"id": user.id},
        include={"posts": True},        # fetch related posts in one go
    )

    # UPDATE
    await db.user.update(where={"id": user.id}, data={"name": "Ada Lovelace"})

    # NESTED WRITE — create a user and their posts atomically
    await db.user.create(data={
        "email": "grace@example.com",
        "posts": {"create": [{"title": "Hello"}, {"title": "World"}]},
    })

    # DELETE
    await db.user.delete(where={"id": user.id})

    await db.disconnect()

asyncio.run(main())

Transactions in Prisma

# Interactive transaction: all-or-nothing (see the Database Transactions section above)
async with db.tx() as transaction:
    await transaction.account.update(
        where={"id": 1}, data={"balance": {"decrement": 100}})
    await transaction.account.update(
        where={"id": 2}, data={"balance": {"increment": 100}})
# commits on clean exit, rolls back on exception

Prisma also exposes raw SQL escape hatches when you outgrow the query builder:

rows = await db.query_raw("SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = $1", "ada@example.com")
•

9. Prisma Migrate

Prisma is declarative: you edit the schema to the desired end state and Prisma diffs it against the database to generate the SQL migration. (Contrast SQLAlchemy/Alembic, which is also autogenerate-capable but where you commonly tweak the imperative migration script.)

prisma migrate dev --name add_user_name     # create + apply a migration in dev
prisma migrate deploy                        # apply pending migrations in prod
prisma db push                               # push schema without a migration (prototyping)

The generated SQL lives in prisma/migrations/ and is version-controlled — reproducible, reviewable, and reversible, just like Alembic.

•

10. Prisma vs SQLAlchemy

Prisma (Client Python)SQLAlchemy
DimensionPrisma (Client Python)SQLAlchemy
Source of truthschema.prisma (one declarative file)Python model classes
PatternGenerated typed client / query builderData Mapper (ORM) + Core
Type safetyStrong — generated, fully typedGood with the 2.0 typed API / Mapped[...]
MigrationsPrisma Migrate (declarative diff)Alembic (autogenerate + editable scripts)
AsyncYes (asyncio interface)Yes (2.0 AsyncSession)
Ecosystem maturity (Python)Smaller, community-maintainedLargest, battle-tested
Raw SQL / complex queriesquery_raw escape hatchFirst-class (Core, hybrid, window funcs)
DX / onboardingExcellent autocompletion, low boilerplateSteeper, but very powerful
Multi-languageSame schema across TS + PythonPython only
•

11. When to choose Prisma vs SQLAlchemy

Lean Prisma whenTypeScript-firstgenerated type-safety + DXPython-centric backendcomplex/analytical SQLHonest take for this hub

Lean Prisma when: - Your team is TypeScript-first and wants one schema/ORM shared across a TS backend and Python services. - You value the generated type-safety + DX and a declarative migration workflow. - Your queries are mostly standard CRUD with relations.

Lean SQLAlchemy when (the default for production Python): - You're building a Python-centric backend and want the most mature, supported ecosystem. - You need complex/analytical SQL, fine-grained control, or heavy performance tuning. - You want the broadest community, docs, and integration (FastAPI, Alembic, SQLModel).

Honest take for this hub: for a pure-Python Backend/AI/ML/DS stack, SQLAlchemy (or SQLModel) is the safer default. Learn Prisma so you can work in polyglot teams and recognize the schema-first/generated-client paradigm — it's increasingly common and a frequent interview talking point.

•

12. Per-role notes & key takeaways

🐍 Python Backend🤖 AI Engineerdual-write📈 ML Engineer📊 Data Scientistread
  • 🐍 Python BackendYou'll most often use SQLAlchemy/SQLModel; understand Prisma to integrate with TS teams or inherit a Prisma schema. The ORM concepts (sessions, N+1, eager loading, transactions) transfer directly.
  • 🤖 AI EngineerApp state for LLM/RAG apps (users, conversations, document metadata) needs a relational store; an ORM keeps that layer clean. Watch the dual-write boundary with vector DBs (see Database Transactions (Deep Dive) §10).
  • 📈 ML EngineerORMs manage metadata (model registry, run/experiment tables, feature metadata); for bulk feature/prediction writes, prefer bulk inserts / COPY over per-row ORM writes.
  • 📊 Data ScientistYou mostly read: an ORM is optional; pandas.read_sql with parameterized SQL is often enough. Still, knowing ORM models helps you understand the schema and relationships you're querying.

Key takeaways - An ORM maps tables↔classes and rows↔objects, giving injection-safe, boilerplate-free, portable data access — at the cost of hidden queries (N+1) and a leaky abstraction. - Active Record (object persists itself, e.g. Django) vs Data Mapper (a session persists plain objects, e.g. SQLAlchemy) are the two classic patterns. - Prisma is a schema-first ORM: declare schema.prisma, prisma generate a type-safe client, and prisma migrate your schema; great DX, TS-first, with a Python client. - For production Python, SQLAlchemy/SQLModel remains the default; know Prisma for polyglot teams and interviews.

API Consumption13 sections

API Consumption and Webhooks — Complete Reference

While 25_FastAPI teaches you how to build APIs (server side), this topic covers acting as a client that consumes other services over HTTP — and the inverse, receiving webhooks when you'd otherwise have to poll. Almost every real backend is both: a FastAPI service (server) that calls a payment provider, a search index, and an LLM API (client).

•

1. Consuming vs Building an API

BuildingConsuming
  • Building (server): you expose endpoints, validate input, return responses → FastAPI/Flask.
  • Consuming (client): you call someone else's endpoints, send auth, and handle the response, retries, timeouts, and failures.

The hard part of consuming isn't the happy path — it's everything that goes wrong: the remote is slow, returns a 500, rate-limits you, rotates a token, or changes its schema. The rest of this guide is mostly about making the unhappy path safe.

•

2. HTTP refresher for clients

MethodsIdempotentnotdon'tRule

Methods (what you intend to do):

MethodPurposeIdempotent?Safe (no side effects)?
GETRead✅✅
POSTCreate / action❌❌
PUTReplace✅❌
PATCHPartial update❌ (usually)❌
DELETERemove✅❌

Idempotent = doing it N times == doing it once. This matters for retries: GET/PUT/DELETE are safe to retry; POST is not unless you add an idempotency key (see §10).

Status code families the client must branch on:

CodeMeaningClient action
2xxSuccess (200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content)Parse body (204 has none)
3xxRedirectUsually followed automatically
400Bad RequestFix payload — don't retry blindly
401UnauthorizedRefresh/supply credentials
403ForbiddenPermission problem — not retryable
404Not FoundResource missing
409ConflictOften a duplicate/version clash
422Unprocessable EntityValidation error (FastAPI default)
429Too Many RequestsBack off; honor Retry-After
5xxServer errorTransient — retry with backoff

Rule: retry only transient failures (429, 5xx, network/timeout). Retrying 4xx (except 429) just wastes calls — the request itself is wrong.

•

3. requests — the synchronous client

The de-facto standard for synchronous HTTP. Simple, blocking, perfect for scripts and sync code.

3.1 Basic requests

import requests

# GET with query params + headers
r = requests.get(
    "https://api.example.com/data",
    params={"limit": 10, "offset": 0},          # → ?limit=10&offset=0
    headers={"Authorization": "Bearer TOKEN"},
    timeout=5,                                   # ALWAYS set one (see §6)
)
r.raise_for_status()                            # raise on 4xx/5xx
data = r.json()                                 # parsed JSON → dict/list

# POST JSON (sets Content-Type: application/json)
requests.post("https://api.example.com/users", json={"name": "Ada"}, timeout=5)

# POST form data (application/x-www-form-urlencoded)
requests.post(url, data={"grant_type": "client_credentials"}, timeout=5)

# Multipart file upload
with open("photo.jpg", "rb") as f:
    requests.post(url, files={"file": ("photo.jpg", f, "image/jpeg")}, timeout=30)

3.2 The Response object

r.status_code      # 200
r.ok               # True for <400
r.json()           # parsed JSON (raises if body isn't JSON)
r.text             # body as decoded str
r.content          # body as raw bytes (images, files)
r.headers          # case-insensitive dict
r.url              # final URL (after redirects)
r.elapsed          # timedelta of the round trip
r.raise_for_status()  # → requests.HTTPError on 4xx/5xx

3.3 Sessions — connection reuse + persistent state

A bare requests.get() opens a fresh TCP+TLS connection every call and throws it away. A Session reuses connections via an underlying urllib3 pool and persists headers/cookies.

with requests.Session() as s:
    s.headers.update({"Authorization": "Bearer TOKEN"})   # sent on every request
    s.get("https://api.example.com/v1/user")              # connection opened
    s.get("https://api.example.com/v1/profile")           # connection REUSED (faster)

Use a Session whenever you hit the same host more than once. In a long-lived app, create it once and reuse it — don't make a new Session per request.

3.4 Built-in retries via an HTTPAdapter

requests has no retry logic by default, but urllib3 does — mount it on a Session:

from requests.adapters import HTTPAdapter
from urllib3.util.retry import Retry

retry = Retry(
    total=5,
    backoff_factor=0.5,                       # sleep = backoff_factor * (2 ** (n-1))
    status_forcelist=[429, 500, 502, 503, 504],  # retry only these statuses
    allowed_methods=["GET", "PUT", "DELETE"],    # idempotent methods only
    respect_retry_after_header=True,             # honor Retry-After on 429
)
s = requests.Session()
s.mount("https://", HTTPAdapter(max_retries=retry))

3.5 Streaming large downloads

Don't load a 2 GB file into memory — stream it in chunks.

with requests.get(url, stream=True, timeout=30) as r:
    r.raise_for_status()
    with open("big.zip", "wb") as f:
        for chunk in r.iter_content(chunk_size=8192):
            f.write(chunk)
•

4. httpx — sync and async

true async clientReuse the client

httpx mirrors the requests API but adds a true async client, HTTP/2, and first-class timeouts. Use it whenever you're in an async context (FastAPI, asyncio) or need concurrency — calling blocking requests inside async def stalls the whole event loop.

4.1 Sync usage (drop-in)

import httpx
r = httpx.get("https://api.example.com/data", timeout=5)
r.raise_for_status()
data = r.json()

4.2 Async usage + concurrency

import asyncio, httpx

async def fetch_all(urls: list[str]) -> list[dict]:
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=10) as client:        # reused pool
        responses = await asyncio.gather(*(client.get(u) for u in urls))
        return [r.json() for r in responses]

asyncio.run(fetch_all(["https://api/a", "https://api/b"]))

4.3 Configuring the client

limits = httpx.Limits(max_connections=100, max_keepalive_connections=20)
timeout = httpx.Timeout(connect=3.0, read=10.0, write=10.0, pool=5.0)

client = httpx.AsyncClient(
    base_url="https://api.example.com",   # then call client.get("/users")
    headers={"Authorization": "Bearer TOKEN"},
    limits=limits,
    timeout=timeout,
    http2=True,                           # multiplex requests over one connection
)

Reuse the client. In FastAPI, create one AsyncClient at startup (lifespan) and share it — creating a client per request defeats connection pooling.

from contextlib import asynccontextmanager

@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app):
    app.state.http = httpx.AsyncClient(base_url="https://api.example.com", timeout=10)
    yield
    await app.state.http.aclose()

4.4 requests vs httpx

requestshttpx
Sync✅✅
Async❌✅ (AsyncClient)
HTTP/2❌✅
Default timeoutNone (waits forever)5s
Best forSimple sync scriptsAsync apps, concurrency, modern code
