5. Authentication schemes

API keyBearer (OAuth2/JWT)BasicHMAC signingmTLS
SchemeHow you send itNotes
API keyHeader (X-API-Key) or query paramSimplest; keep secret
Bearer (OAuth2/JWT)Authorization: Bearer <token>Tokens expire → refresh on 401
BasicAuthorization: Basic base64(user:pass)HTTPS only
HMAC signingSign the request with a shared secretAWS SigV4, some webhooks
mTLSClient TLS certificateService-to-service, high security
# API key in header
requests.get(url, headers={"X-API-Key": key}, timeout=5)

# Basic auth
requests.get(url, auth=("user", "pass"), timeout=5)

# Bearer token
requests.get(url, headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {token}"}, timeout=5)

OAuth2 client-credentials flow (machine-to-machine)

Exchange a client id/secret for a short-lived access token, then send it as a Bearer header and refresh when it expires.

import time, requests

class TokenManager:
    def __init__(self, token_url, client_id, client_secret):
        self._url, self._id, self._secret = token_url, client_id, client_secret
        self._token, self._expires_at = None, 0

    def token(self) -> str:
        if self._token and time.time() < self._expires_at - 60:   # 60s safety margin
            return self._token
        r = requests.post(self._url, data={
            "grant_type": "client_credentials",
            "client_id": self._id,
            "client_secret": self._secret,
        }, timeout=5)
        r.raise_for_status()
        body = r.json()
        self._token = body["access_token"]
        self._expires_at = time.time() + body["expires_in"]
        return self._token
•

6. Timeouts, errors & status handling

foreverConnect timeoutRead timeout

Always set a timeout

By default requests waits forever. A hung remote then blocks your worker indefinitely; under load this exhausts the pool and your service goes down because a dependency did. This is one of the most common production outages.

requests.get(url, timeout=5)          # total budget
requests.get(url, timeout=(3, 30))    # (connect timeout, read timeout)
  • Connect timeoutmax time to establish TCP/TLS. Keep short (2–3s) to fail fast on dead hosts.
  • Read timeoutmax wait between bytes once connected. Allow more for legitimately slow APIs.

Layered exception handling

import requests

try:
    r = requests.get(url, timeout=5)
    r.raise_for_status()
    data = r.json()
except requests.HTTPError as e:          # 4xx / 5xx after raise_for_status()
    log.warning("bad status %s", e.response.status_code)
except requests.Timeout:                 # connect or read timed out
    log.warning("timed out")
except requests.ConnectionError:         # DNS failure, refused, network down
    log.warning("connection failed")
except requests.RequestException as e:   # base class — catch-all safety net
    log.error("request failed: %s", e)

raise_for_status() only converts HTTP error statuses to exceptions. Network failures (timeout, DNS, refused) raise their own exceptions regardless — catch RequestException as the common base.

•

7. Retries, backoff & circuit breakers

ExponentialjitterClosedOpenHalf-openMental model

Retry only transient failures, with exponential backoff + jitter

Fixed-delay retries from many clients synchronize into a "thundering herd" that hammers a recovering server. Exponential backoff (1s, 2s, 4s, 8s) spreads load; jitter (randomness) desynchronizes clients.

from tenacity import (retry, stop_after_attempt, wait_exponential_jitter,
                      retry_if_exception_type)
import requests

@retry(
    retry=retry_if_exception_type((requests.Timeout, requests.ConnectionError)),
    wait=wait_exponential_jitter(initial=1, max=30),   # backoff + randomness
    stop=stop_after_attempt(5),
    reraise=True,
)
def fetch():
    r = requests.get(url, timeout=5)
    r.raise_for_status()
    return r.json()

Circuit breaker — fail fast when a dependency is down

Retries handle transient blips; a circuit breaker handles a dependency that is down, so you stop pouring requests (and tying up workers) into a black hole.

  • Closedcalls flow; failures counted.
  • Openafter a failure threshold it "trips": calls fail instantly (no network) for a cooldown.
  • Half-openafter cooldown, a few trial calls; success closes it, failure re-opens.
import pybreaker, requests

breaker = pybreaker.CircuitBreaker(fail_max=5, reset_timeout=60)

@breaker
def call_dependency():
    r = requests.get(url, timeout=5)
    r.raise_for_status()
    return r.json()
# After 5 consecutive failures, calls raise CircuitBreakerError immediately for 60s.

Mental model: timeout (one call) → retry+backoff (transient) → circuit breaker (sustained outage). Use all three together.

•

8. Respecting rate limits as a client

429 Too Many RequestsRetry-After

APIs cap requests per window; exceeding it returns 429 Too Many Requests. Be a good citizen:

  1. Read headers: X-RateLimit-Remaining, X-RateLimit-Reset.
  2. On 429, honor Retry-After (seconds or an HTTP date) instead of guessing.
  3. Throttle proactively (token/leaky bucket) so you rarely hit the cap.
import time, requests

def get_with_rate_limit(url, **kw):
    while True:
        r = requests.get(url, timeout=5, **kw)
        if r.status_code != 429:
            return r
        wait = int(r.headers.get("Retry-After", 1))
        time.sleep(wait)            # obey the server's instruction
•

9. Pagination

generatorcursor-based

Large result sets are paged. Detect the style and loop until exhausted; a generator keeps memory flat.

StyleRequestTrade-off
Offset/limit?limit=100&offset=200Simple; slow + inconsistent on changing data
Page number?page=3Convenient; same drawbacks as offset
Cursor / keysetresponse returns next_cursorStable + efficient for large/streaming data
def fetch_all(session, url, params=None):
    """Follow next-links/cursors, yielding items lazily."""
    while url:
        r = session.get(url, params=params, timeout=10)
        r.raise_for_status()
        body = r.json()
        yield from body["items"]
        url = body.get("next")     # cursor/next URL; None ends the loop
        params = None              # params already baked into `next`

Prefer cursor-based pagination for large datasets; stream so you never hold everything in memory.

•

10. Webhooks — receiving push events

PollingWebhooksPOSTsraw bytesUse the raw bodyhmac.compare_digest

Polling = the client repeatedly asks "is it done yet?" — wasteful, latency-bound. Webhooks = the provider POSTs to a URL you register when an event happens — event-driven, near-real-time. Webhooks invert the roles: your app becomes a server receiving their request.

10.1 Receiving and verifying (FastAPI)

Your webhook URL is public, so anyone could POST fake events. Verify a cryptographic signature over the raw bytes of the body.

import hmac, hashlib, time
from fastapi import FastAPI, Request, HTTPException

app = FastAPI()
WEBHOOK_SECRET = b"whsec_..."

@app.post("/webhook/stripe")
async def stripe_webhook(request: Request):
    raw = await request.body()                       # RAW bytes — not request.json()
    sig = request.headers.get("Stripe-Signature", "")

    if not verify(raw, sig, WEBHOOK_SECRET):
        raise HTTPException(400, "invalid signature")

    event = await request.json()
    if already_processed(event["id"]):               # idempotency (see 10.3)
        return {"status": "ok"}                       # ack duplicate, do nothing

    enqueue_processing(event)                         # 10.4: ack fast, work async
    mark_processed(event["id"])
    return {"status": "ok"}

def verify(payload: bytes, signature: str, secret: bytes) -> bool:
    expected = hmac.new(secret, payload, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
    return hmac.compare_digest(expected, signature)  # constant-time (no timing leak)

Key points: - Use the raw body, not parsed-then-reserialized JSON — re-serializing changes bytes and breaks the HMAC. - hmac.compare_digest, never == — constant-time comparison avoids timing attacks.

10.2 Replay protection

Reject events whose signed timestamp is too old, so an attacker can't capture and resend a valid request later.

ts = int(request.headers.get("Webhook-Timestamp", "0"))
if abs(time.time() - ts) > 300:            # 5-minute tolerance
    raise HTTPException(400, "stale webhook")

10.3 Idempotency (why handlers must dedupe)

Providers guarantee at-least-once delivery: if your endpoint is slow or returns non-2xx, they retry, so the same event arrives more than once. Dedupe on the provider's event ID so re-delivery is harmless — otherwise you double-charge or double-email. See also 25_FastAPI task queues (same at-least-once model).

10.4 Acknowledge fast, process async

Return 2xx immediately, then do the real work in a background task/queue. If you process inline and exceed the provider's timeout, they assume failure and retry — multiplying load.

•

11. Secrets & configuration

  • Never hard-code or commit secrets; add .env to .gitignore.
  • Load from environment variables, a .env file, or a secrets manager (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager).
  • Use typed, validated config via pydantic-settings.
from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsConfigDict

class Settings(BaseSettings):
    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(env_file=".env")
    api_key: str
    api_base_url: str = "https://api.example.com"

settings = Settings()   # raises at startup if api_key is missing

See 19_Best_Practices for the broader security section.

•

12. Testing API clients

Don't hit real APIs in unit tests — they're slow, flaky, and may cost money. Mock the HTTP layer.

# requests → use `responses`
import responses, requests

@responses.activate
def test_fetch_user():
    responses.add(responses.GET, "https://api/users/1",
                  json={"id": 1, "name": "Ada"}, status=200)
    assert fetch_user(1)["name"] == "Ada"

# httpx → use `respx`
import respx, httpx

@respx.mock
def test_async_client():
    respx.get("https://api/users/1").mock(return_value=httpx.Response(200, json={"id": 1}))
    ...

Also useful: VCR.py records real responses once and replays them (cassettes). Keep retry/backoff logic in functions you can unit-test by injecting failures.

•

13. Best-practice checklist

AlwaysCommon outages this prevents
  • ✅ Always set a timeout (separate connect/read).
  • ✅ Reuse a Session/AsyncClient for connection pooling.
  • ✅ raise_for_status() and catch RequestException as the base.
  • ✅ Retry only transient failures (429, 5xx, network) with exponential backoff + jitter.
  • ✅ Add a circuit breaker for dependencies that can be down, not just flaky.
  • ✅ Honor Retry-After; throttle to stay under rate limits.
  • ✅ Stream large downloads/result sets; paginate with a generator.
  • ✅ Webhooks: verify HMAC over raw body with compare_digest, check timestamp, dedupe on event ID, ack fast + process async.
  • ✅ Secrets from env/secrets-manager via pydantic-settings; never in code.
  • ✅ Mock HTTP in tests (responses/respx/VCR).

Common outages this prevents: missing timeout (worker exhaustion), no idempotency (double-charges), retry storms (no backoff/jitter), and leaked API keys (secrets in code).

Auth and Security18 sections

Auth & Security in Python — Complete Reference

Scope: authentication vs authorization, password hashing (bcrypt/argon2/passlib), secure randomness & tokens (secrets, timing-safe compare), JWT deep-dive, sessions vs tokens, refresh-token rotation & revocation, OAuth2 / OpenID Connect flows, authorization models (RBAC/ABAC/scopes), API keys & service-to-service auth, transport & web security (TLS/HSTS, cookies, CORS, CSRF), injection & deserialization defenses, secrets management, the OWASP Top 10 mapped to Python, the cryptography library, and security tooling.

This is the one place that pulls together auth/security material otherwise spread across [[fastapi]] (§9 Authentication, Production Guide), [[best-practices]] (§14 stdlib security), and [[pydantic]] (validation at the boundary). Architecture-level security (network, secrets infra, zero-trust) lives in 11_System_Design.

•

1. The Security Mindset

CORE PRINCIPLES
  Defense in depth      Multiple independent layers — no single point of failure.
  Least privilege       Grant the minimum access needed, nothing more.
  Fail securely         On error, deny (closed) — never default to "allow".
  Don't roll your own    Use vetted libraries for crypto/auth, never hand-rolled.
  Never trust input     Validate/escape everything crossing a trust boundary.
  Secrets out of code    Config from env/secret store; never commit secrets.
  Assume breach         Limit blast radius; log, rotate, and detect.

A useful framing: every request crosses trust boundaries (client→server, server→DB, service→service). At each boundary you ask three questions — Who are you? (authentication), What are you allowed to do? (authorization), and Is this input safe? (validation). The rest of this doc answers those three for Python.

•

2. Authentication vs Authorization

401 vs 403first
AUTHENTICATION (AuthN)            AUTHORIZATION (AuthZ)
  "Who are you?"                    "What are you allowed to do?"
  Verifies identity                Verifies permissions
  Login, passwords, tokens, MFA    RBAC, scopes, ownership checks
  Failure → 401 Unauthorized       Failure → 403 Forbidden

401 vs 403: 401 = "I don't know who you are — authenticate" (missing/expired/invalid credentials). 403 = "I know who you are, but you may not do this." Returning the wrong one leaks information and confuses clients. (Consistent with [[fastapi]] §5.)

The two are independent steps and run in this order: authenticate first (establish identity), then authorize (check that identity's permissions for the specific resource/action).

•

3. Password Hashing

slow, salted, adaptiveArgon2idbcryptscrypt

Never store plaintext passwords, and never use fast/general-purpose hashes (md5, sha1, sha256) for them. Fast hashes are the problem: a GPU computes billions/sec, so a leaked table is brute-forced quickly. Use a slow, salted, adaptive password hash: Argon2id (modern first choice), bcrypt (battle-tested default), or scrypt.

# ── passlib with bcrypt (the FastAPI-ecosystem standard) ──
from passlib.context import CryptContext

# deprecated="auto" lets you migrate algorithms transparently over time
pwd_context = CryptContext(schemes=["argon2", "bcrypt"], deprecated="auto")

def hash_password(plain: str) -> str:
    return pwd_context.hash(plain)          # salt is generated & embedded automatically

def verify_password(plain: str, hashed: str) -> bool:
    return pwd_context.verify(plain, hashed)  # constant-time internally

# ── Seamless rehash-on-login (upgrade old hashes) ──
def check_and_upgrade(plain: str, stored_hash: str) -> tuple[bool, str | None]:
    if not pwd_context.verify(plain, stored_hash):
        return False, None
    new_hash = pwd_context.hash(plain) if pwd_context.needs_update(stored_hash) else None
    return True, new_hash                    # persist new_hash if not None
# ── argon2-cffi directly (no passlib) ──
from argon2 import PasswordHasher
from argon2.exceptions import VerifyMismatchError

ph = PasswordHasher()                        # sensible defaults (time/memory/parallelism)
h = ph.hash("s3cret")
try:
    ph.verify(h, "s3cret")                   # True or raises
    if ph.check_needs_rehash(h):
        h = ph.hash("s3cret")                # params bumped → rehash
except VerifyMismatchError:
    ...                                      # wrong password

# ── stdlib fallback (no extra deps): PBKDF2 ──
import hashlib, os
salt = os.urandom(16)
dk = hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac("sha256", b"s3cret", salt, 600_000)  # high iteration count
KEY POINTS
  Salt        Unique random value per password — defeats rainbow tables. (Auto with
              bcrypt/argon2; the salt is stored inside the hash string.)
  Pepper      Optional app-wide secret HMAC'd in before hashing, kept OUTSIDE the DB
              (env/HSM) so a DB-only leak is useless. Defense in depth.
  Work factor Tune cost (bcrypt rounds ≈12; argon2 memory/time) so a hash takes
              ~250–500ms — slow for attackers, fine for one login.
  bcrypt cap  bcrypt silently truncates input at 72 bytes — pre-hash long inputs
              (e.g. sha256 then base64) or use argon2.
  Never log   Never log, print, or include the plaintext or hash in error messages.

Replaces the inline snippets in [[fastapi]] (Production Guide §2) and [[best-practices]] §14.

•

4. Secure Randomness & Timing-Safe Comparison

Never use randomsecret

Use secrets (CSPRNG) for anything security-sensitive. Never use random — it's a deterministic Mersenne Twister, predictable from a few outputs.

import secrets

secrets.token_urlsafe(32)     # URL-safe token, ~43 chars — session IDs, reset/API tokens
secrets.token_hex(16)         # 32 hex chars
secrets.token_bytes(32)       # raw bytes (e.g. as a signing key)
secrets.choice(alphabet)      # secure random pick (e.g. OTP / temp password)
secrets.randbelow(1_000_000)  # secure int in [0, n)
# ── Timing-safe comparison — defeats timing side-channels ──
import hmac
hmac.compare_digest(provided_token, expected_token)   # ✅ constant-time
# if provided_token == expected_token:                 # ❌ short-circuits → leaks length/prefix

Use hmac.compare_digest (or secrets.compare_digest) whenever you compare a secret — API keys, tokens, HMAC signatures, CSRF tokens. A naive == returns faster on an early-mismatch, and an attacker can measure that to recover the secret byte by byte.

•

5. JWT — Deep Dive

JWTsignedbearer tokens

A JWT is a compact, URL-safe, signed (not encrypted by default) token. Anyone can read the payload — only the holder of the key can forge a valid one.

HEADER.PAYLOAD.SIGNATURE   (three base64url segments joined by dots)

  HEADER     {"alg": "HS256", "typ": "JWT"}
  PAYLOAD    {"sub": "user123", "exp": 1717000000, "role": "admin", "iss": "myapp"}
  SIGNATURE  HMAC-SHA256( base64(header) + "." + base64(payload), SECRET_KEY )

REGISTERED CLAIMS
  sub  subject (user id)      exp  expiry (UNIX ts)     iat  issued-at
  iss  issuer                 aud  audience             nbf  not-before
  jti  unique token id (use for revocation / replay defense)
# ── PyJWT (recommended) — encode/decode with full validation ──
import jwt                       # pip install pyjwt
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone

SECRET = "load-from-env-not-here"
ALGO = "HS256"

def create_token(sub: str, role: str, minutes: int = 15) -> str:
    now = datetime.now(timezone.utc)
    payload = {
        "sub": sub, "role": role,
        "iat": now,
        "exp": now + timedelta(minutes=minutes),
        "iss": "myapp", "aud": "myapp-clients",
    }
    return jwt.encode(payload, SECRET, algorithm=ALGO)

def decode_token(token: str) -> dict:
    return jwt.decode(
        token, SECRET,
        algorithms=[ALGO],            # ✅ pin allowed algs — never trust the header's alg
        audience="myapp-clients",     # validate aud
        issuer="myapp",               # validate iss
        options={"require": ["exp", "iat", "sub"]},
    )                                  # raises ExpiredSignatureError / InvalidTokenError
SECURITY PITFALLS (the classic JWT footguns)
  alg=none attack    Attacker sets header alg to "none" to skip the signature.
                     → ALWAYS pass algorithms=[...] explicitly; never decode without it.
  alg confusion      Attacker swaps RS256→HS256 and signs with the public key as the
                     HMAC secret. → Pin the exact algorithm; don't accept a list mixing
                     symmetric & asymmetric.
  No expiry          Tokens valid forever. → Always set short exp (15–60 min).
  Secrets in payload Payload is only base64, NOT encrypted. → Never put PII/secrets in it.
  Can't revoke       A signed JWT is valid until exp. → Keep access tokens short; use a
                     jti denylist or refresh-token rotation for logout/revocation.
  Weak key           HS256 with a short/guessable secret is brute-forceable.
                     → ≥256-bit random secret, or RS256/ES256 for multi-service.
HS256 vs RS256
  HS256 (symmetric)   One shared SECRET signs AND verifies. Simple; good for a single
                      service that both issues and checks tokens.
  RS256 (asymmetric)  Private key signs, PUBLIC key verifies. Use across microservices /
                      with third-party identity providers — verifiers never hold the
                      signing key. ES256 = same idea, smaller keys (elliptic curve).

JWTs are bearer tokens: whoever holds one is the user. Always transport over HTTPS, keep them short-lived, and store them carefully on the client (prefer an HttpOnly cookie over localStorage, which is XSS-readable — see §12).

•

6. Sessions vs Tokens

Two ways to keep a user logged in after authentication:

                 SERVER-SIDE SESSIONS              STATELESS TOKENS (JWT)
  State          Session store (Redis/DB);         No server state; all data in the
                 client holds only a session id    signed token itself
  Revocation     Instant — delete the session      Hard — valid until exp (need denylist)
  Scaling        Needs shared/sticky store         Trivial — any node can verify
  Transport      Cookie (HttpOnly, Secure)         Authorization: Bearer header (or cookie)
  Size           Tiny id                            Larger (sent on every request)
  Best for       Browser apps, easy logout         APIs, microservices, mobile, SPAs
# ── Opaque server-side token/session (stateful) ──
import secrets, time

SESSIONS: dict[str, dict] = {}                # use Redis with TTL in production

def create_session(user_id: str, ttl: int = 3600) -> str:
    sid = secrets.token_urlsafe(32)           # opaque, unguessable, carries no data
    SESSIONS[sid] = {"user_id": user_id, "expires": time.time() + ttl}
    return sid

def get_session(sid: str) -> dict | None:
    s = SESSIONS.get(sid)
    if not s or s["expires"] < time.time():
        SESSIONS.pop(sid, None)               # expired → evict, fail closed
        return None
    return s

def destroy_session(sid: str) -> None:        # instant logout/revocation
    SESSIONS.pop(sid, None)

A common hybrid: short-lived JWT access token + long-lived opaque refresh token — you get stateless verification on the hot path and real revocation via the refresh store (§7).

•

7. Refresh Tokens — Rotation & Revocation

Short access-token lifetimes limit damage from a leak, but forcing re-login every 15 minutes is hostile. Refresh tokens solve this: a long-lived credential that mints new access tokens.

FLOW
  Login        → issue access (15 min, JWT) + refresh (7–30 days, opaque, stored hashed)
  API calls    → send access token; verify statelessly
  Access expired → POST /refresh with the refresh token → new access (+ rotated refresh)
  Logout       → delete the refresh token server-side (access dies on its own soon after)
import secrets, hashlib
from datetime import datetime, timezone

# Store only the HASH of refresh tokens (treat them like passwords)
REFRESH_DB: dict[str, dict] = {}              # token_hash -> {user, expires, revoked}

def _h(token: str) -> str:
    return hashlib.sha256(token.encode()).hexdigest()

def issue_refresh(user_id: str, days: int = 30) -> str:
    token = secrets.token_urlsafe(48)
    REFRESH_DB[_h(token)] = {"user": user_id, "revoked": False,
                             "exp": datetime.now(timezone.utc).timestamp() + days * 86400}
    return token

def rotate(old: str) -> tuple[str, str] | None:
    rec = REFRESH_DB.get(_h(old))
    if not rec or rec["revoked"] or rec["exp"] < datetime.now(timezone.utc).timestamp():
        # Reuse of a rotated/used token = likely theft → revoke the whole family
        return None
    rec["revoked"] = True                      # one-time use: invalidate the old token
    new_refresh = issue_refresh(rec["user"])
    new_access = create_token(rec["user"], role="user")   # from §5
    return new_access, new_refresh
HARDENING
  Rotation        Each refresh issues a NEW refresh token and invalidates the old one.
  Reuse detection If a previously-rotated token is presented again → assume theft, revoke
                  the entire token family and force re-login.
  Hash at rest    Store refresh tokens hashed (sha256) so a DB leak can't replay them.
  Bind & scope    Optionally bind to device/IP; keep refresh tokens out of JS (HttpOnly).
•

8. OAuth2 & OpenID Connect

OAuth2OpenID Connect (OIDC)ID tokenOAuth2 = access, OIDC = identity

OAuth2 is an authorization framework — it lets an app obtain limited access to a resource on a user's behalf without handling their password (the "Sign in with Google" delegation). OpenID Connect (OIDC) is a thin authentication layer on top of OAuth2 that adds an ID token (a JWT identifying the user). Rule of thumb: OAuth2 = access, OIDC = identity.

GRANT TYPES (flows) — pick by client type
  Authorization Code + PKCE   Web/SPA/mobile logging in a USER via a provider. PKCE
                              (Proof Key for Code Exchange) is mandatory for public
                              clients — defeats auth-code interception.
  Client Credentials          Machine-to-machine (no user). Service authenticates with
                              its own client_id/secret to call another service.
  Refresh Token               Exchange a refresh token for a fresh access token.
  Password (ROPC)             User's password sent directly to your app. LEGACY — only
                              for first-party trusted clients; avoid for third parties.
  Device Code                 Input-constrained devices (TVs, CLIs).
  ❌ Implicit                  Deprecated (tokens in the URL fragment) — use Code+PKCE.
# ── Calling a provider's token endpoint (Authorization Code) with httpx ──
import httpx

async def exchange_code(code: str, verifier: str) -> dict:
    async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:
        resp = await client.post("https://provider.com/oauth/token", data={
            "grant_type": "authorization_code",
            "code": code,
            "redirect_uri": "https://myapp.com/callback",
            "client_id": CLIENT_ID,
            "client_secret": CLIENT_SECRET,
            "code_verifier": verifier,        # PKCE: proves we started the flow
        })
        resp.raise_for_status()
        return resp.json()                    # {access_token, id_token, refresh_token, ...}

# ── Validate an OIDC id_token from a JWKS endpoint (RS256) ──
import jwt
from jwt import PyJWKClient

def verify_id_token(id_token: str) -> dict:
    jwks = PyJWKClient("https://provider.com/.well-known/jwks.json")
    signing_key = jwks.get_signing_key_from_jwt(id_token).key
    return jwt.decode(id_token, signing_key, algorithms=["RS256"],
                      audience=CLIENT_ID, issuer="https://provider.com")

For real apps prefer a maintained client (authlib, or the provider's SDK) over hand-rolling redirects, state/nonce, and PKCE. Always validate state (CSRF for the flow) and nonce.

•

9. Authorization Models (RBAC, ABAC, Scopes)

RBAC (Role-Based)        Permissions attach to ROLES; users get roles. Coarse, simple,
                         most common. e.g. admin / editor / viewer.
ABAC (Attribute-Based)   Decisions from ATTRIBUTES of user+resource+context.
                         e.g. "editors may edit docs in their own department before 6pm."
Scopes (OAuth2)          Token-embedded permissions limiting what a CLIENT may do.
                         e.g. "read:orders write:orders". Orthogonal to user roles.
Ownership / object-level Check the user owns/relates to THIS specific row — the most
                         commonly forgotten check (OWASP "Broken Object Level Auth").
# ── RBAC: permission-aware dependency factory ──
from enum import Enum
from fastapi import Depends, HTTPException, status

class Role(str, Enum):
    admin = "admin"; editor = "editor"; viewer = "viewer"

ROLE_PERMISSIONS = {
    Role.admin:  {"read", "write", "delete"},
    Role.editor: {"read", "write"},
    Role.viewer: {"read"},
}

def require_permission(perm: str):
    def checker(user=Depends(get_current_user)):
        if perm not in ROLE_PERMISSIONS.get(Role(user["role"]), set()):
            raise HTTPException(status.HTTP_403_FORBIDDEN, "Insufficient permissions")
        return user
    return checker

@app.delete("/items/{item_id}")
def delete_item(item_id: int, user=Depends(require_permission("delete"))):
    ...

# ── Object-level (ownership) check — don't forget this one ──
def get_owned_order(order_id: int, user=Depends(get_current_user)):
    order = db.get_order(order_id)
    if order is None:
        raise HTTPException(404, "Not found")
    if order.user_id != user["sub"] and user["role"] != Role.admin:
        raise HTTPException(403, "Not your order")   # authorize the SPECIFIC object
    return order

Enforce authorization on the server, per request, close to the data — never rely on the UI hiding a button. A hidden button is not a permission check.

•

10. End-to-End Auth in FastAPI

A complete password-login + JWT example. (This is the canonical version; [[fastapi]] §9 shows the same pattern in its web-framework context.)

from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone
from fastapi import FastAPI, Depends, HTTPException, status
from fastapi.security import OAuth2PasswordBearer, OAuth2PasswordRequestForm
from passlib.context import CryptContext
from pydantic import BaseModel
import jwt

app = FastAPI()
pwd = CryptContext(schemes=["bcrypt"], deprecated="auto")
oauth2 = OAuth2PasswordBearer(tokenUrl="token")
SECRET, ALGO = "load-from-env", "HS256"

class TokenOut(BaseModel):
    access_token: str
    token_type: str = "bearer"

def authenticate(username: str, password: str):
    user = db.get_user(username)                       # None if missing
    if not user or not pwd.verify(password, user.hashed_password):
        return None                                    # same error for both → no user enumeration
    return user

def create_access_token(sub: str, minutes: int = 30) -> str:
    exp = datetime.now(timezone.utc) + timedelta(minutes=minutes)
    return jwt.encode({"sub": sub, "exp": exp}, SECRET, algorithm=ALGO)

async def current_user(token: str = Depends(oauth2)):
    cred_exc = HTTPException(status.HTTP_401_UNAUTHORIZED, "Could not validate credentials",
                            headers={"WWW-Authenticate": "Bearer"})
    try:
        payload = jwt.decode(token, SECRET, algorithms=[ALGO])
    except jwt.PyJWTError:
        raise cred_exc
    user = db.get_user(payload.get("sub", ""))
    if user is None:
        raise cred_exc
    return user

@app.post("/token", response_model=TokenOut)
async def login(form: OAuth2PasswordRequestForm = Depends()):
    user = authenticate(form.username, form.password)
    if not user:
        raise HTTPException(status.HTTP_401_UNAUTHORIZED, "Incorrect username or password")
    return TokenOut(access_token=create_access_token(user.username))

@app.get("/users/me")
async def me(user=Depends(current_user)):
    return {"username": user.username}

11. API Keys & Service-to-Service Auth

# ── API key in a header (compare in constant time) ──
from fastapi import Security, HTTPException
from fastapi.security import APIKeyHeader
import hmac

api_key_header = APIKeyHeader(name="X-API-Key")
VALID_KEYS = {...}   # store HASHED keys; look up by hash

def check_api_key(key: str = Security(api_key_header)):
    # constant-time membership: hash the presented key, compare to stored hashes
    presented = hashlib.sha256(key.encode()).hexdigest()
    if not any(hmac.compare_digest(presented, k) for k in VALID_KEYS):
        raise HTTPException(401, "Invalid API key")
# ── HMAC request signing (webhooks / partner APIs) ──
import hmac, hashlib, time

def sign(secret: bytes, body: bytes, ts: str) -> str:
    msg = ts.encode() + b"." + body
    return hmac.new(secret, msg, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()

def verify_webhook(secret: bytes, body: bytes, ts: str, signature: str, tol: int = 300) -> bool:
    if abs(time.time() - int(ts)) > tol:          # reject stale → replay protection
        return False
    return hmac.compare_digest(sign(secret, body, ts), signature)   # constant-time
SERVICE-TO-SERVICE OPTIONS
  API key (hashed)          Simplest; rotate regularly; one key per consumer.
  HMAC-signed requests      Proves integrity + authenticity; add a timestamp/nonce vs replay.
  OAuth2 client credentials Standard for internal microservices; short-lived tokens.
  mTLS                       Mutual TLS — both sides present certs; strong zero-trust option.

This consolidates the API-key / bearer-token / webhook-signing snippets from [[fastapi]] §9 and [[api-consumption]].

•

12. Transport & Web Security (TLS, Cookies, CORS, CSRF)

# ── Force HTTPS + HSTS (terminate TLS at a proxy in prod) ──
from fastapi.middleware.httpsredirect import HTTPSRedirectMiddleware
app.add_middleware(HTTPSRedirectMiddleware)
# HSTS header tells browsers "HTTPS only from now on":
#   Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains; preload

# ── Secure session cookies ──
response.set_cookie(
    "session", value=sid,
    httponly=True,     # JS cannot read it → mitigates XSS token theft
    secure=True,       # only sent over HTTPS
    samesite="lax",    # "strict"/"lax" mitigate CSRF; "none" REQUIRES secure=True
    max_age=3600, path="/",
)
# ── CORS: be explicit; never wildcard origins WITH credentials ──
from fastapi.middleware.cors import CORSMiddleware
app.add_middleware(
    CORSMiddleware,
    allow_origins=["https://myapp.com"],   # ❌ ["*"] with allow_credentials=True is invalid/unsafe
    allow_credentials=True,
    allow_methods=["GET", "POST"],
    allow_headers=["Authorization", "Content-Type"],
)
THE BROWSER THREATS
  XSS  (Cross-Site Scripting)   Injected JS runs in your page → steals tokens, acts as user.
        Defend: escape/encode output, Content-Security-Policy, HttpOnly cookies, never
        render untrusted HTML; never build pages via string concat with user input.
  CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery)  A malicious site makes the browser send an authenticated
        request using the victim's cookie. Defend: SameSite cookies + a CSRF token (double-submit
        or per-session) for state-changing form posts. Token-in-header APIs (Bearer) are largely
        immune since the attacker can't read/set the header cross-origin.
  Clickjacking                  Your page framed by an attacker. Defend: X-Frame-Options: DENY
        / CSP frame-ancestors.
  CORS                          NOT a server protection — it relaxes the browser's same-origin
        policy. Misconfigured (reflecting any Origin + credentials) it leaks data.

CORS is not authentication. It only controls which browser origins may read responses; it does nothing for non-browser clients and is not a substitute for authn/authz.

•

13. Injection & Deserialization Defenses

# ── SQL injection → ALWAYS parameterize (never f-string SQL) ──
cur.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = %s", (email,))     # ✅ driver escapes
# cur.execute(f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '{email}'")     # ❌ injectable
session.execute(text("SELECT * FROM u WHERE id = :id"), {"id": uid})  # ✅ SQLAlchemy bind

# ── Command injection → list args, never shell=True with user input ──
import subprocess
subprocess.run(["ping", "-c", "1", host], check=True, timeout=5)  # ✅ no shell
# subprocess.run(f"ping -c 1 {host}", shell=True)                  # ❌ "host=; rm -rf /"
# Never: os.system(...), eval(user_input), exec(user_input)

# ── Path traversal → resolve and confine to a base dir ──
from pathlib import Path
def safe_path(base: Path, user_part: str) -> Path:
    target = (base / user_part).resolve()
    if not target.is_relative_to(base.resolve()):     # 3.9+
        raise ValueError("Path traversal blocked")    # blocks "../../etc/passwd"
    return target

# ── SSRF → validate/allowlist outbound URLs; block internal ranges ──
from urllib.parse import urlparse
def safe_url(url: str) -> bool:
    host = urlparse(url).hostname or ""
    return host in ALLOWED_HOSTS               # deny localhost/169.254.169.254/internal IPs

# ── Insecure deserialization → NEVER unpickle/yaml.load untrusted data ──
import pickle, yaml, json
# pickle.loads(untrusted)        # ❌ arbitrary code execution
# yaml.load(untrusted)           # ❌ — use yaml.safe_load(untrusted)
json.loads(untrusted)            # ✅ data-only; can't execute code
THE RULE BEHIND ALL OF THESE
  Separate CODE from DATA. Injection happens when attacker DATA is interpreted as CODE
  (SQL, shell, HTML, a pickle stream, a path). Use parameterized/allow-listed interfaces
  that keep that boundary; validate input shape at the edge (Pydantic — see [[pydantic]]).

Mirrors and expands [[best-practices]] §14 (sqlite parameterization, subprocess, pickle warning).

•

14. Secrets Management

# ── 12-factor: secrets from the environment, validated at startup ──
from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsConfigDict
from pydantic import SecretStr

class Settings(BaseSettings):
    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(env_file=".env")
    secret_key: SecretStr                  # SecretStr won't print in logs/repr
    database_url: SecretStr

    @property
    def jwt_key(self) -> str:
        return self.secret_key.get_secret_value()

settings = Settings()   # raises immediately if a required secret is missing → fail fast
RULES
  Never commit secrets   .gitignore the .env; commit a .env.example with blank values.
  Rotate                 Rotate keys/tokens on a schedule and immediately on suspected leak.
  Least privilege        Scope each credential to exactly what it needs (read-only DB user, etc.).
  Don't log              Use SecretStr/redaction; scrub secrets from logs and error reports.
  Use a vault in prod    AWS Secrets Manager / GCP Secret Manager / HashiCorp Vault — not env
                         files baked into images.
  Scan history           If a secret was ever committed, it's compromised — rotate it AND purge
                         history; "deleting" the file is not enough.

If you accidentally commit a secret: rotate it first (assume it's already scraped), then remove it from history (git filter-repo / BFG) and force-push.

•

15. Cryptography in Python (the cryptography library)

Don't implement crypto primitives yourself. Use the cryptography package; reach for hashlib only for non-secret hashing/checksums.

# ── Symmetric encryption made safe: Fernet (AES-128-CBC + HMAC, authenticated) ──
from cryptography.fernet import Fernet

key = Fernet.generate_key()           # store as a secret (env/vault)
f = Fernet(key)
token = f.encrypt(b"sensitive data")  # versioned, timestamped, authenticated ciphertext
plain = f.decrypt(token)              # raises InvalidToken if tampered/expired
# f.decrypt(token, ttl=3600)          # optional max age

# ── File integrity / checksums (NOT for passwords) ──
import hashlib
def sha256_file(path) -> str:
    h = hashlib.sha256()
    with open(path, "rb") as fh:
        while chunk := fh.read(8192):
            h.update(chunk)
    return h.hexdigest()
PICK THE RIGHT TOOL
  Passwords            argon2 / bcrypt (§3)            — slow, salted
  Random secrets/IDs   secrets (§4)                    — CSPRNG
  Symmetric encrypt    cryptography.Fernet             — authenticated, hard to misuse
  Asymmetric / signing cryptography (RSA/Ed25519)      — keys, signatures
  Hashing/checksums    hashlib (sha256+)               — integrity, NOT passwords
  Constant-time check  hmac.compare_digest             — comparing secrets
  ❌ Never             md5/sha1 for security, DIY ciphers, ECB mode, hardcoded keys/IVs
•

16. OWASP Top 10 — Mapped to Python

A01 Broken Access Control     Missing object-level checks. → enforce authz per request &
                              per object (§9); deny by default.
A02 Cryptographic Failures    Plaintext/weak hashing, http, hardcoded keys. → §3/§12/§15.
A03 Injection                 SQL/command/path/SSRF. → parameterize & allow-list (§13).
A04 Insecure Design           No threat model/rate limits. → design with §1; add throttling.
A05 Security Misconfiguration debug=True in prod, permissive CORS, default creds, verbose
                              errors leaking stack traces. → harden config; generic errors.
A06 Vulnerable Components     Outdated deps with CVEs. → pip-audit / Dependabot (§17).
A07 Identification & AuthN    Weak passwords, no MFA, no lockout, session fixation. → §3–§7.
A08 Software/Data Integrity   Unsigned updates, insecure deserialization. → §13 (no pickle).
A09 Logging & Monitoring      Can't detect/respond to breaches. → log authn events (never
                              secrets); alert on anomalies.
A10 SSRF                      Server fetches attacker URLs. → validate/allow-list outbound (§13).

17. Security Tooling

# ── Static analysis for insecure code (SAST) ──
pip install bandit && bandit -r src/          # flags eval, shell=True, weak hashes, etc.
ruff check --select S .                         # Ruff's bandit rules (S = flake8-bandit)

# ── Dependency vulnerability scanning (SCA) ──
pip install pip-audit && pip-audit             # checks installed deps vs the advisory DB
pip install safety && safety check             # alternative scanner
# In CI: enable GitHub Dependabot / Renovate for automated upgrade PRs.

# ── Secret scanning ──
pip install detect-secrets && detect-secrets scan > .secrets.baseline
# pre-commit hooks: detect-secrets, detect-private-key, gitleaks (see [[best-practices]] §21)
LAYERED PIPELINE
  pre-commit   detect-secrets, ruff (S rules)        — block at commit time
  CI           bandit, pip-audit, ruff --select S    — block on PR
  Runtime      rate limiting, WAF, structured authn logging, alerting
•

18. Production Security Checklist

Summarythenargon2/bcryptsecretshmac.compare_digestpinned algorithm + short expiry
AUTHENTICATION & SESSIONS
  ✅ Passwords hashed with argon2/bcrypt (never plaintext, never md5/sha1)
  ✅ Same generic error for bad-user and bad-password (no account enumeration)
  ✅ Short-lived access tokens (15–60 min) + rotating refresh tokens
  ✅ JWTs decoded with an explicit algorithms=[...]; exp/iss/aud validated
  ✅ Logout/revocation works (session delete or refresh-token denylist)
  ✅ Rate-limit + lockout/backoff on login; MFA for sensitive accounts

AUTHORIZATION
  ✅ Authz enforced server-side, per request, per object (ownership checks)
  ✅ Deny by default; 401 vs 403 used correctly; least privilege everywhere

TRANSPORT & WEB
  ✅ HTTPS everywhere + HSTS; cookies HttpOnly + Secure + SameSite
  ✅ CORS locked to known origins (no "*" with credentials)
  ✅ Security headers (CSP, X-Frame-Options); CSRF protection for cookie-auth forms

INPUT & DATA
  ✅ All SQL parameterized; no shell=True / eval / exec on user input
  ✅ Path traversal & SSRF guarded; only safe_load/json for untrusted data
  ✅ Input validated at the boundary with Pydantic; response models prevent field leakage

SECRETS & DEPENDENCIES
  ✅ Secrets from env/vault, never committed; SecretStr/redaction in logs
  ✅ Keys rotated on schedule and on suspected leak
  ✅ bandit + pip-audit + secret scanning in CI; deps pinned & monitored

OPERATIONS
  ✅ debug=False in prod; generic error pages (no stack traces to clients)
  ✅ Authn/authz events logged (never log secrets/tokens/passwords)
  ✅ Backups encrypted; PII minimized and access-controlled

Summary: authenticate (verify identity) then authorize (check permissions), and treat all input as hostile. Hash passwords with argon2/bcrypt, generate secrets with secrets, compare them with hmac.compare_digest, sign JWTs with a pinned algorithm + short expiry, pair them with rotating refresh tokens for real revocation, enforce object-level authz, lock down TLS/cookies/CORS/CSRF, parameterize/allow-list every interpreter boundary, keep secrets out of code, and let bandit/pip-audit guard the pipeline. Don't roll your own crypto.
